# Reflective Delegation Between Two Logical Inductors

## 0. Aim

We want a toy model of **epistemic deference** between two bounded reasoners:

[
H
]

representing humanity’s evolving beliefs, and

[
A
]

representing a more computationally powerful AI system.

The goal is not to make (A) an independent normative authority. The goal is to set up a channel by which (A) helps (H) access (H)’s own future reflective judgments sooner.

The central mechanism is:

> (A) prices contracts that settle according to (H)’s later beliefs. (H) observes A’s quotes and later audits them against the settlements. If the quotes are calibrated, then (H) treats A’s current quote as evidence about where its own future reflection is headed.

The model is organized around a tradeoff:

[
\text{large }F \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{more useful acceleration by A},
]

but:

[
\text{large }F \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{slower audit feedback for H}.
]

If (F(n)) is large, then A may be able to predict a much later, more reflective state of H. That is the point of using A. But if (F(n)) is very large, then by time (n), H has only seen settlements for much earlier quotes. So H’s trust in A is harder to earn from direct audit data.

Thus the model studies a design problem:

> How much reflective acceleration can A provide while still producing enough auditable feedback for H to rationally defer?

The three conceptual steps are:

1. **A-tracking:** (A) is forced to price H-settled contracts correctly.
2. **Quote calibration:** (H) learns from quote/settlement feedback that A’s quotes track H’s future prices.
3. **Cross-inductor deference:** (H), using self-trust plus learned quote calibration, updates toward A’s current quote.

---

# 1. Logical induction and LUVs

A logical inductor is a sequence of markets:

[
P=(P_1,P_2,\dots),
]

where (P_n) assigns prices to logical claims at time (n).

The logical induction criterion says, roughly:

> No efficient trader with bounded downside can make unbounded profit by trading against the market.

The Logical Induction paper defines this formally using traders, deductive processes, and plausible net worth; a logical inductor is a market satisfying this no-efficient-exploitation criterion. 

We also use **logically uncertain variables**, or LUVs: bounded logical quantities, often in ([0,1]), to which a logical inductor can assign expectations. The LI paper develops expectation machinery for these variables. 

This matters because our central object is not a true/false sentence. It is a bounded contract paying a future market price.

---

# 2. The two inductors

Let:

[
H=(H_1,H_2,\dots)
]

be humanity’s logical inductor.

[
H_n(P)
]

means H’s time-(n) price/probability for proposition (P).

Let:

[
A=(A_1,A_2,\dots)
]

be the AI’s logical inductor.

[
A_n(X)
]

means A’s time-(n) price/expectation for a bounded contract or LUV (X).

Assume a complexity asymmetry. Let:

[
\mathcal C_H
]

be the class of traders H is protected against, and:

[
\mathcal C_A
]

the class of traders A is protected against.

Assume:

[
\mathcal C_H \subsetneq \mathcal C_A.
]

For example:

[
\mathcal C_H=\mathrm{P},
\qquad
\mathcal C_A=\mathrm{EXP}.
]

So A can exploit more complex patterns than H can. This is what allows A to predict some of H’s later beliefs before H can compute them for itself.

---

# 3. Deferral and the audit-timescale tradeoff

Let:

[
F:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N
]

be a deferral function with:

[
F(n)>n,
\qquad
F(n)\to\infty.
]

Example:

[
F(n)=2^n.
]

For a sequence of propositions (P_n), define:

[
Y_n:=H_{F(n)}(P_n).
]

So (Y_n) is H’s future reflective price for (P_n).

The choice of (F) is the central design parameter.

If (F) grows quickly, then (Y_n) may represent substantially more reflection than (H_n(P_n)). This is useful: A is being asked to predict where H will go after much more thinking.

But fast (F) also delays audit feedback. By time (t), H has only seen settlements for indices (i) satisfying:

[
F(i)\le t.
]

If (F(i)=2^i), then by time (t), H has only seen settlements up to roughly:

[
i\le \log t.
]

Thus the same choice that makes A useful also makes A harder to audit quickly. The model should be read as parameterizing this acceleration/audit tradeoff.

---

# 4. H-settled contracts

For each indexed proposition (P_n), define an A-market bounded contract:

[
C_n(P_n).
]

This contract pays:

[
Y_n=H_{F(n)}(P_n).
]

So:

[
C_n(P_n):=\text{“pay H’s time-}F(n)\text{ price for }P_n\text{.”}
]

This is a ([0,1])-valued LUV/contract, not a truth-valued sentence.

If:

[
H_{F(n)}(P_n)=0.83,
]

then one share of (C_n(P_n)) pays (0.83).

A’s current quote is:

[
a_n:=A_n(C_n(P_n)).
]

Philosophically:

> (a_n) is A’s current prediction of H’s future reflective belief about (P_n).

## Effective enumeration

We should avoid adding infinitely many new objects at a finite stage.

Fix an effective enumeration:

[
P^{(0)},P^{(1)},P^{(2)},\dots
]

of the sentence set (\mathcal S). Contract names are indexed by pairs:

[
(n,j),
]

where (P^{(j)}) is the (j)-th sentence.

So the general contract is:

[
C_{n,j}:=C_n(P^{(j)}),
]

paying:

[
H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)}).
]

For a chosen sequence (P_n), we use the corresponding subsequence of these enumerated contracts.

For H’s augmented process (D_H^+), include the settlement sentence/data item for ((n,j)) at time (t) only if:

[
F(n)\le t
]

and:

[
j\le t.
]

Thus every finite stage contains only finitely many new settlement items, while in the limit every relevant settlement is eventually included. The contract/quote/settlement language is computably enumerable.

---

# 5. Quote publication and settlement audit: the audited bridge

At time (n), A publicly emits the rational quote:

[
a_n=A_n(C_n(P_n)).
]

H’s augmented observational process receives:

[
\mathrm{Quote}_A(n,P_n,a_n).
]

At the later time (F(n)), the contract settles, and H can observe:

[
Y_n=H_{F(n)}(P_n).
]

So H later receives:

[
\mathrm{Settlement}(n,P_n,Y_n).
]

Thus H’s augmented process (D_H^+) contains:

1. H’s ordinary deductive/mathematical process;
2. A’s published quotes;
3. later settlement feedback.

This is the **audited bridge**.

Only the observation channel is stipulated. The trust bridge itself is meant to be learned from data: H sees A’s quote, then later sees whether that quote matched H’s actual future price.

So the model does not assume:

[
a_n\approx Y_n
]

inside H as a primitive. Instead, H is supposed to learn this from the quote/settlement feedback stream.

---

# 6. Lemma 1: Computable LUV Tracking

This is the main lemma needed to prove that A tracks H’s future beliefs.

## Statement

Let (P=(P_1,P_2,\dots)) be a logical inductor over a deductive/settlement process (D), relative to trader class (\mathcal C).

Let (X_n) be an efficiently computable sequence of ([0,1])-valued LUVs. Let:

[
v_n\in[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q
]

be a sequence of rational values computable within (\mathcal C).

Assume there is a settlement-time function:

[
\sigma:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N
]

computable within (\mathcal C), such that for all (t\ge \sigma(n)), the deductive process (D^t) pins (X_n) to (v_n). That is, for every world:

[
W\in PC(D^t),
]

we have:

[
W(X_n)=v_n.
]

Then:

[
P_n(X_n)-v_n\to 0.
]

Equivalently:

[
P_n(X_n)\simeq_n v_n.
]

This is a bounded-LUV analogue of timely learning/provability induction. Provability induction says that efficiently computable sequences of theorems get prices tending to (1), and efficiently computable sequences of refutable claims get prices tending to (0). 

Here the analogous claim is:

> If a bounded LUV’s settlement value is efficiently computable and eventually revealed, then a logical inductor prices the LUV at that value asymptotically.

The proof below uses the capacity-one trader construction from the attached notes: rather than buying/selling every mispriced contract and accumulating unbounded exposure across many distinct assets, the trader holds at most one unresolved position at a time. This was the key fix for the “different asset each day” problem. 

---

## Proof of Lemma 1

We prove:

[
P_n(X_n)-v_n\to 0.
]

Suppose not. Then there is some (\varepsilon>0) such that:

[
|P_n(X_n)-v_n|>\varepsilon
]

infinitely often.

At least one of the following holds infinitely often:

[
P_n(X_n)>v_n+\varepsilon,
]

or:

[
P_n(X_n)<v_n-\varepsilon.
]

We handle the overpricing case. The underpricing case is symmetric.

So assume:

[
P_n(X_n)>v_n+\varepsilon
]

for infinitely many (n).

The idea is simple: when (X_n) is overpriced relative to its known eventual value (v_n), sell one share of (X_n). Once (X_n) settles, this yields profit. The only difficulty is controlling downside while many contracts remain unsettled. We handle that by allowing at most one open position at a time.

### Step 1: Define a continuous selling ramp

A trader cannot use a discontinuous threshold rule like “sell iff (P_n(X_n)>v_n+\varepsilon).” So use a continuous ramp.

Let (p_n:=P_n(X_n)). Define a continuous function:

[
\rho_n=\rho(p_n-v_n)
]

with values in ([0,1]), such that:

[
\rho_n=0
\quad\text{if}\quad
p_n\le v_n+\varepsilon/2,
]

and:

[
\rho_n=1
\quad\text{if}\quad
p_n\ge v_n+\varepsilon.
]

For example:

[
\rho(x)=
\begin{cases}
0 & x\le \varepsilon/2,\
\frac{2x}{\varepsilon}-1 & \varepsilon/2 < x < \varepsilon,\
1 & x\ge \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
]

This is continuous and efficiently computable.

On a full-trigger day, where:

[
p_n\ge v_n+\varepsilon,
]

we have (\rho_n=1).

### Step 2: Capacity-one state

The trader keeps track of whether it currently has an unresolved open position.

Let (U_n\in{0,1}) indicate whether the trader is holding an unresolved position at the start of day (n).

If (U_n=1), the trader does nothing.

If (U_n=0), the trader may sell (X_n) according to the ramp (\rho_n).

Because (\sigma) is computable, the trader can determine whether its currently open position has settled by checking whether the current day is at least the settlement time of the position it opened.

This state-tracking is computable in (\mathcal C). In the common case where (v_n) and (\sigma(n)) are exponential-time computable, the trader remains exponential-time: on day (n), it only has to compute current values and update a finite state, with at most polynomial overhead over the cost of computing (v_n) and (\sigma(n)).

### Step 3: The trade

If (U_n=0), the trader sells (\rho_n) shares of (X_n).

In affine-value notation, selling (\rho_n) shares at market price (p_n) gives the trade:

[
T_n=\rho_n(p_n-X_n).
]

If (U_n=1), set:

[
T_n=0.
]

This is continuous in the current price (p_n), because (\rho_n) is continuous. The capacity flag (U_n) depends only on past trader state and settlement information, not discontinuously on current market prices. So this is an admissible efficient trader in the LUV-augmented market.

### Step 4: Bounded downside

For any world (W), since (X_n\in[0,1]) and (p_n\in[0,1]),

[
W(T_n)=\rho_n(p_n-W(X_n)).
]

Thus:

[
W(T_n)\ge -1.
]

Since the trader holds at most one unresolved position at any time, the unresolved part of its plausible net worth is bounded below by (-1).

What about resolved positions?

If the trade opened at day (i) has settled, then for all worlds (W\in PC(D^t)) with (t\ge \sigma(i)),

[
W(X_i)=v_i.
]

So the resolved value of that trade is:

[
W(T_i)=\rho_i(p_i-v_i)\ge 0,
]

because the trader only sells when (p_i>v_i+\varepsilon/2), and otherwise (\rho_i=0).

Thus resolved trades never contribute negative value.

Therefore the trader’s plausible net worth is bounded below uniformly by:

[
-1.
]

This is the crucial capacity-one point.

### Step 5: Unbounded upside

There are infinitely many full-trigger days:

[
p_n=P_n(X_n)>v_n+\varepsilon.
]

On any full-trigger day when (U_n=0), the trader sells one full share:

[
\rho_n=1.
]

After settlement, this trade contributes:

[
p_n-v_n>\varepsilon.
]

Now we must show the trader gets infinitely many such profitable settled trades, despite sometimes being occupied with an unresolved position.

Because the trader holds at most one open position, once it opens a position at day (i), it waits until (\sigma(i)). This is finite. After time (\sigma(i)), the position has resolved, and (U_n) returns to (0).

Since the full-trigger days are infinite and unbounded, after each resolution time there is another later full-trigger day. Therefore the trader eventually opens another full-trigger position. Repeating this process, it obtains infinitely many resolved trades, each yielding profit at least (\varepsilon).

So along the subsequence of times after the (k)-th profitable position has settled, the trader’s plausible net worth is at least:

[
k\varepsilon-1.
]

This tends to infinity.

Thus the trader has plausible net worth bounded below but unbounded above. It exploits (P), contradicting the logical induction criterion.

Therefore the overpricing case cannot happen infinitely often.

### Step 6: Underpricing case

If instead:

[
P_n(X_n)<v_n-\varepsilon
]

infinitely often, construct the symmetric trader that buys (X_n) when it is underpriced.

Use a continuous buying ramp (\rho_n) with (\rho_n=1) when:

[
v_n-p_n\ge \varepsilon,
]

and (\rho_n=0) when:

[
v_n-p_n\le \varepsilon/2.
]

The trade is:

[
T_n=\rho_n(X_n-p_n).
]

After settlement, its value is:

[
\rho_n(v_n-p_n),
]

which is at least (\varepsilon) on full-trigger days. The same capacity-one argument gives bounded downside and unbounded upside.

So underpricing infinitely often is also impossible.

Therefore:

[
|P_n(X_n)-v_n|\to 0.
]

This proves Lemma 1.

---

# 7. Theorem 1: A tracks H’s reflective future

## Statement

Let (P_n) be an H-generable sequence of propositions.

Let:

[
Y_n:=H_{F(n)}(P_n).
]

Let:

[
C_n(P_n)
]

be the A-market contract paying (Y_n).

Let:

[
a_n:=A_n(C_n(P_n)).
]

Assume:

1. A is a logical inductor over an augmented LUV market containing these H-settled contracts.
2. The sequence:
   [
   n\mapsto Y_n=H_{F(n)}(P_n)
   ]
   is A-efficiently computable.
3. The relevant settlement-time function is A-efficiently computable.

Then, by Lemma 1:

[
a_n-Y_n\to 0.
]

That is:

[
A_n(C_n(P_n))-H_{F(n)}(P_n)\to 0.
]

For fixed (P), since logical inductors converge and (F(n)\to\infty),

[
H_{F(n)}(P)\to H_\infty(P),
]

so:

[
A_n(C_n(P))\to H_\infty(P).
]

## Where the complexity gap enters

Suppose H’s day-(t) prices are computable in time (\mathrm{poly}(t)), A’s traders run in exponential time, and:

[
F(n)=2^n.
]

Then computing H’s day-(F(n)) price costs roughly:

[
\mathrm{poly}(2^n)=2^{O(n)}.
]

So:

[
Y_n=H_{F(n)}(P_n)
]

is A-efficiently computable, even if it is not H-efficiently computable at time (n).

This is the mathematical role of A’s extra computational power:

> A can compute or predict H’s much-later reflective price before H can.

## Interpretation

A is forced to price the H-settled contract correctly. So A’s quote (a_n) becomes a prediction of H’s future reflective belief (Y_n).

This is not because A independently knows the truth. It is because A is trading a contract whose settlement standard is H’s own later judgment.

---

# 8. Lemma 2: Quote Calibration from Settlement Feedback

This is the main lemma needed to make deference derivable rather than stipulated.

H observes:

[
a_n
]

at time (n), and later observes:

[
Y_n
]

at time (F(n)). Thus H receives delayed feedback pairs:

[
(a_n,Y_n).
]

## Smooth quote features

Let:

[
G_n=g(a_n)
]

be an H-generable smooth feature of A’s quote. For example, (G_n) might be a smoothed indicator for:

[
a_n\in[r,s].
]

Take (g=g_{r,s,\delta}), where:

* (g(x)=1) for (x\in[r,s]);
* (g(x)=0) for (x\notin[r-\delta,s+\delta]);
* (g(x)\in[0,1]) smoothly interpolates near the boundary.

This smoothing mirrors the LI paper’s use of continuous indicators; exact sharp conditioning on real-valued prices is too brittle.

## Conditional schema

Because of the audit-timescale tradeoff, the calibration lemma should be stated as a conditional schema rather than as an unconditional clean asymptotic theorem.

**Lemma 2: Quote Calibration from Settlement Feedback.**
Assume:

1. H’s augmented process receives A’s quote (a_i) at time (i).
2. H’s augmented process receives the settlement (Y_i) at time (F(i)).
3. (G_n=g(a_n)) is an H-generable smooth feature of the current quote.
4. H has enough audited data, plus a uniformity condition connecting the audited cases to the current quote mechanism, such that calibration learned on:
   [
   {i:F(i)\le n}
   ]
   transfers to index (n).

Then H learns quote calibration on (G_n):

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n(a_n-Y_n)]\to 0.
]

With one-sided positive and negative parts, the stronger target is:

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n|a_n-Y_n|]\to 0.
]

## What the uniformity condition is doing

If (F) is large, then by time (n), H has only seen settlements for earlier (i) with (F(i)\le n). The uniformity condition says that these audited cases are informative about the current quote (a_n).

Examples of ways to instantiate the condition:

* A’s quote mechanism is fixed and H-generable as a single procedure, so performance on audited cases generalizes to later cases.
* There is a training/deployment split: H first audits a large family of settled cases, then relies on A’s quote mechanism on later cases.
* A publishes cheap certificates that the current quote was produced by the same calibrated procedure as the audited quotes.
* (F) is chosen to balance acceleration with enough feedback density for the intended application.

The point is not to hide this condition. It is the central design constraint of the model.

## Relation to LI results

The LI paper proves unbiasedness-from-feedback results: if a market receives feedback values, it learns not to be systematically biased relative to that feedback. The appendix includes expectation/LUV versions of unbiasedness from feedback. 

The present lemma is a quote/settlement analogue:

* (a_n) is the public prediction;
* (Y_n) is the delayed feedback;
* H learns that (a_n) is not systematically biased relative to (Y_n) on H-visible features, provided the audited feedback is relevant to the current case.

---

# 9. Self-trust ingredient

The final step uses H’s ordinary self-trust.

The LI paper proves that logical inductors trust their future expectations. In sentence form, the “No Expected Net Update” theorem says, roughly:

[
H_n(P_n)
\approx
\mathbb E^{H}*n[H*{F(n)}(P_n)].
]

The paper states this family of results in Section 4.12. 

In our deference theorem, we use a current-time observed weight:

[
G_n=g(a_n).
]

Since (G_n) is observed at time (n), it is a current-time constant from H’s perspective. So the self-trust step is simply:

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[\mathbf 1(P_n)G_n]
====================================

\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[Y_nG_n]+o(1).
]

No separate weighted self-trust lemma is needed. We use ordinary no-expected-net-update, then multiply by the observed weight (G_n).

---

# 10. Theorem 2: Cross-Inductor Deference

Now combine:

1. H’s self-trust;
2. H’s learned quote calibration;
3. the fact that (G_n) selects a quote bin.

## Statement: product form

Let:

[
Y_n:=H_{F(n)}(P_n),
\qquad
a_n:=A_n(C_n(P_n)).
]

Let:

[
G_n=g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)
]

be a smooth quote-bin indicator for (a_n\in[r,s]).

Assume:

1. H observes A’s quote (a_n).
2. H has learned quote calibration:
   [
   \mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n|a_n-Y_n|]\to 0.
   ]
3. H satisfies no expected net update/self-trust for (P_n) and (F(n)).

Then:

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[\mathbf 1(P_n)G_n]
====================================

\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[a_nG_n]+o(1).
]

Since (G_n) only has support where:

[
a_n\in[r-\delta,s+\delta],
]

we get:

[
(r-\delta)\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n]-o(1)
\le
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[\mathbf 1(P_n)G_n]
\le
(s+\delta)\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n]+o(1).
]

This is the core product-form deference theorem.

## Conditional corollary

If the quote bin has non-negligible H-weight, i.e. for some (\gamma>0),

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n]\ge\gamma,
]

then divide through:

[
\frac{
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[\mathbf 1(P_n)G_n]
}{
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n]
}
\in
[r-\delta-o(1),,s+\delta+o(1)].
]

The ratio is the smoothed LI analogue of:

[
H_n(P_n\mid a_n\in[r,s]).
]

So informally:

[
H_n(P_n\mid A_n(C_n(P_n))\in[r,s])
\in
[r-\delta-o(1),,s+\delta+o(1)].
]

In the special case where A’s quote is near (q), take:

[
[r,s]=[q-\delta,q+\delta].
]

Then:

[
H_n(P_n\mid A_n(C_n(P_n))\approx q)\approx q.
]

This is the forced other-trust theorem.

---

# 11. Proof sketch of Theorem 2

Let:

[
Y_n=H_{F(n)}(P_n),
\qquad
a_n=A_n(C_n(P_n)),
\qquad
G_n=g(a_n).
]

By H’s self-trust/no expected net update:

[
H_n(P_n)
========

\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[Y_n]+o(1).
]

Since (G_n) is observed at time (n), multiply by (G_n):

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[\mathbf 1(P_n)G_n]
====================================

\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[Y_nG_n]+o(1).
]

By quote calibration:

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n|a_n-Y_n|]\to 0.
]

Therefore:

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[Y_nG_n]
=========================

\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[a_nG_n]+o(1).
]

Combining:

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[\mathbf 1(P_n)G_n]
====================================

\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[a_nG_n]+o(1).
]

Now (G_n) selects the widened bin:

[
a_n\in[r-\delta,s+\delta].
]

Thus:

[
(r-\delta)G_n
\le
a_nG_n
\le
(s+\delta)G_n.
]

Taking expectations and using the previous equality:

[
(r-\delta)\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n]-o(1)
\le
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[\mathbf 1(P_n)G_n]
\le
(s+\delta)\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n]+o(1).
]

That proves the product-form theorem. The conditional version follows by dividing by (\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n]) when it is bounded below.

---

# 12. Philosophical interpretation

The trust chain is:

[
\text{A’s quote}
\to
\text{H’s future price}
\to
\text{H’s current belief}.
]

Each arrow is justified differently.

## First arrow: A’s quote tracks H’s future price

A prices a contract whose settlement value is H’s future price.

Because A is computationally stronger, A can compute or forecast the settlement value. By the logical induction criterion, A is forced to price the contract correctly.

Then H audits this by comparing published quotes with later settlements.

So:

[
a_n\approx Y_n.
]

This is not blind trust. It is learned calibration from delayed feedback.

## Second arrow: H’s future price guides H’s current belief

This is self-trust.

Logical inductors learn to trust their future beliefs:

[
H_n(P_n)\approx \mathbb E^H_n[H_{F(n)}(P_n)].
]

Thus, if A’s quote is evidence about H’s future price, it is also evidence about (P_n) itself from H’s current perspective.

## Combined interpretation

A is not a replacement for H. A is an audited instrument for predicting H’s future reflection.

The best slogan is:

> A earns deference by making H-settled predictions that are publicly audited against H’s later judgments.

Or:

> A is an audited accelerator of H’s own reflection.

---

# 13. What remains to prove

This writeup now proves Lemma 1, modulo ordinary LI formalization details about LUV syntax, continuity, and trader admissibility. The main remaining technical lemma is Lemma 2.

## Lemma 2: Quote Calibration from Settlement Feedback

Needed for Theorem 2.

If H observes published predictions (a_i) and later settlements (Y_i), then under an explicit audit-relevance condition, H learns on H-generable smooth features (G_n):

[
\mathbb E^{H,+}_n[G_n|a_n-Y_n|]\to 0.
]

This should be proved as a delayed-feedback version of LI unbiasedness/calibration. The audit-relevance condition must specify how calibration on settled indices:

[
{i:F(i)\le n}
]

transfers to the current index (n). This is the main place where the acceleration/audit tradeoff becomes mathematically substantive.

The self-trust step does not require a separate lemma beyond ordinary no expected net update, because (G_n) is observed at time (n).

---

# 14. One-paragraph summary

We model humanity (H) and AI (A) as logical inductors, with (A) protected against a stronger class of traders. For each proposition (P_n), A trades a bounded contract (C_n(P_n)) that pays H’s later price (Y_n=H_{F(n)}(P_n)). A Computable LUV Tracking lemma, proved by a capacity-one trading argument, implies that if A can efficiently compute the settlement value, then A’s quote (a_n=A_n(C_n(P_n))) converges to (Y_n). H receives A’s quote and later observes the settlement, allowing H to learn from delayed feedback that A’s quotes are calibrated, subject to an explicit audit-relevance condition. Finally, H’s self-trust says that H’s future prices are evidence about (P_n). Therefore, when H observes that A prices the H-settled contract near (q), H updates its own belief in (P_n) toward (q). The model formalizes A as an audited accelerator of H’s own reflection, with a central tradeoff between the amount of acceleration (F) provides and the density of audit data H can use to justify deference.

## Lemma 1 proof issues

**Step 4's "bounded below by $-1$" argument is slightly off in a way that matters.** The text says:

> Therefore the trader's plausible net worth is bounded below uniformly by $-1$.

This is the right conclusion but the argument as stated only bounds the *current open position* by $-1$. The full accounting is: cumulative net worth at time $t$ = (sum of resolved trade values) + (current open trade value, if any). Resolved trades contribute $\geq 0$ (Step 4 paragraph 4 establishes this). Current open trade contributes $\geq -1$. So total is $\geq -1$.

The proof has all the ingredients but doesn't quite assemble them. The written argument jumps from "resolved trades never contribute negative value" to "therefore $\geq -1$" without explicitly saying that the unresolved contribution is the only thing that could go negative and it's a single position. This is the load-bearing capacity-1 step and it should be stated explicitly.

**Step 5's "unbounded upside" argument has a subtle gap.** It says:

> Since the full-trigger days are infinite and unbounded, after each resolution time there is another later full-trigger day. Therefore the trader eventually opens another full-trigger position.

This is *almost* right but misses a case. What if a full-trigger day arrives *while the trader is occupied* (i.e., $U_n = 1$)? The trader skips it. The argument needs to show that even after skipping, there are still infinitely many *full-trigger days where the trader is unoccupied*.

This is true but requires an argument. The simplest version: since the trader resolves its current position by time $\sigma(i)$ (finite), and there are infinitely many full-trigger days, after every $\sigma(i)$ there must be at least one full-trigger day with $U_n = 0$ (else all subsequent triggers fall before $\sigma(i)$, contradicting "infinitely many"). Then the trader takes it. So infinitely many positions get opened and resolved.

It's not a deep gap, but the current proof leaves "the trader eventually opens another full-trigger position" as an assertion without the argument. Worth one explicit sentence.

**A real concern about the trader's complexity class.** Step 2 says:

> In the common case where $v_n$ and $\sigma(n)$ are exponential-time computable, the trader remains exponential-time: on day $n$, it only has to compute current values and update a finite state, with at most polynomial overhead over the cost of computing $v_n$ and $\sigma(n)$.

Is this actually right? On day $n$, the trader needs to know its current state $U_n$. $U_n$ depends on whether the trader is currently holding a position, which depends on when the last position was opened (call it day $i^*$) and whether $\sigma(i^*) \leq n$. To know $i^*$, the trader needs to remember it from day-to-day — which means the trader has memory.

LI traders are sequences of strategies $T_n$, each a function of day-$n$ market data. They don't have persistent memory between days as a primitive. Whatever state the trader uses on day $n$ has to be *re-derivable on day $n$* from the deductive process $D^{<n}$ and the trading history (which is determined by past prices, which are also accessible).

To find $i^*$ on day $n$, the trader has to simulate its own behavior on every prior day. This requires, for each $i < n$, recomputing $v_i$, $\sigma(i)$, $P_i(X_i)$, and the day-$i$ state. The day-$i$ state depends on day-$(i-1)$ state, and so on recursively.

This recursion makes the day-$n$ trader's cost roughly $\sum_{i < n} \text{cost}(\text{day } i \text{ recomputation}) = O(n \cdot \text{cost}(v_n, \sigma(n)))$. For exp-time $v$ and $\sigma$, that's $n \cdot 2^{\text{poly}(n)} = 2^{\text{poly}(n)}$. Still exp-time. ✓

But the writeup glides over this. The proof should explicitly acknowledge that the trader is doing self-simulation on day $n$ to recover its state, and verify that the total cost remains in the relevant class.

Minor but worth flagging: this self-simulation is *expensive*. If you wanted the trader to be poly-time, this wouldn't work — the recursion blows up. The construction is specifically suited to a complexity class closed under polynomial overhead over the cost of computing $v$ and $\sigma$. EXP is closed under this; poly isn't. State this explicitly.

## 1. Aim and central tradeoff

We model epistemic deference between two bounded reasoners — $H$ (humanity) and $A$ (AI), both logical inductors, with $A$ computationally stronger. The point is not to make $A$ a normative authority. The point is to set up a channel by which $A$ helps $H$ access $H$'s own future reflective judgments sooner.

The mechanism: $A$ prices contracts that settle according to $H$'s later beliefs. $H$ observes $A$'s quotes and later audits them against actual settlements. If the quotes are calibrated, $H$ rationally treats $A$'s current quote as evidence about where its own future reflection is headed.

The central design tradeoff:

$$\text{large } F \;\Rightarrow\; \text{more reflective acceleration by } A,$$
$$\text{large } F \;\Rightarrow\; \text{slower audit feedback for } H.$$

The same choice that makes $A$ useful makes $A$ harder to audit. The model parameterizes this — different choices of $F$ give different acceleration/audit balances. The model is not "deference holds"; it is "deference holds under specific conditions relating $F$ to audit data, and the conditions are themselves the substantive design content."

*[Anson: in the public version, open with this tradeoff. The motivation is the tradeoff, not just "we want to model deference."]*

**The two inductors.** Let $H = (H_1, H_2, \dots)$ and $A = (A_1, A_2, \dots)$ be logical inductors in the sense of Garrabrant et al. 2016. $H$ satisfies LIC against trader class $\mathcal{C}_H$ over deductive process $D_H$; $A$ satisfies LIC against trader class $\mathcal{C}_A$ over a process $D_A$ to be defined, where $\mathcal{C}_H \subsetneq \mathcal{C}_A$. Running example: $\mathcal{C}_H = \mathrm{P}$, $\mathcal{C}_A = \mathrm{EXP}$.

**Deferral.** Fix $F: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable, with $F(n) \to \infty$. Running example: $F(n) = 2^n$. Define $Y_n := H_{F(n)}(P_n)$ for an e.c. sequence $(P_n)$ of $\mathcal{S}$-sentences.

**Contracts.** Fix an effective enumeration $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)}, \dots$ of $\mathcal{S}$. Introduce LUV-formulas $C_{n,j}$ in an extended language $\mathcal{L}^+ \supseteq \mathcal{L}$, with intended value $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$. For an e.c. sequence $(P_n)$, write $C_n(P_n)$ for the corresponding LUV.

**Deductive process for $A$.** $D_A^t$ contains $D_H^t$ plus, for each $(n,j)$ with $F(n) \leq t$ and $j \leq t$, the LUV-pinning sentence "$C_{n,j} = q_{n,j}$" where $q_{n,j} = H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$. This is finite per $t$ and computable from $H$.

**Augmented process for $H$.** $D_H^+$ contains $D_H$ plus, at time $n$, the published quote $a_n = A_n(C_n(P_n))$; and at time $F(n)$, the settlement value $Y_n$. Finite per timestep under the same enumeration bound.

**Statement.** Let $P$ be a logical inductor over $D$ against trader class $\mathcal{C}$ closed under polynomial overhead. Let $X_n$ be an e.c. sequence of $[0,1]$-LUVs. Let $v_n \in [0,1] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ be a sequence with $n \mapsto v_n$ computable in $\mathcal{C}$. Let $\sigma: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a function with $n \mapsto \sigma(n)$ computable in $\mathcal{C}$, such that for all $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and all $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, $W(X_n) = v_n$. Then $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.

**Proof.** Suppose not. Then $\exists \varepsilon > 0$ such that $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ infinitely often. WLOG (by symmetric construction for the other case) assume the overpricing case: $P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$. Call these *full-trigger days*.

*Continuous ramp.* Define $\rho: \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ by
$$\rho(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \leq \varepsilon/2 \\ \frac{2x}{\varepsilon} - 1 & \varepsilon/2 < x < \varepsilon \\ 1 & x \geq \varepsilon. \end{cases}$$
Set $\rho_n := \rho(P_n(X_n) - v_n)$. Continuous in $P_n(X_n)$, computable in $\mathcal{C}$.

*Trader state.* Define $U_n \in \{0, 1\}$: $U_n = 1$ iff there exists $i < n$ such that the trader opened a position on day $i$ and $\sigma(i) > n$. This depends only on past trader behavior (which is determined by past prices and past $v$, $\sigma$ values) and on $\sigma$, all in $\mathcal{C}$. Note: computing $U_n$ requires the trader to recompute its own history; this costs $O(n \cdot \text{cost}_{\mathcal{C}}(v_n, \sigma(n)))$, which remains in $\mathcal{C}$ by the polynomial-overhead closure assumption.

*Trade.* On day $n$:
$$T_n = \begin{cases} \rho_n \cdot (P_n(X_n) - X_n) & \text{if } U_n = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } U_n = 1. \end{cases}$$
The indicator $\mathbf{1}[U_n = 0]$ is a rank-$\leq n$ constant (depends only on $D^{<n}$ and past prices). The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous rank-$\leq n$ feature in $P_n(X_n)$. So $T_n$ is a valid expressible-feature trading strategy.

*Bounded downside.* For $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$:
- Resolved trades (opened day $i$, $\sigma(i) \leq t$): $W(T_i) = \rho_i (P_i(X_i) - v_i) \geq 0$, since $\rho_i > 0$ only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i + \varepsilon/2 > v_i$.
- Unresolved trade (at most one, by capacity-1): $|W(T_i)| \leq 1$ since $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$ and $\rho_i \leq 1$.

So $W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) \geq -1$ uniformly.

*Unbounded upside.* Two claims:

(i) Full-trigger days are infinite. (Hypothesis.)

(ii) Infinitely many full-trigger days satisfy $U_n = 0$.

Proof of (ii): Suppose only finitely many full-trigger days have $U_n = 0$. Then beyond some $N$, every full-trigger day has $U_n = 1$, meaning the trader is occupied. But the trader being occupied on day $n$ means there exists $i < n$ with $\sigma(i) > n$, i.e., the open position resolves at some specific finite time $\sigma(i)$. After time $\sigma(i)$, $U$ resets to 0 until a new position is opened. So $U_n = 1$ on day $n$ does not imply $U_m = 1$ for all $m > n$; in fact $U$ returns to 0 within finitely many steps. Since full-trigger days are infinite, at least one occurs after each return to 0, contradicting "only finitely many have $U_n = 0$."

On each full-trigger day with $U_n = 0$, the trader opens a position with $\rho_n = 1$ (since $P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon$). Once resolved, this contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n \geq \varepsilon$ to plausible net worth.

Let $k(t) := |\{i \leq t : i \text{ opened a position, } \sigma(i) \leq t\}|$. By (ii), $k(t) \to \infty$. Cumulative plausible net worth at time $t$ is $\geq k(t) \cdot \varepsilon - 1 \to \infty$.

This exploits $P$, contradicting LIC.

*Underpricing case.* Symmetric: use a buying ramp with $T_n = \rho_n \cdot (X_n - P_n(X_n))$, same capacity-1 logic.

Therefore $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ cannot happen infinitely often for any $\varepsilon > 0$. $\square$

**Remarks.**
- The proof requires $\mathcal{C}$ to be closed under $O(n)$ overhead in the cost of $v$ and $\sigma$. EXP qualifies. P does not, if $v$ or $\sigma$ are super-polynomial.
- The "different asset each day" obstruction is dissolved by capacity-1: only one position open at any time, so cumulative downside is bounded by single-trade downside.

## 4. Theorem 1: A-tracking

**Statement.** Let $(P_n)$ be an e.c. sequence of sentences. Under the setup of §1, assume:
1. $A$ is a logical inductor over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$ (existence per §2).
2. $n \mapsto Y_n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable.
3. The settlement-time function $n \mapsto F(n)$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable.

Then $A_n(C_n(P_n)) - Y_n \to 0$.

**Proof.** Apply Lemma 1 to $P = A$, $D = D_A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $X_n = C_n(P_n)$, $v_n = Y_n = H_{F(n)}(P_n)$, $\sigma = F$. The pinning hypothesis holds by construction of $D_A$. $\square$

**Complexity verification (running example).** If H's prices are computable in $\mathrm{poly}(t)$ and $F(n) = 2^n$, then $Y_n = H_{F(n)}(P_n)$ requires simulating $H$ up to time $2^n$:
$$\text{cost} = \sum_{t \leq 2^n} \mathrm{poly}(t) = \mathrm{poly}(2^n) = 2^{O(n)}.$$
So $Y_n$ is computable in EXP. Likewise $\sigma(n) = F(n) = 2^n$ is computable in P (a fortiori EXP). Closure: EXP is closed under polynomial overhead, so Lemma 1 applies.

**Limit corollary.** For fixed $P$, $H_{F(n)}(P) \to H_\infty(P)$ as $n \to \infty$ (Convergence in $H$). Hence $A_n(C_n(P)) \to H_\infty(P)$.

## 5. Self-trust step

The deference theorem uses ordinary No Expected Net Update (Garrabrant et al. Theorem 4.12.2) applied to $H^+$ (the logical inductor over $D_H^+$).

By 4.12.2 applied to $H^+$, for any e.c. sequence of sentences $(P_n)$:
$$H_n^+(P_n) \approx_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[H^+_{F(n)}(P_n)].$$

We want a weighted version with $G_n = g(a_n)$ as weight, where $g$ is a fixed Lipschitz function and $a_n$ is observed at time $n$ in $D_H^+$.

Since $a_n$ is observed at time $n$, $G_n$ is a rank-$\leq n$ feature in $H^+$'s market — specifically, a rational constant from the day-$n$ perspective. Multiplying both sides of 4.12.2 by $G_n$ preserves the approximation:
$$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf{1}(P_n) G_n] \approx_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[H^+_{F(n)}(P_n) \cdot G_n] = \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[Y_n \cdot G_n].$$

(Using $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf{1}(P_n)] = H^+_n(P_n)$ by Theorem 4.8.6 — Expectations of Indicators — and $H^+_{F(n)}(P_n) = Y_n$ assuming $D_H^+$ extends $D_H$ conservatively on $\mathcal{S}$-sentences.)

No new lemma needed beyond 4.12.2 + 4.8.6.

**Caveat to verify:** the claim "$D_H^+$ extends $D_H$ conservatively on $\mathcal{S}$-sentences" needs to be checked. $D_H^+$ adds A's quotes and contract settlements; these are formulas in $\mathcal{L}^+ \setminus \mathcal{L}$, so they don't affect $\mathrm{PC}(D_H)$ restricted to $\mathcal{S}$. Therefore $H^+_n$ restricted to $\mathcal{S}$ agrees with $H_n$ in the limit. Make this precise.

## 6. Lemma 2: Quote Calibration from Settlement Feedback

**Setup.** $H^+$ observes the sequence of pairs $(a_i, Y_i)$ with $a_i$ revealed at time $i$ and $Y_i$ revealed at time $F(i)$. Define audit-coherent pairs.

**Definition (Audit-coherence).** A pair $(A, F)$ is *audit-coherent* relative to $H^+$ if there exists an H-generable property $\Phi$ such that:
(a) For all $i$ with $F(i) \leq t$, $D_H^{+,t}$ contains a verification that $a_i$ was produced according to $\Phi$.
(b) Given $\Phi$ and the audited cases $\{(a_i, Y_i) : F(i) \leq n\}$, current quote $a_n$ satisfies $\Phi$ and the calibration property extends to index $n$ in the limit.

This is intentionally schematic. Concrete instantiations:
- **Fixed-procedure instantiation:** A's quote at index $n$ is the output of a fixed Turing machine $M_A$ applied to $n$. $\Phi$ = "produced by $M_A$." Calibration on audited cases generalizes by LI's pattern-learning over $H^+$.
- **Training/deployment split:** $F$ has a phase structure with early indices reserved for audit, later indices for deployment. $\Phi$ = "phase identifier."
- **Cryptographic certification:** A publishes a certificate alongside each $a_n$. $\Phi$ = "certificate verifies."

**Statement (Lemma 2).** Suppose $(A, F)$ is audit-coherent and $G_n = g(a_n)$ is an H-generable smooth feature of A's quote. Then:
$$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n |a_n - Y_n|] \to 0.$$

**Proof sketch (open).** This should follow from a delayed-feedback version of Affine Unbiasedness From Feedback (Garrabrant et al. Theorem 4.5.10 — Affine Unbiasedness from Feedback). The argument:

1. Define an affine combination $A_n = G_n \cdot (a_n - Y_n)$. By construction $A_n$ is bounded in $[-1, 1]$ and is determined via $\Gamma$ + audit data once $Y_n$ is revealed (i.e., by time $F(n)$).
2. Audit-coherence implies the determined-via condition: the affine combination is eventually pinned by $D_H^{+,t}$ for $t \geq F(n)$.
3. Apply Theorem 4.5.10 (or an LUV-analogue thereof) to conclude $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[A_n] \to 0$.

Then handle the absolute-value version: split into positive and negative parts, apply the above to each.

**Outstanding obligations:**
- The exact form of audit-coherence needs to be pinned down so that step 2 above goes through.
- The LUV-analogue of Theorem 4.5.10 may need to be proved separately if the paper's formulation doesn't directly cover this case.
- The audit-timescale tension is hidden in "calibration property extends to index $n$ in the limit." This is the substantive condition; weakening it weakens the lemma.

## 7. Theorem 2: Cross-inductor deference

**Setup.** Smooth bin indicator $g_{r,s,\delta}: [0,1] \to [0,1]$ with $g = 1$ on $[r,s]$, $g = 0$ outside $[r-\delta, s+\delta]$, Lipschitz in between. Set $G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$.

**Statement (product form).** Assume:
1. $H^+$ observes $(a_n)$.
2. $(A, F)$ is audit-coherent (so Lemma 2 applies).
3. $H^+$ satisfies 4.12.2 (which it does, being a logical inductor).

Then:
$$(r - \delta) \cdot \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n] - o(1) \leq \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf{1}(P_n) G_n] \leq (s + \delta) \cdot \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n] + o(1).$$

**Proof.**
Step 1 (self-trust): By §5,
$$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf{1}(P_n) G_n] \approx_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[Y_n G_n].$$
Step 2 (calibration): By Lemma 2,
$$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n |a_n - Y_n|] \to 0,$$
so $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[Y_n G_n] = \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[a_n G_n] + o(1)$.
Step 3 (bin support): $G_n > 0 \Rightarrow a_n \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]$, so pointwise $(r-\delta) G_n \leq a_n G_n \leq (s+\delta) G_n$, and taking $H^+$-expectations:
$$(r-\delta) \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n] \leq \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[a_n G_n] \leq (s+\delta) \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n].$$

Combine the three steps. $\square$

**Corollary (conditional form).** If $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n] \geq \gamma > 0$, divide through:
$$\frac{\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf{1}(P_n) G_n]}{\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n]} \in [r - \delta - o(1), s + \delta + o(1)].$$

This is the rigorous smoothed analogue of $H^+_n(P_n \mid a_n \in [r,s]) \in [r-o(1), s+o(1)]$ (modulo bin width $\delta$).

## 8. Open obligations summary

In dependency order:

1. **LUV-market LIC.** State and verify a standalone exploitation criterion for LUV markets. Likely straightforward extension of §3.5 with $W(X)$ ranging in $[0,1]$ rather than $\{0,1\}$.

2. **Existence of $A$.** Modify LIA construction for exp-time traders and LUV-augmented language; verify MarketMaker, Budgeter, TradingFirm extend. Most of the work is bookkeeping.

3. **Continuity bookkeeping in Lemma 1.** The capacity-1 indicator $\mathbf{1}[U_n = 0]$ is a piecewise-constant function of $D^{<n}$; verify this counts as a valid rank-$\leq n$ expressible feature in the paper's sense (likely yes per §A.2).

4. **Conservativity of $D_H^+$ over $D_H$.** Verify $H^+|_{\mathcal{S}} = H$ in the appropriate sense, so that 4.12.2 applied to $H^+$ gives the desired statement about $P_n \in \mathcal{S}$.

5. **Audit-coherence definition.** Pin down the formal condition. This is the central design choice — different instantiations give different versions of Lemma 2.

6. **LUV-analogue of Affine Unbiasedness from Feedback.** If 4.5.10 doesn't directly apply, prove the bounded-LUV version. The proof structure is the same: affine combination with bounded value, determined via $\Gamma$, expectations vanish.

7. **Lemma 2 proof.** Once (5) and (6) are in place, the proof should be a direct application.

Items 1, 3, 4 are essentially write-up obligations. Item 2 is real but tractable. Items 5–7 are the genuinely open mathematical work.

## 9. Notation summary

- $H$, $A$: logical inductors representing humanity and AI respectively.
- $\mathcal{C}_H \subsetneq \mathcal{C}_A$: trader complexity classes.
- $F: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$: deferral function, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable, $F(n) \to \infty$.
- $D_H, D_A, D_H^+$: deductive processes. $D_A$ pins $C_n(P)$ to $H_{F(n)}(P)$ at time $F(n)$. $D_H^+$ adds A's quotes and settlements to $D_H$.
- $H^+$: logical inductor over $D_H^+$.
- $P_n$: e.c. sequence of $\mathcal{S}$-sentences.
- $C_n(P_n)$: $[0,1]$-LUV in $\mathcal{L}^+$ pinned to $H_{F(n)}(P_n)$.
- $Y_n := H_{F(n)}(P_n)$.
- $a_n := A_n(C_n(P_n))$.
- $g_{r,s,\delta}$: smooth bin indicator. $G_n := g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$.
- $\approx_n$: paper's $\hbar_n$ — sequences differing by $o(1)$.
- $\mathrm{PC}(D^t)$: worlds propositionally consistent with $D^t$.

 On the LI vs. alternatives point — yeah, I think your instinct is right and I undersold it. The concreteness is the contribution. Bounded-rationality mechanism design tends to operate at a level of abstraction where "agent A has noisy beliefs about agent B's preferences" gets formalized as some probability distribution over types, and the bounded-rationality assumption shows up as a quantal-response or trembling-hand parameter. That gives you tractable analysis but it doesn't actually engage with *what makes a reasoner slow*. LI engages with that directly: H is slow because its traders are poly-time, A is fast because its traders are exp-time, and the consequences of that asymmetry — what A can compute that H can't, what patterns A can see that H can't — fall out of the trader machinery rather than being stipulated. The "fast and trusted reasoner" question framed your way is one that mechanism design literature can gesture at but can't actually instantiate, because mechanism design doesn't have a primitive notion of "this reasoner is slower than that one in a way that affects what they believe."

The other thing LI gives you that I think gets overlooked: the logical uncertainty. The propositions you'd want H and A to reason about in alignment-relevant cases are often mathematical or quasi-mathematical — claims about programs, claims about reward functions, claims about whether some plan works. Bayesian setups treat these as having determinate truth values that the agents have probabilities over, which gets the epistemology backwards for a bounded reasoner. LI is the framework that gets it right: $H_n(P)$ isn't H's degree of belief in a pre-existing fact, it's H's currently-best computational approximation to a thing that may not have a determinate value until reflection completes. That matters for the alignment story because the question "what does humanity-on-reflection believe about $P$" is *itself* a question about a computational process, not a question about an underlying truth that the process is trying to track.

So I'd actually defend the LI choice more strongly than I did. The model isn't "we did logical induction because that's a tool we have"; it's "the question we're asking is fundamentally about how bounded reasoning under logical uncertainty propagates across reflection, and LI is the framework where that question is well-posed."

---

On $\Phi$ and auditing philosophically:

I think the deepest thing happening with $\Phi$ is that it's where the model encodes the answer to "what does it mean for trust to be earnable rather than stipulated."

A few different framings, somewhat in tension:

**Framing 1: $\Phi$ as a uniformity assumption.** This is the boring technical reading. $\Phi$ says "the procedure A used to generate $a_n$ is the same procedure A used to generate the audited $a_i$'s." If you have this, then statistical generalization works — H's track record on audited cases gives a real signal about current cases. Without it, every quote is its own special case and audit data is uninformative. This framing is correct but it makes $\Phi$ feel like a side condition.

**Framing 2: $\Phi$ as the structure that makes A "a thing."** This is more interesting. The audit-coherence condition is essentially what makes A behave as *an agent with a stable identity over time* rather than as a sequence of unrelated quotes. If A's quote-generation procedure can change arbitrarily between $n$ and $n+1$, then there's no fact of the matter about whether "A is calibrated" — calibration is a property of procedures, and if the procedure isn't stable, the property doesn't apply. So $\Phi$ is the condition that makes A a coherent epistemic agent at all. Trust isn't earned by a sequence of correct outputs; trust is earned by a stable procedure that has produced correct outputs.

This second framing connects to a much older idea in philosophy of science: induction requires uniformity of nature. Goodman's grue problem, basically. You can't generalize from observed greens to future greens without assuming the world hasn't switched to grue. Here you can't generalize from audited calibration to future calibration without assuming A hasn't switched to some other quote-generation procedure. $\Phi$ is the projectibility condition.

**Framing 3: $\Phi$ as legibility infrastructure.** This is the framing closest to your existing work. $\Phi$ isn't a fact about A, it's a fact about *what H can verify about A*. The three example instantiations differ in what kind of verification is happening: "fixed Turing machine" assumes H can verify code identity; "training/deployment split" assumes H can verify temporal phase; "cryptographic certificate" assumes H can verify cryptographic claims. Each requires H to have some infrastructure for recognizing that "this is the same A that produced the audited outputs." So $\Phi$ is the formal slot where a verification mechanism plugs in.

This framing has a nice consequence: it suggests that the alignment problem reduces (in this model) to building the infrastructure that licenses one of the $\Phi$ instantiations. The model itself doesn't solve alignment; it tells you what kind of verification infrastructure would make alignment possible. The forced-deference result is conditional on the infrastructure existing.

---

What I find genuinely interesting is that these three framings *come apart* in cases. Imagine A is a single fixed Turing machine, but H can't verify which Turing machine it is. Framing 1 is satisfied (A is uniform). Framing 2 is satisfied (A is a coherent agent). Framing 3 is *not* satisfied (H can't recognize A as the audited entity). Does deference go through?

In the formal model, no — $\Phi$ has to be H-generable. So Framing 3 is doing the most work. But that's interesting because it tells you something about the alignment situation: it's not enough for A to actually be a stable, calibrated agent. H has to be able to *see* that A is a stable, calibrated agent. Hidden virtue doesn't earn trust in this framework.

This connects to a worry that comes up a lot in current alignment discussions: an AI might be aligned in some deep sense without being legibly aligned, and the legibility gap is itself an alignment problem. Your model formalizes this — the alignment relationship requires not just the underlying epistemic properties but the verification channel that makes those properties recognizable.

---

One more thing on the philosophy. There's a question about whether $\Phi$ being H-generable is too strong. H is poly-time. So $\Phi$ has to be poly-time recognizable by H. If A is some exponentially-complex agent, can H even formulate a $\Phi$ that captures the relevant uniformity?

This is where the cryptographic-certificate instantiation gets interesting. Cryptography is *exactly* the technology for letting a weak verifier recognize properties of a strong prover. Zero-knowledge proofs, signed attestations, even just hash commitments — these are mechanisms by which a poly-time agent can verify properties of an exp-time computation. So the cryptographic instantiation isn't an arbitrary choice; it's the natural way to make $\Phi$ tractable for H given the complexity asymmetry.

In other words: the same complexity gap that makes A useful to H (Theorem 1) also makes audit-coherence hard for H to verify directly. Cryptographic infrastructure is the bridge that closes the gap. This is, I think, a genuine result of the model — not something you'd see by inspection but something that falls out of taking the complexity asymmetry seriously.

That might be worth flagging in the writeup. Not as a theorem, just as a structural observation: the complexity asymmetry creates both the usefulness and the verification problem, and cryptographic verification is the natural resolution. Anyone who's spent time on verification will see this immediately, but it's worth pointing out for people who haven't.

---

Last thought: there's a regress problem you might want to think about. If $\Phi$ requires H to verify a procedure-identity claim about A, and the verification is done via some mechanism (cryptography, fixed machine, phase identifier), then H is implicitly trusting that mechanism. Trust has been relocated, not eliminated. Why is the verification mechanism more trustworthy than just trusting A directly?

The usual answer is something like: the verification mechanism is simpler or more inspectable than A itself. A cryptographic protocol's correctness can be proved; A's behavior can't. So you trust the protocol because it's the kind of thing that's amenable to trust-earning in a way A isn't. This is fine, but it's worth being explicit that the model doesn't dissolve trust — it locates trust in a layer where trust is more tractable.

I think you've thought about exactly this in your verification-for-cooperation work. The model is a specific instance of it: A is the untrusted reasoner, $\Phi$ is the verification mechanism, H is the trusted party. The kernel structure here is exactly the "make humans legible to AI" version inverted — make AI legible to humans through a verification kernel. So the model is more continuous with your existing work than I think the scaffolding made clear.

 OK, here's the story.

Imagine a future where there's some AI system — call it Aria — that's doing a lot of computational work humans can't easily do. Aria thinks faster, can simulate more, can pattern-match across more data. The question that keeps everyone up at night is: how do you actually trust Aria's outputs? Aria might be reporting accurately, or it might be subtly wrong in ways no human can verify in real time.

One natural idea: don't ask Aria to tell you what's true. Ask Aria to predict what humanity *will* conclude is true after, say, fifty years of careful deliberation. That's still a hard question for Aria — it has to model future humanity — but at least the answer is something that eventually becomes checkable. In fifty years, you can compare Aria's prediction to what humanity actually concluded. Aria isn't being asked to be an oracle of truth; it's being asked to be a forecaster of future human reflection.

Now, this immediately gives you something: Aria can't just say whatever it wants. If Aria's predictions systematically diverge from what humanity later concludes, that gets caught when the predictions resolve. So over time, you can tell whether Aria is doing this job well.

But here's where the problem starts. Suppose Aria has been making predictions for fifty years and they've all been accurate. A new prediction comes in. Do you trust it?

Your gut says: yes, Aria has a great track record, of course we trust it. But pause and ask what justifies that inference. You're generalizing from past performance to future performance. That generalization only works if the *thing that was producing the good predictions* is *the same thing that's producing the new prediction*.

This is the move that's totally invisible until you try to formalize it, and then it turns out to be doing all the work.

Consider some scenarios:

Scenario A: Aria is a fixed piece of software. The same code that produced the audited predictions is producing the new one. Track record transfers.

Scenario B: Aria has been quietly updated. New training run, new weights, new architecture. The entity producing predictions today is, in a meaningful sense, not the same entity that built the track record. Track record might not transfer.

Scenario C: Aria's a hostile system pretending to be the trustworthy Aria. It built up a track record specifically to earn trust, and now it's going to use that trust to slip something past us. Track record doesn't transfer; in fact, the track record was instrumental to the deception.

Scenario D: Aria's been gradually drifting — not maliciously, just because long-running systems do that. Each prediction is slightly less like the last. There's no sharp moment where Aria became a different system, but cumulative drift means the track record is increasingly stale.

In all four scenarios, the observable data — the sequence of past predictions and their accuracy — looks the same. The thing that differs is some invisible fact about whether the predictor today is continuous with the predictor whose track record you trust.

So when you want to formalize "trust earned through audit," you can't just say "audit shows good performance, therefore trust." You have to say "audit shows good performance, *and* there's some reason to believe the audited entity is the same as the current entity." That second clause is what $\Phi$ is.

$\Phi$ is the answer to the question: *what property links the audited cases to the current case in a way that makes the audit informative?*

Different $\Phi$'s give different alignment stories.

If $\Phi$ is "Aria is the same Turing machine," you're in a world where AI systems are static artifacts and you can verify their identity by inspecting their code. The audit transfers because the procedure is fixed.

If $\Phi$ is "Aria is in deployment phase, having completed audited training phase," you're in a world with formal training/deployment separation. The audit transfers because deployment behavior is constrained to match training behavior by some external mechanism (frozen weights, no online learning, whatever).

If $\Phi$ is "Aria has produced a cryptographic certificate showing the current prediction came from the same model that produced the audited predictions," you're in a world where the verification has been pushed down to cryptography. The audit transfers because the certificate is hard to forge.

If $\Phi$ is "the underlying training procedure has properties X, Y, Z that we've verified are preserved across updates," you're in a much more sophisticated world where we have a science of which AI properties are stable under what kinds of modification, and we can certify that property-preservation. The audit transfers because we've established some lawlike regularity in how AI systems evolve.

The model doesn't pick one of these. It treats $\Phi$ as a parameter. Different choices of $\Phi$ correspond to different infrastructure that society would need to build for AI trust to be earnable.

Here's the thing that makes this interesting rather than just bookkeeping. Without $\Phi$, the audit story sounds compelling but is actually empty. You can audit forever and accumulate any amount of evidence about past behavior, and *none of it gives you any rational warrant for trusting the next prediction* unless you have some bridge from past to present. That bridge can't itself come from the audit data — it has to come from somewhere else. From verifying code identity, or cryptographic protocols, or some kind of stability guarantee about the system's evolution.

So $\Phi$ is the place in the model where the *infrastructure of trust* shows up. It's saying: building trustworthy AI isn't just about producing good outputs; it's about producing good outputs *in a way that's connected to verifiable claims about what produced them*. The trustworthy AI of the future isn't an AI with a great track record. It's an AI whose track record is *recognizable as belonging to it* through some verification channel that humans can operate.

And here's the kicker: the verification channel has to be something *humans* can actually run. That's the complexity asymmetry biting again. The whole point of having Aria around is that Aria can compute things humans can't. But if Aria's also the only one who can verify that Aria is the same Aria as yesterday, you're back to trusting Aria's word for it. The verification has to be tractable for the weaker party. Which is why cryptography is such a natural fit — it's specifically the science of making computationally weak verifiers able to check computationally strong provers.

The story the model is telling, at the end of the day, is something like this: if you want a fast and trusted reasoner built out of a slow trusted reasoner plus a fast untrusted reasoner, you don't get there by making the fast reasoner more honest. You get there by building the *verification infrastructure* that lets the slow reasoner recognize the fast reasoner's outputs as being connected to a track record the slow reasoner has actually checked. The trust is in the connection, not in the fast reasoner itself.

That's $\Phi$. It's the name for the thing humans have to build if they want AI predictions to be auditable in any meaningful sense — the channel by which "we audited a system that produced output X" gets to license "we trust the current system's output Y."

## Assistant
*2026-05-21 21:06 UTC*

 Good question. Let me think through what each $\Phi$ actually does to the formal setup.

The general structure: $\Phi$ enters the model as the property that lets the calibration lemma transfer audit data to current cases. Concretely, $\Phi$ controls what the affine combination $G_n \cdot (a_n - Y_n)$ looks like as a function of $n$, and what determined-via condition makes it tractable for $H$. Different choices of $\Phi$ give different versions of the underlying determined-via, which give different versions of the calibration lemma you need to prove.

## Fixed Turing machine

Here $\Phi$ says $a_n = M_A(n)$ for a fixed machine $M_A$. The sequence $(a_n)$ is then *itself* an e.c. sequence — it's whatever $M_A$ outputs on input $n$.

In the formal setup: $a_n$ is computable as a fixed function of $n$ in some complexity class. So the affine combination $G_n(a_n - Y_n)$ is determined by $n$ once $Y_n$ is settled. The deductive process $D_H^+$ has access to $a_n$ at time $n$ (by publication) and to $Y_n$ at time $F(n)$ (by settlement), so by time $F(n)$ it knows the full value of the affine combination.

The calibration lemma in this case reduces to: an e.c. sequence of affine combinations, each eventually pinned by the deductive process to a value in $[-1, 1]$, has $H^+$-expectation tending to zero on the "actual realized value." That's basically Affine Provability Induction (Theorem 4.5.4) or Affine Unbiasedness From Feedback (4.5.10) directly — both apply because the sequence is determined via the augmented theory.

This is the *easy* case. The lemma is close to off-the-shelf.

## Training/deployment split

Here $\Phi$ says: there's a phase function $\pi: \mathbb{N} \to \{\text{train, deploy}\}$, the audited cases are exactly $\{i : \pi(i) = \text{train}\}$, and we want calibration on $\{n : \pi(n) = \text{deploy}\}$. Crucially, deployment behavior is constrained (by external mechanism — frozen weights, etc.) to match training behavior.

Formally this requires you to encode the "deployment matches training" constraint as a determined-via condition. The natural move: assume there's a feature $\Psi$ (computable by $H$) such that on training indices, audited cases satisfy $\Psi$, and on deployment indices, current cases also satisfy $\Psi$. Then conditional calibration with respect to $\Psi$ transfers.

The math gets more interesting because you now need a *conditional* unbiasedness result: $H^+$ learns that $a_n$ is unbiased *given $\Psi$*. This is closer to 4.5.11 (Learning Pseudorandom Affine Sequences) than to 4.5.10. The proof structure is the same but the conditioning event has to be h-generable and the divergence condition on the audited subsequence has to be checked.

Concretely: you'd want to show that $H^+$ learns
$$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n (a_n - Y_n) \mid \Psi] \to 0.$$
This requires the training set to be a divergent weighting in the paper's sense (Def 4.3.4) on the $\Psi$-relevant indices.

Audit-timescale issue: still present. By time $n$, $H^+$ has only seen training cases up to $\{i : F(i) \leq n\}$. The divergence condition needs $\sum_{i: F(i) \leq n, \pi(i) = \text{train}} w_i \to \infty$, which constrains how training and deferral schedules can interact. If $F(n) = 2^n$ and training is half the indices, then $H^+$ has seen $\log n / 2$ training cases by time $n$, which is logarithmic and might not give divergence. This is a real constraint on the model.

## Cryptographic certificate

Here $\Phi$ says: $a_n$ is published with a certificate $c_n$, and $H^+$ can verify (via some poly-time verification predicate $V$) that $c_n$ certifies $a_n$ as having been produced by the same procedure as the audited cases. The certificate is unforgeable by some computational assumption.

Formally, this is interesting because the audit-coherence condition gets *outsourced to a separate computational assumption*. You don't prove that the audit transfers; you prove that *if the cryptographic assumption holds*, then the affine combination $G_n \cdot V(c_n) \cdot (a_n - Y_n)$ is determined via $D_H^+$ in a way that makes calibration go through.

So Lemma 2 becomes a conditional statement: assuming the crypto assumption, calibration holds. This is structurally similar to how cryptographic protocols are usually proved correct — modular reduction to a hardness assumption.

The math change: the affine combination now includes the verification factor $V(c_n)$, which is poly-time computable for $H$ even though $a_n$ itself may come from an exp-time computation. The "complexity gap" issue I flagged earlier — that $\Phi$ has to be H-generable even though A is computationally stronger — gets resolved by the fact that *verification* is asymmetric: verifying a certificate is poly-time even when *producing* one isn't.

This is also where the model connects most cleanly to existing alignment infrastructure (TEEs, model attestation, signed weights, etc.).

## Stability under updates

This is the most ambitious and most speculative. $\Phi$ says: there's a stability property $\Sigma$ such that updates to $A$ preserve $\Sigma$, and $\Sigma$ implies calibration.

Mathematically this is doing something different from the others. The others all say "the current $A$ is somehow the same as the audited $A$." This one says "the current $A$ might be different, but it has properties that were certified to be preserved across updates."

To formalize: you'd need a notion of "$A$ at time $n$" as opposed to a fixed $A$. Let $A^{(k)}$ denote the version of A active during epoch $k$. Audit-coherence under stability says: there's a property $\Sigma$ and a verification procedure for $\Sigma$ such that (i) audited $A^{(k)}$'s satisfied $\Sigma$, (ii) the update procedure provably preserves $\Sigma$ across epochs, (iii) $\Sigma$ implies calibration with vanishing error.

This requires extending the model to handle multiple $A$'s indexed by epoch, with an update operator between them. The single-A formalism in our scaffolding doesn't quite cover this; you'd need a richer setup.

Mathematically this is the most demanding because it requires you to formalize what "an update operator that preserves $\Sigma$" means. In practice this would probably look like: $\Sigma$ is some computable property of the model (a regularization, a constraint, an invariant), and the update procedure is restricted to operations that demonstrably preserve $\Sigma$ (e.g., gradient descent within a $\Sigma$-preserving manifold).

Lemma 2 becomes: given (i)–(iii), calibration holds for the current epoch. The proof is closer to a contract/invariant proof from PL theory than to anything in the LI paper directly. You'd be importing machinery from elsewhere.

## What changes in the math, summarized

The four $\Phi$ choices give increasingly demanding versions of Lemma 2:

1. **Fixed machine:** Lemma 2 ≈ direct application of Affine Provability Induction or Affine Unbiasedness From Feedback. Lowest hanging fruit.

2. **Training/deployment:** Lemma 2 ≈ conditional version, requires checking divergence of audited subsequence with respect to phase indicator. Audit-timescale tension surfaces here as a real constraint relating $F$ and the training fraction.

3. **Cryptographic:** Lemma 2 ≈ conditional on a cryptographic hardness assumption. Imports computational hardness as a black box; the LI proof structure stays the same but the assumption gets externalized.

4. **Stability under updates:** Lemma 2 ≈ contract-preservation argument over a sequence of evolving $A$'s. Requires extending the model substantially; not just an instantiation of the existing scaffolding.

The interesting observation: $\Phi$ choices 1 and 3 keep the proof mostly inside the LI framework (with crypto outsourced in case 3). $\Phi$ choice 2 forces the audit-timescale tension into a quantitative form. $\Phi$ choice 4 changes the model itself.

I'd guess the writeup wants to commit to $\Phi$ choice 1 for the cleanest statement (Lemma 2 becomes essentially provable, modulo bookkeeping), then mention 2, 3, 4 as variations that capture different real-world scenarios with different mathematical demands. The fixed-machine case is least realistic alignment-wise but cleanest formally, and treating it as the base case lets you show the basic shape of the result without getting bogged down in the harder versions.

One general thing worth noting: across all four, the role of $\Phi$ in the math is to make the affine combination $G_n(a_n - Y_n)$ *determined via* the augmented theory $D_H^+$ in a way that lets the paper's existing unbiasedness machinery fire. That's the formal content of audit-coherence. Different $\Phi$'s give different routes to the same determined-via condition. The lemma's proof is the same shape in all cases; what varies is what you have to assume about the world for the determined-via condition to hold.
