 Yeah, a few. Loosely ordered from most interesting to most bookkeeping.

**The model is asymmetric about what "deference" means.** Theorem 1 says A is forced to predict H's future beliefs. Theorem 2 says H updates toward A's quote. These look like complementary directions of a single trust relationship, but they're actually quite different in character. A's deference to H is *structural* — it falls out of the contract design and is involuntary on A's part. H's deference to A is *epistemic* — it requires H to actually update its own beliefs, and the update only happens if H satisfies self-trust and recognizes the audit. The asymmetry is fine but it's worth being explicit about: A defers because of how the contracts are set up; H defers because of how its own reasoning works.

This has a consequence for the alignment story. If you wanted, you could imagine a version of the model where H is irrational — doesn't satisfy self-trust, doesn't recognize the audit channel. In that version, A still defers to H (Theorem 1 still holds), but H doesn't defer to A (Theorem 2 fails). The asymmetry means H's epistemic standing is doing real work; the model isn't just "set up the contracts and trust falls out." A trusts H mechanically; H has to actually be a good reasoner to trust A back.

**There's a weird thing about what A is predicting.** A is predicting $H_{F(n)}(P_n)$ — H's price at a specific future time. But why $F(n)$ in particular? If you take $F(n)$ very large, A is predicting humanity-after-much-reflection. If you take $F(n)$ moderate, A is predicting humanity-soon. These are very different predictions and the model treats them uniformly.

The interesting question is: what's the limit of $H_{F(n)}(P)$ as $F(n) \to \infty$? By Convergence, it's $H_\infty(P)$. So in some sense the "ideal" target is humanity's limiting belief, and any finite $F(n)$ is an approximation. But the closer you get to the limit, the less audit data you have (the audit-timescale tradeoff). The model has a natural "sweet spot" in the choice of $F$ that the current writeup doesn't really highlight — fast enough to give you useful acceleration, slow enough to give you audit data, both expressed in terms of how close $H_{F(n)}$ is to $H_\infty$.

There might be something to say here about *why* you'd want to predict an intermediate-future H rather than $H_\infty$ directly. The answer is probably that $H_\infty$ isn't operationalizable — you can never observe it, so contracts couldn't settle. $H_{F(n)}$ is the strongest operationalizable proxy. But this means the model is implicitly committing to a kind of finitism about reflective endpoints: there's no "humanity on full reflection," just humanity at increasingly later finite times.

**The complexity asymmetry is doing two different jobs.** The asymmetry $\mathcal{C}_H \subsetneq \mathcal{C}_A$ shows up in two places. First, in making A *useful*: A can predict things H can't compute (because $Y_n$ is in $\mathcal{C}_A$ but maybe not $\mathcal{C}_H$). Second, in making A *forced to be useful*: A can simulate H, so any pattern in H's prices is visible to A's traders, so A can't get away with mispricing.

These are conceptually distinct. You could have a model where A is more powerful than H in some specific dimension (e.g., A can solve certain kinds of computational problems H can't) without A being uniformly more powerful. In that case the second job would still work but the first might be limited to specific propositions. The current model collapses these by assuming uniform complexity dominance, which is convenient but probably stronger than needed.

This connects to a real-world worry: AI systems aren't uniformly stronger than humans. They're stronger in some ways (computational speed, certain kinds of pattern recognition) and weaker in others (common sense, certain kinds of robustness). The model's clean complexity asymmetry doesn't capture this. A more realistic version would have heterogeneous complexity classes — A is stronger than H on some computations, weaker on others — and the forced-deference result would only hold for propositions where the relevant computations fall in A's stronger domain.

I don't think this is a problem for the toy model, but it's worth knowing as a limitation.

**The model doesn't distinguish "H predicts what H will believe" from "H predicts what H *should* believe."** This is a place where the LI framework has a built-in normative commitment that you might want to surface. Logical induction takes the limiting prices as the right answer — $H_\infty(P)$ is what H ought to believe about $P$. But there's no separate normative standard; whatever H converges to is by definition the right answer.

For the alignment story this is convenient (it lets you identify "humanity's verdict" with "humanity's eventual prices") but it's also kind of a strong commitment. It assumes that whatever humanity converges to on reflection is *normatively correct* — that there's no further question of whether humanity got it right. Some moral realists would push back on this; most metaethical positions short of strong constructivism would distinguish "what we converge to" from "what's true."

You might not care about this for the toy model. But Demski might, depending on his metaethical commitments. Worth being aware that the model has a built-in idealized-observer theory of normativity baked into the LI machinery.

**The "two inductors" framing might be doing less work than it looks like.** Reading the model carefully, the action is mostly in A's contracts and H's augmented process. H itself, as a logical inductor in its own right, doesn't do much beyond providing the settlement values for A's contracts. You could imagine a stripped-down version where H is just a black-box belief sequence (not necessarily a logical inductor) and A is forced to track it. The forced-tracking result (Theorem 1) doesn't actually use H being a logical inductor — it just uses H being a computable belief sequence.

What you do need H being a logical inductor for is Theorem 2 (the self-trust step). H needs to satisfy 4.12.2 to update on A's quotes.

So the model has an asymmetric requirement: A needs full LI machinery (to be forced to track); H needs LI machinery only for the self-trust step (to be forced to defer). You could weaken H's requirements substantially if you only wanted Theorem 1, or strengthen them appropriately if you wanted more from Theorem 2.

This might suggest a generalization: what's the *minimal* epistemic requirement on H for the deference result to hold? If it's weaker than full LI, that's interesting because real humans probably don't satisfy full LI but might satisfy some weaker self-trust-like property.

**There's an interesting structural feature about what propositions are in scope.** The sequence $(P_n)$ is required to be e.c. (efficiently computable). So the model is about deference on propositions that can be efficiently enumerated. This rules out some natural alignment targets — e.g., propositions about specific real-world situations that would only be formulated as they arise, not as part of any pre-specified enumeration.

You could try to handle this by having a "rich" enumeration that includes lots of propositions, most of which are never actually queried. But there's a real question about whether the model captures *responsive* deference (H asks A about something specific, A answers) vs. *batch* deference (A makes predictions on a pre-specified sequence, H later checks them). The current setup is batch. A responsive version would be a different model.

**Smallest thing: there's an unstated assumption that A's quote $a_n$ is rational.** The contract pays $H_{F(n)}(P)$, which is rational since H's prices are in $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$. A's price for that contract should also be in $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ since A is a market with rational prices. So $a_n$ is rational and publication works (you can transmit a rational exactly). Worth checking once that this is clean — that A's market on LUV-valued contracts gives rational prices — but I think it's fine.

---

Stepping back: the model is a clean instance of a more general pattern that I think is worth being aware of even if you don't write about it. The pattern is *deference via a designed channel*. You have two parties with different epistemic strengths. You want one to be able to trust the other. The solution is to design a structured channel between them — a market, a contract, a verification protocol — such that trust falls out of the channel's properties rather than requiring direct epistemic comparison.

This pattern shows up in lots of places. Prediction markets in general. Cryptographic verification. Peer review. Expert testimony in court. The contracts in your model are one instance of this pattern, specifically suited to a logical-uncertainty setting where the parties are bounded reasoners.

Recognizing the pattern might help you situate the contribution. You're not solving "how do humans trust AI" in general; you're showing what a specific *designed channel* — H-settled prediction contracts — buys you in a specific formal setting. The contribution is the concreteness, and the limitations are the conditions under which the channel design actually delivers trust. The audit-coherence requirement is one such limitation; the responsive-vs-batch distinction is another; the metaethical commitment about $H_\infty$ being normative is another.

If you want a one-sentence framing of what the model contributes: "Designed prediction channels can convert a complexity asymmetry into a trust relationship, but only under specified verification infrastructure and at the cost of certain modeling commitments about what 'humanity's beliefs' means in the limit."

- $Y_n := H_{F(n)}(P_n)$ — H's future price for $P_n$.
- $a_n := A_n(C_n(P_n))$ — A's current quote for the H-settled contract on $P_n$.
- $G_n := g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ — a smooth indicator with $G_n = 1$ when $a_n \in [r,s]$, $G_n = 0$ when $a_n \notin [r-\delta, s+\delta]$.

Let $H^+$ be H's logical inductor over the augmented process $D_H^+$, which receives A's quotes at time $n$ and contract settlements at time $F(n)$.

**Assumptions.**
1. $H^+$ observes $a_n$ at time $n$.
2. $(A, F)$ is audit-coherent, so by Lemma 2: $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n \cdot |a_n - Y_n|] \to 0$.
3. $H^+$ satisfies No Expected Net Update (Theorem 4.12.2 of the LI paper, which it does by being a logical inductor).

**Conclusion.** As $n \to \infty$:

$$(r - \delta) \cdot \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n] - o(1) \;\leq\; \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf{1}(P_n) \cdot G_n] \;\leq\; (s + \delta) \cdot \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n] + o(1).$$

## Corollary (conditional form)

**Additional assumption.** $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n] \geq \gamma > 0$ for all sufficiently large $n$ — the bin has non-negligible H-weight.

**Conclusion.**

$$\frac{\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf{1}(P_n) \cdot G_n]}{\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n]} \;\in\; [r - \delta - o(1), \; s + \delta + o(1)].$$

The ratio on the left is the rigorous smoothed analogue of the conditional probability $H^+_n(P_n \mid a_n \in [r,s])$. So informally:

$$H^+_n(P_n \mid A_n(C_n(P_n)) \in [r,s]) \;\in\; [r - \delta - o(1), \; s + \delta + o(1)].$$

In the special case where A's quote lies in a narrow window around $q$ (take $[r,s] = [q-\delta, q+\delta]$):

$$H^+_n(P_n \mid A_n(C_n(P_n)) \approx q) \;\approx\; q.$$

## Alignment gloss

The question you asked is the right one: does this give us what we want?

**What we wanted.** A formal statement of the form: "when humanity learns what the AI's prediction is, humanity is forced — on pain of incoherence — to update its own belief toward that prediction."

**What the theorem says.** When H observes that A's quote on $P_n$ lies in some bin $[r,s]$, H's conditional belief in $P_n$ (in the smoothed sense formalized by the ratio above) lies in essentially the same bin, modulo $\delta$ and asymptotic error. If A is quoting $q$ for the contract, H's belief in $P_n$ is approximately $q$.

So yes, the theorem delivers what we wanted. H is forced — by its own self-trust plus the audit-licensed bridge — to align its belief about $P_n$ with A's quote about the H-settled contract.

**What "forced" means here.** Three things in combination, and worth being precise about because the philosophical content depends on the precision.

First, "forced" is *epistemically* compelled, not *structurally* compelled. The model doesn't make H mechanically take A's quote as its belief. It says that *if H is a coherent reasoner (satisfies LIC over its augmented process)*, then H's belief will track A's quote. A coherent H that didn't update toward A's quote could be exploited by a trader who sees both A's quote and H's belief and arbitrages the gap. So the force is the same force that makes any logical inductor's beliefs cohere — exploitability of incoherent positions.

Second, "forced" presupposes that the audit-coherence condition holds. Without $\Phi$, the lemma doesn't fire, and H isn't forced to update on A's quote at all. So the deference is conditional on the verification infrastructure being in place. The model doesn't say "trust AI"; it says "given verification infrastructure $\Phi$, an AI's quotes become evidence H is forced to update on."

Third, "forced" is asymmetric in an important way. H is forced to update *toward A's quote*, but only because A's quote tracks $Y_n$ (H's own future belief). The trust chain runs through H's future self, not through A's authority. H isn't deferring to A because A is smart; H is deferring to A because A is an audited predictor of H's own future reflection.

**The alignment payoff.** If you accept the model, you get a precise statement of a structure that's been informally floating around alignment discussions for years: the trustworthy AI of the future is one whose outputs are audited predictions of what humanity-on-reflection would endorse, and humans are (rationally) compelled to update on those predictions to the extent that the audit infrastructure is in place.

This is a stronger result than "humans should trust AI under certain conditions." It's "humans are logically committed to updating on AI outputs under certain conditions, and not doing so would constitute a coherence failure on the human side." That's a different kind of normative claim — it puts the burden of justification on *not* deferring rather than on deferring.

**One caveat that's worth flagging.** The forced update is on $P_n$, not on every proposition. H is forced to defer to A on the specific propositions covered by the contracts. The model doesn't license general deference; it licenses deference on the audited prediction domain. If A makes a claim outside that domain — about some proposition $P^*$ that hasn't been part of the contract sequence — Theorem 2 says nothing. So the model is naturally giving you *scoped* trust, which is probably more aligned with what you'd want anyway than universal trust.

**The honest assessment.** Yes, this is what we wanted. The conditional corollary is the form alignment people would most easily recognize as the "forced trust" theorem. The product form is the technically clean version. The two together say: under audit-coherence, observing that A quotes $q$ on the H-settled contract for $P_n$ forces H's belief in $P_n$ toward $q$.

Whether it's a *satisfying* answer depends on how much weight the audit-coherence condition can bear. If the condition is easy to satisfy — fixed Turing machine, cryptographic verification — then the model gives you forced deference under realistic infrastructure. If the condition turns out to require something much stronger in practice, then the forced-deference theorem becomes more like a conditional possibility theorem ("forced deference is possible given the right infrastructure") than an action-guiding result ("here's how to set up trustworthy AI").

I think the honest answer is: the model formalizes the *structure* of forced deference cleanly, and reduces the practical question to "can we build $\Phi$?". That's progress even if it doesn't dissolve the alignment problem — it tells you what kind of work the alignment problem actually requires.

The lemma wants: $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n |a_n - Y_n|] \to 0$.

The thing that makes the inference legitimate rather than circular is that the condition should be about something H can *check on the audited cases* and that *provably extends* to the current case — not about the current case directly.

The fix has to separate "H can verify the *structure* of A's quote process" from "H can compute the *values* of A's quotes." That's the key distinction.

The crucial move: $H^+$ knows *that* $a_n = M_A(n)$ without being able to *compute* $M_A(n)$ in time. H recognizes the generating process but can't simulate it.

Under this condition, the sequence $(a_n)$ is determined by the fixed program $M_A$. **Definition (Audit-coherence).** A pair $(A, F)$ is *audit-coherent* relative to $H^+$ if there is a fixed program $M_A$ and a deferral schedule $F$ such that:

(C2) **Verified provenance.** For every $i$, the sentence $\text{Prov}_i := \ulcorner a_i = M_A(i) \urcorner$ is contained in $D_H^{+,t}$ for all $t \geq i$. (H observes not just the quote but a verification that the quote came from $M_A$.)

The condition does *not* assume the conclusion. Let me check this carefully, because it's the whole point.

The conclusion is $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[G_n |a_n - Y_n|] \to 0$ — a statement about H's *current* expectation of the *current* quote's accuracy.

- **Settlement-calibration**: A's quotes are *actually* accurate on the audited record. This is the "A is actually good" condition. It's about A's quality.

The lemma says: infrastructure + actual accuracy ⟹ H learns to defer. Neither condition alone suffices, and crucially, the infrastructure condition is the one that's a genuine modeling assumption about the world, while the accuracy condition is the thing A has to earn.

With this decomposition, the proof becomes:

3. By settlement-calibration, the realized $G$-weighted errors on audited cases vanish.

This is the formal version of the audit-timescale tradeoff: fast $F$ (large computational advantage) gives slow audit convergence (logarithmic in $n$); slow $F$ gives faster audit convergence but less advantage. The tradeoff is now a precise statement about convergence rates, not just a hand-wave. The condition I'd commit to is the (C1)–(C4) audit-coherence definition, *plus* a separate settlement-calibration condition, with the lemma stated as "audit-coherence + settlement-calibration ⟹ H learns calibration." ## The encoding

For each contract index $(n, j)$ — recall $P^{(j)}$ is the $j$-th sentence — the value we want to encode is the rational $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$. A belief state at any fixed timestep has finite support and rational values, so $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ is a rational with some denominator. Let $d(n)$ be a bound on the denominator of $H$'s prices at timestep $F(n)$ — this is computable in $\mathcal{C}_A$ alongside the value itself, since you compute the value by simulating $H$ and can read off its denominator.

Introduce, for each $(n, j)$ and each $k \in \{0, 1, \dots, d(n)\}$, a fresh propositional atom

$$\theta_{n,j,k} \;:\equiv\; \text{“}C_{n}(P^{(j)}) \geq k / d(n)\text{”}.$$

These are ordinary $\{0,1\}$-valued sentences in the extended language $\mathcal{L}^+$. The intended reading: $\theta_{n,j,k}$ is true iff the contract's value is at least $k/d(n)$. The bundle $\{\theta_{n,j,k}\}_k$ encodes a single rational value via its threshold profile.

A world $W$ assigns the contract a value by reading off the thresholds:

$$\text{val}_W(n,j) := \max\{\,k/d(n) : W(\theta_{n,j,k}) = 1\,\}$$

(with the convention $\theta_{n,j,0}$ is always true, so the max is well-defined). This is the discrete analogue of the LUV supremum construction, but built from finitely many ordinary sentences instead of a formula with $\Gamma$-provable uniqueness.

## Coherence axioms for the thresholds

You want worlds to assign *sensible* threshold profiles — monotone, so that "value $\geq k/d$" implies "value $\geq (k-1)/d$." Add to the background theory $\Gamma^+$ the monotonicity schema

$$\theta_{n,j,k} \to \theta_{n,j,k-1} \quad \text{for all } n, j, k \geq 1.$$

These are purely syntactic axioms — they don't reference $H$. They just say the threshold sentences for a given contract are nested. With them, every $\Gamma^+$-consistent world assigns each contract a unique value in $\{0, 1/d(n), \dots, 1\}$, determined by where the threshold profile flips from 1 to 0.

This gives you the "unique value" property *without* needing $\Gamma^+$ to prove anything about $H$. The uniqueness comes from the monotonicity axioms (cheap, syntactic), not from representing $H$'s computation (expensive, and what forced the LUV assumption earlier).

## The deductive process settles the thresholds

Now the deductive process $D_A$ does the work of pinning values, by asserting the correct threshold sentences. At the settlement time $\sigma(n)$ — the time by which $D_A$ has surfaced the value of contract $(n,j)$ — $D_A^{\sigma(n)}$ contains, for the true value $q^*_{n,j} = H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$:

$$\theta_{n,j,k} \text{ for all } k \text{ with } k/d(n) \leq q^*_{n,j}, \qquad \neg\,\theta_{n,j,k} \text{ for all } k \text{ with } k/d(n) > q^*_{n,j}.$$

So once $t \geq \sigma(n)$, every world $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ has $\text{val}_W(n,j) = q^*_{n,j}$ exactly. The value is propositionally pinned, by ordinary sentence assertions, exactly as the standard deductive-process framework intends.

The key point: $D_A$ *asserts* the threshold truth values as observations (it computes $q^*_{n,j}$ by simulating $H$, then writes down the corresponding thresholds). It does *not* require $\Gamma^+$ to *prove* them from $H$'s code. $\Gamma^+$ only needs the cheap monotonicity axioms. The expensive computation lives in $D_A$'s construction (which is allowed to be any computable nested sequence of finite sentence sets), not in $\Gamma^+$.

This is the move that buys you out of the $\Gamma_A$-represents-$H$ assumption. The LUV definition required $\Gamma \vdash$ uniqueness, which for a value defined as $H$'s output meant $\Gamma$ had to represent $H$. The threshold version requires only $\Gamma^+ \vdash$ monotonicity (trivial) plus $D_A$ asserting the right thresholds (allowed, since $D_A$ is just required to be computable).

Per timestep, how many threshold sentences enter? For contract $(n,j)$, there are $d(n) + 1$ thresholds. Using the enumeration bound from before (include $(n,j)$ only when $F(n) \leq t$ and $j \leq t$), the number of new threshold sentences at time $t$ is at most

$$\sum_{(n,j): F(n) \leq t,\, j \leq t} (d(n) + 1),$$

which is finite for each $t$ (finitely many $(n,j)$ pairs, each contributing finitely many thresholds). So $D_A^t$ is finite. ✓

Computability: to assert the thresholds for $(n,j)$, $D_A$ computes $q^*_{n,j} = H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ and $d(n)$, both in $\mathcal{C}_A$ (simulate $H$ to timestep $F(n)$, cost $\mathrm{poly}(F(n)) = 2^{O(n)}$). So $D_A$ is computable. ✓

Trader access in Lemma 1: the exploiting trader on day $n$ needs to know the target value to compute the ramp. It computes $q^*_{n,j}$ in $\mathcal{C}_A$ (same simulation). The number of thresholds $d(n)+1$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, so the trader can address the right threshold sentences. The ramp resolution $\varepsilon$ has to be coarse enough relative to $1/d(n)$ — i.e., you need $d(n) \gtrsim 1/\varepsilon$ so the thresholds can distinguish prices at scale $\varepsilon$. Since $d(n)$ grows (denominators of $H$'s prices generally increase with timestep), this is fine for large $n$; for small $n$ you can just take $\varepsilon$ adaptively or note the result is asymptotic anyway. Add this to the ledger as a constraint: *threshold resolution $1/d(n)$ must eventually be finer than the arbitrage gap $\varepsilon$*. ✓ (with the caveat to verify)

The trader trades the contract by trading its threshold sentences. So "one share of the contract" = the portfolio $\frac{1}{d(n)} \sum_{k=1}^{d(n)} (\text{one share of } \theta_{n,j,k})$.

The trader's price for this portfolio at day $n$ is $\frac{1}{d(n)} \sum_k A_n(\theta_{n,j,k})$, which is $A$'s implied price for the contract. The arbitrage argument compares this to $q^*_{n,j}$ exactly as before. The capacity-1 logic is unchanged. You can either *define* $A_n(C_n(P))$ as this sum (making the contract price a derived quantity from threshold prices) or add coherence requirements tying them. The cleaner choice is to *define* the contract price as the threshold-portfolio price; then $a_n$ is by definition a function of ordinary sentence prices, and there's nothing extra to assume.

## What this buys and what it costs

**Buys:**
- No LUV abstraction. Everything is ordinary sentences; standard LIC applies to Lemma 1 directly.
- No $\Gamma_A$-represents-$H$ assumption. $\Gamma^+$ only needs monotonicity axioms.
- The contract price $a_n$ becomes a *defined* quantity (threshold-portfolio price), not a primitive, so you don't need a separate LUV-market existence argument for it.
- Worlds assign contract values by a finite, transparent rule.

**Costs:**
- The number of sentences per contract grows with $d(n)$, so the bookkeeping has a size parameter you have to track. Manageable, but it's there.
- The threshold resolution constraint ($d(n) \gtrsim 1/\varepsilon$ eventually) is a new ledger item to verify.
- For Theorem 2's self-trust step, you *still* need expectations of $H$'s future price, which is intrinsically real-valued. The threshold encoding helps Lemma 1 and possibly Lemma 2, but it does not eliminate the expectation operator from the self-trust citation. That part still cites 4.12.2.

## Where this leaves the self-trust step

Worth being explicit since the threshold trick doesn't fully reach it. In Theorem 2 you want $H_n^+(P_n) \approx_n \mathbb{E}_n^+[\text{"}H_{F(n)}(P_n)\text{"}]$. The right side is an expectation of H's future price. Two options:

(a) Cite 4.12.2 directly, which is stated with the future price as a LUV-valued expectation. You're using one finished theorem; you don't develop LUV theory, you invoke it. Clean.

(b) Threshold-encode H's future price too: introduce threshold sentences for "$H_{F(n)}(P_n) \geq k/d(n)$" and express the expectation as a sum over threshold probabilities, $\mathbb{E}_n^+[\text{"}H_{F(n)}(P_n)\text{"}] = \frac{1}{d(n)}\sum_k H_n^+(\text{"}H_{F(n)}(P_n) \geq k/d(n)\text{"})$. Then self-trust becomes a statement about ordinary sentence prices, and you'd invoke No-Expected-Net-Update at the *threshold-sentence* level (4.12.2 for each threshold sentence) and sum.

Option (b) keeps the whole development in ordinary sentences and is more uniform with the rest, at the cost of a slightly fiddly "sum over thresholds" in the self-trust step. Option (a) is less work but reintroduces the expectation operator as a citation. I'd lean (b) for uniformity if you've already committed to threshold encodings everywhere else — it means the *entire* paper is in ordinary-sentence LIC with no expectation machinery developed, only cited at the threshold level. That's a clean story: "we never leave the sentence-based framework; real values are always finite threshold bundles."

If you go (b), there's a subtlety: 4.12.2 is about $P_n(\phi_n) \approx_n \mathbb{E}_n[P_{f(n)}(\phi_n)]$, and you'd be applying it with $\phi_n$ being the threshold sentence "$H_{F(n)}(P_n) \geq k/d(n)$" — but that's a sentence about *H's* future price, and you're asking *$H^+$* to have self-trust about it. So you need $H^+$ to satisfy 4.12.2 with respect to these threshold sentences, which requires the threshold sentences to be in $H^+$'s language and settled in $D_H^+$. That's fine — $D_H^+$ receives the settlements — but it's another ledger entry: the threshold sentences for $H$'s future prices must be $D_H^+$-settled at the appropriate time, just like the contract thresholds are $D_A$-settled.

## Suggested setup ordering with thresholds

So the clean setup order becomes: fix languages; fix the threshold atoms $\theta_{n,j,k}$ and the monotonicity axioms (this is now where "contracts" are defined, as threshold bundles); define contract value in a world and contract price as the threshold-portfolio price; fix $D_A$ as asserting the correct thresholds at $\sigma(n)$; fix $D_H^+$ as asserting contract-quote thresholds at time $n$ and both contract-settlement and H-future-price thresholds at $F(n)$; state the complexity ledger including the new resolution constraint $d(n) \gtrsim 1/\varepsilon$. Then Lemma 1 is pure sentence-LIC, Theorem 1 is its corollary, and the self-trust step is threshold-summed 4.12.2.

The thing I'd flag to double check before committing: the threshold-portfolio definition of the contract price means $A$'s "contract price" is whatever $A$'s threshold prices imply, and you're relying on $A$ (as a logical inductor over the threshold sentences) to price the thresholds coherently. Limit Coherence (4.1.2) gives you that the limiting threshold prices form a coherent distribution, so the implied contract price converges to a sensible value. But at finite $n$, the implied contract price $\frac{1}{d(n)}\sum_k A_n(\theta_{n,j,k})$ is just whatever it is — you don't get to assume it's well-behaved, you derive its behavior from Lemma 1. That's the right direction of inference, but make sure you never accidentally assume contract-price coherence as a hypothesis when it should be a conclusion.

Let me make the language and contract construction precise. I'll be careful about what's a symbol, what's a sentence, what's an axiom, and what's asserted by the deductive process — since the whole point of this version is that those distinctions do the work.

## The base setup

$\mathcal{L}$ is the language of $H$'s logical inductor — a language of propositional logic in the paper's sense (propositional variables standing in for prime sentences of some first-order theory, per the paper's §2 setup). $\mathcal{S}$ is its sentence set, $\Gamma$ its theory, $D_H$ a $\Gamma$-complete deductive process. Fix an effective enumeration $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)}, \dots$ of $\mathcal{S}$.

$H = (H_1, H_2, \dots)$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}$: each $H_t : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ is a computable rational pricing, and $H$ satisfies the LIC against $\mathcal{C}_H$.

One fact about $H$ we lean on: at each timestep $t$, $H_t$ is a *belief state* (finite support, rational values), so $H_t(P)$ is a rational whose denominator we can bound. Define

$$d(n) := \text{lcm of the denominators of } \{H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)}) : j \leq n\},$$

or any $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable common-denominator bound for the prices we care about at timestep $F(n)$. The point is just that $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ is an integer multiple of $1/d(n)$ for the relevant $j$, and $d(n)$ is computable in $\mathcal{C}_A$ by simulating $H$.

## The extended language $\mathcal{L}^+$

$\mathcal{L}^+$ extends $\mathcal{L}$ by adding, for each triple $(n, j, k)$ with $n \geq 1$, $j \geq 0$, and $1 \leq k \leq d(n)$, a new propositional atom

$$\theta_{n,j,k}.$$

These are fresh atoms — they are not built from the propositional variables of $\mathcal{L}$. So $\mathcal{S}^+ \supsetneq \mathcal{S}$: the sentences of $\mathcal{L}^+$ include all of $\mathcal{S}$ plus everything you can build from the $\theta$ atoms (and Boolean combinations mixing the two).

Intended reading of the atom: $\theta_{n,j,k}$ is "the contract for $P^{(j)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value $\geq k/d(n)$." But — and this is the crucial discipline — *that reading is not encoded in any axiom that references $H$*. The atom is just a fresh propositional symbol. Its intended meaning is enforced entirely by (i) the monotonicity axioms below, which make the bundle behave like a threshold encoding of *some* value, and (ii) the deductive process $D_A$, which later asserts *which* value by fixing the atoms' truth values.

I include $k$ from $1$ to $d(n)$ (not $0$); the "$\geq 0$" threshold is trivially true so needs no atom. The value read-off uses this convention below.

## The extended theory $\Gamma^+$

$$\Gamma^+ := \Gamma \;\cup\; \{\, \theta_{n,j,k} \to \theta_{n,j,k-1} \;:\; n \geq 1,\, j \geq 0,\, 2 \leq k \leq d(n) \,\}.$$

That is, $\Gamma$ plus the monotonicity schema: for a fixed contract $(n,j)$, the threshold atoms are nested — being above $k/d(n)$ implies being above $(k-1)/d(n)$.

This is the *entire* addition to the theory. Note what's absent: there is no axiom saying "$\theta_{n,j,k}$ iff $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)}) \geq k/d(n)$." Such an axiom would require $\Gamma^+$ to represent $H$, which is exactly what we're avoiding. The connection to $H$ is made by $D_A$ asserting truth values, not by $\Gamma^+$ proving equivalences.

$\Gamma^+$ is conservative over $\Gamma$ for $\mathcal{S}$-sentences: the new axioms only involve $\theta$ atoms, which don't appear in any $\mathcal{S}$-sentence, so $\Gamma^+ \vdash \phi \iff \Gamma \vdash \phi$ for $\phi \in \mathcal{S}$. (Standard conservativity of adding fresh atoms with axioms only among themselves.)

## Value of a contract in a world

A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W : \mathcal{S}^+ \to \{0,1\}$. For $W \in \mathrm{PC}(\Gamma^+)$ — propositionally consistent with $\Gamma^+$, hence respecting monotonicity — define the value of contract $(n,j)$ in $W$:

$$\text{val}_W(n,j) := \frac{1}{d(n)} \cdot \big|\{\, k : 1 \leq k \leq d(n),\ W(\theta_{n,j,k}) = 1 \,\}\big|.$$

By monotonicity, the set of true thresholds is a down-closed initial segment $\{1, \dots, m\}$ for some $0 \leq m \leq d(n)$, so $\text{val}_W(n,j) = m/d(n)$. The value is well-defined and lies in $\{0, 1/d(n), 2/d(n), \dots, 1\}$. No supremum gymnastics needed — the monotonicity axioms guarantee a clean initial-segment profile, so the value is just "how many thresholds are true, over $d(n)$."

This is the threshold analogue of the LUV value, but the uniqueness comes from monotonicity (cheap, syntactic) rather than from $\Gamma$-provable functional-ness of $H$ (expensive).

## The contract as a tradeable object

A market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ prices each atom: $A_t(\theta_{n,j,k}) \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$. Define the *contract* $C_n(P^{(j)})$ not as a new symbol to be priced, but as the affine combination of atoms

$$C_n(P^{(j)}) := \frac{1}{d(n)} \sum_{k=1}^{d(n)} \theta_{n,j,k}.$$

This is a $\mathbb{Q}$-combination of sentences in the paper's sense (an affine combination with rational coefficients). Its value in a world $W$ is, by linearity, exactly $\text{val}_W(n,j)$ — the read-off above. Its price according to $A_t$ is, again by linearity,

$$A_t(C_n(P^{(j)})) := \frac{1}{d(n)} \sum_{k=1}^{d(n)} A_t(\theta_{n,j,k}).$$

So the "contract price" $a_n = A_n(C_n(P_n))$ is a *derived* quantity — a rational combination of ordinary atom prices — not a primitive that needs its own market column or its own existence argument. $A$ is just an ordinary logical inductor over $\mathcal{L}^+$, pricing the atoms; the contract and its price are bookkeeping on top.

This is the cleanest part of the threshold approach: a "contract" is literally an affine combination of sentences, which is an object the LI framework already handles natively (trades *are* affine combinations of sentences). So trading the contract is trading the corresponding bundle, and no new machinery is introduced.

## The deductive process $D_A$ asserts values

$D_A$ is a computable nested sequence of finite sets of $\mathcal{L}^+$-sentences, $\Gamma^+$-complete in the limit, defined so that it eventually pins each contract to its intended value.

Construction. Let $\sigma(n)$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable settlement-time function (the time by which $D_A$ has surfaced contract $(n,j)$'s value — at minimum large enough to have simulated $H$ to step $F(n)$ and run the deductive enumeration; you can take $\sigma(n)$ to be any convenient $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable bound $\geq$ the cost of that simulation). At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains:

1. $D_H^t$ (so $D_A$ extends $H$'s process on $\mathcal{S}$-sentences);
2. the monotonicity axioms for all $(n,j,k)$ with $n, j \leq t$ (finitely many);
3. for each $(n,j)$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$ and $j \leq t$: the literals fixing the threshold profile to the true value $q^*_{n,j} := H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$. Writing $m^*_{n,j} := q^*_{n,j} \cdot d(n) \in \{0,\dots,d(n)\}$, these literals are
$$\theta_{n,j,k} \ \text{for } k \leq m^*_{n,j}, \qquad \neg\,\theta_{n,j,k} \ \text{for } k > m^*_{n,j}.$$

Finiteness per timestep: items 2 and 3 range over $(n,j)$ with $n,j \leq t$ and $k \leq d(n)$, finitely many. ✓

Computability: computing $q^*_{n,j}$ and $d(n)$ requires simulating $H$ to step $F(n)$, cost $\mathrm{poly}(F(n)) = 2^{O(n)} \in \mathcal{C}_A$. So $D_A$ is computable. ✓

Effect: for $t \geq \sigma(n)$ (and $j \leq t$), every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ has $W(\theta_{n,j,k}) = \mathbb{1}[k \leq m^*_{n,j}]$, hence $\text{val}_W(n,j) = q^*_{n,j} = H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ exactly. The contract is propositionally pinned to its intended value. This is what Lemma 1's pinning hypothesis requires — and it's achieved by ordinary literal assertion in a computable deductive process, with no theory-level representation of $H$.

## What $A$ is, precisely

$A = (A_1, A_2, \dots)$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ (pricing all $\mathcal{S}^+$-sentences, in particular the atoms $\theta_{n,j,k}$) satisfying the LIC against $\mathcal{C}_A$-traders relative to $D_A$. Existence: the standard LIA construction over the language $\mathcal{L}^+$ and process $D_A$, with the trader enumeration taken over $\mathcal{C}_A$ (exp-time) rather than poly-time. No LUV-market existence result is needed because $A$ prices ordinary sentences; the contracts are affine combinations, not new primitives.

The contract price $a_n = A_n(C_n(P_n)) = \frac{1}{d(n)}\sum_k A_n(\theta_{n,j(n),k})$ where $j(n)$ is the index with $P_n = P^{(j(n))}$. Since $A$'s atom prices are rational, $a_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$, so it can be published exactly to $D_H^+$.

## How Lemma 1 sees all this

Lemma 1, stated at full generality: for any e.c. sequence of sentences $(\psi_m)$ in $\mathcal{S}^+$ with $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable truth values $v_m \in \{0,1\}$ eventually pinned by $D_A$ at $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable times, $A_m(\psi_m) - v_m \to 0$.

Apply it to the doubly-indexed family of *threshold atoms* $\psi_{(n,k)} := \theta_{n,j(n),k}$ with target values $v_{(n,k)} := \mathbb{1}[k \leq m^*_{n,j(n)}]$. The capacity-1 trader gives $A_n(\theta_{n,j(n),k}) \to v_{(n,k)}$ uniformly over the family.

Then the contract-price convergence follows by averaging:
$$|a_n - Y_n| = \Big|\tfrac{1}{d(n)}\textstyle\sum_k A_n(\theta_{n,j(n),k}) - \tfrac{1}{d(n)}\sum_k v_{(n,k)}\Big| \leq \tfrac{1}{d(n)}\sum_k |A_n(\theta_{n,j(n),k}) - v_{(n,k)}|,$$
the average threshold error, which $\to 0$ since the threshold errors are uniformly small. The $1/d(n)$ normalization makes this an average, not a sum, so growing $d(n)$ doesn't hurt. That's Theorem 1.

## The one piece of fine print

The atom $\theta_{n,j,k}$ exists in $\mathcal{L}^+$ only for $k \leq d(n)$, and $d(n)$ is itself defined via $H$'s prices at step $F(n)$. So the *language* $\mathcal{L}^+$ depends on $H$ through $d(\cdot)$. This is fine — $\mathcal{L}^+$ is still an effectively presented language, since $d(n)$ is computable — but you should note it: the language is computably presented relative to $H$. If you'd rather not have the language depend on $H$, you can instead fix a single resolution growth rate independent of $H$ (say $d(n) = 2^n$, atoms $\theta_{n,j,k}$ for $k \leq 2^n$) and have $D_A$ assert the *nearest* threshold profile to $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$, accepting a rounding error of $\leq 2^{-n}$ in the pinned value. The rounding error vanishes, so Theorem 1's conclusion is unaffected, and the language is now $H$-independent and cleaner to present. I'd take this version — fix $d(n) = 2^n$ (or any explicit $H$-independent rate with $1/d(n) \to 0$ fast enough to beat the arbitrage gap), assert nearest-threshold profiles, absorb the rounding into the $o(1)$.

That removes the last place $H$ leaked into the foundational objects. The language and theory are now fixed and $H$-independent; all the $H$-dependence lives in $D_A$'s assertions, which is exactly where it belongs.

We want to collapse that bundle of truth values into a single number in $[0,1]$: the value of the contract in that world. The formula is the recipe for doing that.

## Reading the formula

$$\text{val}_W(n,j) := \frac{1}{d(n)} \cdot \big|\{\, k : 1 \leq k \leq d(n),\ W(\theta_{n,j,k}) = 1 \,\}\big|.$$

The inner part, $\{k : 1 \leq k \leq d(n),\ W(\theta_{n,j,k}) = 1\}$, is the **set of indices $k$ whose atom is true in $W$**. The vertical bars $|\cdots|$ around it mean **the size of that set** — how many atoms are true. Then you multiply by $\frac{1}{d(n)}$.

So in words: **count how many of the contract's threshold atoms are true, then divide by the total number of thresholds.** It's a fraction — (true atoms) / (total atoms).

## Why this gives the right value

Remember the intended meaning of each atom: $\theta_{n,j,k}$ says "the contract's value is at least $k/d(n)$." So the atoms are a thermometer. $\theta_{n,j,1}$ is the lowest mark ("value $\geq 1/d(n)$"), $\theta_{n,j,2}$ the next ("value $\geq 2/d(n)$"), up to $\theta_{n,j,d(n)}$ at the top ("value $\geq 1$").

The monotonicity axiom — $\theta_{n,j,k} \to \theta_{n,j,k-1}$ — forces the thermometer to fill from the bottom. If "value $\geq 5/d(n)$" is true, then "value $\geq 4/d(n)$", "$\geq 3/d(n)$", etc. are all true too. So in any consistent world, the true atoms form an unbroken initial run: $\theta_{n,j,1}, \dots, \theta_{n,j,m}$ are true and $\theta_{n,j,m+1}, \dots$ are false, for some cutoff $m$.

That cutoff $m$ is exactly "how high the thermometer reads." And $m$ is exactly the *count* of true atoms (since they're the first $m$ of them). So:

$$\text{val}_W(n,j) = \frac{m}{d(n)},$$

which is what the formula computes. The mercury rose to the $m$-th mark, the value is $m/d(n)$.

## A concrete example

Take $d(n) = 4$, so the contract has atoms $\theta_{n,j,1}, \theta_{n,j,2}, \theta_{n,j,3}, \theta_{n,j,4}$, encoding the thresholds $\geq 1/4, \geq 2/4, \geq 3/4, \geq 4/4$.

Suppose in world $W$ the value is meant to be $3/4$. Then a consistent $W$ sets:
- $\theta_{n,j,1}$ ("$\geq 1/4$") = **true** ✓
- $\theta_{n,j,2}$ ("$\geq 2/4$") = **true** ✓
- $\theta_{n,j,3}$ ("$\geq 3/4$") = **true** ✓
- $\theta_{n,j,4}$ ("$\geq 4/4$") = **false** ✗

Three atoms are true. The formula gives $\frac{1}{4} \cdot 3 = 3/4$. Correct.

And monotonicity rules out nonsense like (true, false, true, false), which wouldn't correspond to any single value — there'd be no clean cutoff. Monotonicity guarantees the true atoms are always a bottom-up run, so the count always corresponds to a genuine threshold reading.

## Why it's built this way rather than just "use a number"

You might ask: why not just have one symbol that directly holds the value $3/4$? Because the LI framework deals in propositional sentences that worlds make true or false. It doesn't have a native "this symbol equals $0.75$" object — that's what the LUV machinery in the paper provides, at the cost (as we discussed) of needing $\Gamma$ to prove the value is unique. The threshold trick gets the same effect — a real value emerging from the framework — using only ordinary true/false sentences plus the cheap monotonicity axioms. The value isn't stored directly; it's *encoded* in how many threshold-sentences come out true.

So the formula is the decoder: it takes the raw true/false pattern and turns it back into the number the pattern was encoding.

It's the property that lets you compose a $\mathcal{C}_A$ computation with a polynomial amount of extra work and stay in $\mathcal{C}_A$. Let me be precise about what "extra work" means here, because there are two slightly different versions and you want the right one.

A complexity class (as a class of *functions* computable within some time bound, which is how you're using it — "traders computable in $\mathcal{C}_A$") is **closed under polynomial overhead** if: whenever $f$ is computable within the class's time bound $T(n)$, then any function computable in time $\mathrm{poly}(n) \cdot T(n)$ — or that makes $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ calls to $f$ plus $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ additional steps — is also within the class.

For EXP specifically: a function is in EXP if it's computable in time $2^{n^c}$ for some constant $c$. Take such an $f$ with bound $2^{n^c}$. Now do $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ work on top — say $n^a$ calls to $f$ plus $n^b$ extra steps. Total time is at most $n^a \cdot 2^{n^c} + n^b \leq 2^{n^{c'}}$ for a slightly larger constant $c'$ (since $n^a \cdot 2^{n^c} = 2^{n^c + a\log n} \leq 2^{n^{c+1}}$ for large $n$). So you're still in EXP. The exponential bound swallows the polynomial factor by bumping the constant in the exponent. That's the closure.

Why your trader needs it, concretely. The capacity-1 trader on day $n$ has to:
- compute the target value $H_{F(n)}(P_n)$ — this is the base $\mathcal{C}_A$ computation, cost $T(n) = 2^{O(n)}$;
- determine its own current state $U_n$ (am I holding a position?), which requires recovering what it did on prior days — and since the trader has no persistent memory in the LI framework, it recomputes its history by re-simulating its day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$, each of which costs another $T(i) \leq T(n)$.

So the day-$n$ cost is roughly $n \cdot T(n)$ — a factor of $n$ (polynomial) on top of the base cost $T(n)$. Closure under polynomial overhead is exactly the statement that $n \cdot T(n)$ is still within the class, so the trader is a legitimate $\mathcal{C}_A$-trader. Without closure, the self-simulation could in principle kick the trader out of $\mathcal{C}_A$, and it wouldn't be a valid trader to use against $A$ in the exploitation argument.

The reason I'd state it as an explicit hypothesis rather than just saying "EXP" is that it isolates *what* about EXP you're using. You're not using anything specific about exponential time — you're only using that the class absorbs the polynomial self-simulation overhead. Stating it abstractly ("$\mathcal{C}_A$ closed under polynomial overhead") makes the lemma apply to any such class and makes clear that the result isn't an artifact of picking EXP. P is also closed under polynomial overhead, incidentally — the issue with P was never closure, it was that P isn't rich enough to compute $H_{F(n)}$ in the first place when $F$ is super-polynomial. So the two requirements on $\mathcal{C}_A$ are genuinely separate: rich enough to simulate $H$ to depth $F$ (this is what rules out P for large $F$), and closed under poly overhead (this is what makes the self-simulating trader legal, satisfied by most classes including both P and EXP).

One precision note if you want to state it carefully: "closed under polynomial overhead" should be stated relative to $n$, the trader's day index, not relative to the size of $H_{F(n)}$'s output or anything else. The overhead is $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ many re-simulations. So the clean statement is: *if $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then any function computable with $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ many oracle calls to $g$ and $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ additional steps is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable.* That's the exact form the trader construction needs.

Consider a logical inductor $H = (H_1, H_2,\ldots)$ over language $\mathcal{L}$ with sentence set $\mathcal{S}$, theory $\Gamma$, and $\Gamma$-complete deductive process $D_H$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in the complexity class $\mathcal{C}_H$. Fix an effective enumeration $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)},\ldots$ of the sentences of $\mathcal{S}$. Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function $F: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$. Also choose a non-decreasing, computable ``resolution" function $d: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such that $\frac{1}{d(n)}\to 0$.
For each triple $(n,j,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ j\geq 0,\ 1\leq k\leq d(n)$, define a new propositional symbol $\theta_{n,j,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(j)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{d(n)}$." Define a new language $\mathcal{L}^+$ that extends $\mathcal{L}$ with all the $\theta$ symbols, and define $\mathcal{S}^+$ to be the sentence set over $\mathcal{L}^+$. Define the theory $\Gamma^+$ as $\Gamma \cup \{\theta_{n,j,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,j,k-1}: n\geq 1, j\geq 0, 2\leq k\leq d(n)\}$, in other words extend $\Gamma$ with an axiom schema of monotonicity that informally says ``being above $\frac{k}{d(n)}$ implies being above $\frac{k-1}{d(n)}$." 
A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with $\Gamma^+$, define the value of a contract $(n,j)$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n,j) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq d(n),\ W(\theta_{n,j,k})=1\}}{d(n)}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq d(n)$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n,j)=\frac{m}{d(n)}$. 
Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $(n,j) \mapsto H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ for $j\leq n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n)\geq n$ and $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n)$ steps for $j\leq n$.

Without that, the theorems are vacuously true (statements about an empty class of objects), and a careful reader — Demski certainly — will ask "does such an $A$ exist, or have you proved theorems about nothing?" This is exactly the role Theorem 3.6.1 / the LIA construction plays in the original paper: it guarantees the class of logical inductors is nonempty so that all the "for any logical inductor" theorems aren't vacuous.

The strength of the result is that *any* LI over $D_A$ tracks $H$, regardless of how it's built. This is the part of $D_A$ that does the actual work — it's where the deductive process "settles" each contract by writing down the truth values of its threshold atoms. Let me walk through what it's doing and what to watch for, translating to your single-index ($j = n$) convention as I go.

In your Option B notation, this becomes: for each $n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$, let $q^*_n := H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ be the true value the contract should pay, let $m^*_n$ be the integer in $\{0, \dots, d(n)\}$ minimizing $|m/d(n) - q^*_n|$, and assert $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k \leq m^*_n$ and $\neg\theta_{n,k}$ for $k > m^*_n$.

## What it accomplishes

It converts a real number, $q^*_n = H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, into a pattern of truth-value assertions over the threshold atoms. The value $q^*_n$ is some rational in $[0,1]$; you can't assert "the contract equals $0.617$" directly because there's no atom that says that. What you have are the threshold atoms $\theta_{n,k}$ = "value $\geq k/d(n)$." So you encode $q^*_n$ by saying which thresholds it clears: all the ones at or below it (assert those true), none of the ones above (assert those false). That fills the thermometer up to level $m^*_n$ and caps it there.

The rounding to $m^*_n$ is forced because the grid is discrete. $q^*_n$ might be $0.617$ while the grid (say $d(n) = 100$) only has marks at $0.61, 0.62, \dots$. You pick the nearest mark — $m^*_n = 62$, value $0.62$ — and assert that profile. The error is at most half a grid step, $\leq 1/(2d(n))$, which vanishes since $1/d(n) \to 0$.

## What "assert" means here, precisely

The literals $\theta_{n,k}$ (for $k \leq m^*_n$) and $\neg\theta_{n,k}$ (for $k > m^*_n$) are added to $D_A^t$ as elements of the deductive set. Recall a deductive process is a nested sequence of finite sets of sentences, interpreted as "what's been proven/revealed by time $t$." So adding these literals means: by time $t$, $D_A$ has revealed exactly which thresholds hold. Any world $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ must respect every sentence in $D_A^t$, so $W$ must set $\theta_{n,k} = 1$ for $k \leq m^*_n$ and $\theta_{n,k} = 0$ for $k > m^*_n$. There's no freedom left — the contract's threshold profile is pinned, and therefore $\text{val}_W(n) = m^*_n/d(n)$ for every plausible world.

That total pinning is the payoff: before time $\sigma(n)$, worlds could disagree about the contract's value (the atoms are unconstrained, except by monotonicity); after $\sigma(n)$, all plausible worlds agree exactly. This is the "settlement" event that Lemma 1's pinning hypothesis requires.

## Things to get right

**Consistency with monotonicity.** The asserted profile (true up to $m^*_n$, false above) is automatically monotone — it's an initial segment, exactly the shape the monotonicity axioms demand. So the literals you assert never contradict $\Gamma^+$. Worth a half-sentence noting this: the nearest-grid-point profile is consistent with the monotonicity schema, so $D_A^t$ stays consistent. (If you ever asserted a non-initial-segment pattern, you'd contradict the axioms and $\mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ would be empty — a disaster. Nearest-grid-point rounding can't do that, since it always produces an initial segment, but it's the kind of thing worth a clause confirming.)

**The "closest" can tie.** If $q^*_n$ lands exactly halfway between two grid points, "the integer with $m/d(n)$ closest to $q^*_n$" is ambiguous — two integers tie. Break it deterministically (round down, say, or round to even) so $m^*_n$ is a well-defined function. Otherwise $D_A$ isn't well-defined as a computable function. One clause: "ties broken by rounding down." Trivial but needed for $D_A$ to be a function.

**Computability of the profile.** To assert the profile, $D_A$ computes $q^*_n$ (needs simulating $H$ to step $F(n)$, which $\sigma(n)$ guarantees is doable in $\mathcal{C}_A$), computes $d(n)$ (computable by assumption), and computes $m^*_n$ (one division and rounding — trivial). So the whole profile is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, which is what makes $D_A$ a computable deductive process. This is the place where the $d$-computability point we discussed actually cashes out: you need $d(n)$ to form $m^*_n$, so if $d$ weren't computable you couldn't assert the profile. Since you assumed $d$ computable, fine — just note that the profile computation uses both $q^*_n$ and $d(n)$.

**Finiteness.** At each $t$, the contracts being settled are those with $\sigma(n) \leq t$. Since $\sigma(n) \geq n$, only finitely many $n$ satisfy $\sigma(n) \leq t$ (at most $n \leq t$). Each contributes $d(n)$ literals. So finitely many literals per timestep. ✓ Note the diagonal convention helped here — you're settling one contract per eligible $n$, not a grid of $(n,j)$ pairs.

**The "value within $1/d(n)$" statement for Lemma 1.** State the consequence explicitly as the deliverable: for $t \geq \sigma(n)$, every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ has $\text{val}_W(n) = m^*_n/d(n)$, and $|m^*_n/d(n) - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})| \leq 1/(2d(n)) \to 0$. The first equality is exact pinning; the second is the vanishing rounding. Lemma 1 will use the exact pinning to a known computable value $m^*_n/d(n)$, and Theorem 1 will use the rounding bound to convert "tracks $m^*_n/d(n)$" into "tracks $H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$."

## One subtlety worth thinking about

There's a question of whether $D_A$ should also, before settlement, assert *anything* about the contract — or leave it totally free until $\sigma(n)$. In your construction, before $\sigma(n)$ the only constraints on $\theta_{n,k}$ are the monotonicity axioms (which are in $D_A^t$ once $n \leq t$). So pre-settlement, plausible worlds can assign the contract any monotone profile, i.e., any value in $\{0, 1/d(n), \dots, 1\}$. That's the right behavior — the contract's value is genuinely undetermined until settlement, and the market $A$ has to price it under that uncertainty. The trader in Lemma 1 exploits the gap between $A$'s price and the eventually-revealed value. So leaving it free pre-settlement is correct and intended; don't assert anything beyond monotonicity before $\sigma(n)$.

Worth confirming this ordering holds: monotonicity at $t \geq n$, settlement at $t \geq \sigma(n) \geq n$, so axioms never arrive after settlement. ✓

Roughly: "At time $t$, for each $n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$, $D_A^t$ contains the following literals settling contract $n$. The relationship you need between them is a *computability/timing* constraint: by $A$'s time $\sigma(n)$, the value $H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ must have been computed. To compute $H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, you simulate $H$ out to its timestep $F(n)$. That simulation costs roughly $\text{poly}(F(n))$ elementary steps (sum over $H$'s timesteps up to $F(n)$, each a $\mathcal{C}_H$ computation). So the requirement "$H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ computable within $\sigma(n)$ steps" forces

$$\sigma(n) \gtrsim \text{poly}(F(n)).$$

In the running example, $F(n) = 2^n$, so $\sigma(n) \gtrsim \text{poly}(2^n) = 2^{O(n)}$. So $\sigma$ grows at least like the simulation cost of $F$. This is the explicit mathematical link: **$\sigma$ must dominate the cost of evaluating $H$ at depth $F$.** $\sigma(n) \geq c \cdot \text{poly}(F(n))$ for whatever polynomial bounds $H$'s per-step cost.

That's the relationship. It's a lower bound on $\sigma$ in terms of $F$ (and $H$'s complexity). You don't need an upper bound — $\sigma$ can be as large as you like, settlement can be lazy — you just need it at least large enough to have done the computation.

I'll give the general version (an arbitrary e.c. family of threshold-style sentences with computable, eventually-pinned values) since that's what makes it serve both the contract-tracking use and the averaging step cleanly, and then note how it specializes.

Let me state it at the atom level first, because that's where the capacity-1 argument actually runs, and the contract-level conclusion follows by averaging.

```
\begin{lemma}[Computable Tracking]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let $(\psi_i)_{i \geq 1}$ be a sequence of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ and $(v_i)_{i \geq 1}$ a sequence of values $v_i \in \{0,1\}$ 
such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $i \mapsto \psi_i$ is computable, and the map $i \mapsto v_i$ 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to 
        \mathbb{N}^+$ such that for every $t \geq \tau(i)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, we have $W(\psi_i) = v_i$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $P_i(\psi_i) - v_i \to 0$ as $i \to \infty$.
\end{lemma}
```

A few notes on why it's phrased this way, and what each hypothesis is buying:

The sentences are indexed by a single index $i$, and the values $v_i$ are $\{0,1\}$ — this is the *atom-level* statement, where each $\psi_i$ is a threshold atom and $v_i$ is its settled truth value. You apply it to the family of all threshold atoms $\theta_{n,j,k}$ under some computable bijection $i \leftrightarrow (n,j,k)$, with $v_i$ the settled truth value $\mathbb{1}[k \leq m^*_{n,j}]$ and $\tau(i) = \sigma(n,j)$.

Hypothesis 1 splits the computability: the *sentence* map only needs to be computable (you're just naming which atom), but the *value* map $i \mapsto v_i$ must be in $\mathcal{C}$, because the exploiting trader has to compute the target value within its budget. This is the place $\mathcal{C}_A$-computability of $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ enters — $v_i$ for a threshold atom is $\mathbb{1}[k \leq m^*_{n,j}]$, and computing $m^*_{n,j}$ needs the $H$-simulation.

Hypothesis 2 is the pinning condition, stated exactly as your $D_A$ delivers it: past the settlement time $\tau(i)$, every plausible world agrees that $\psi_i = v_i$. The $\mathcal{C}$-computability of $\tau$ matters because the trader uses it to track which positions have resolved (the capacity-1 bookkeeping).

The conclusion $P_i(\psi_i) - v_i \to 0$ is the asymptotic tracking of each atom's settled value.

The closure-under-polynomial-overhead hypothesis on $\mathcal{C}$ is what licenses the capacity-1 trader to reconstruct its own state by self-simulation within $\mathcal{C}$, as we discussed.

Now the corollary you actually want for Theorem 1, derived by averaging:

```
\begin{corollary}[Contract Tracking]
Under the setup above, for the contracts $C_{n,j}$ settled by $D_A$, 
\[
A_n(C_{n,j}) - H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)}) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
\]
(along any $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable choice of $j = j(n)$ with the contract 
settled by an appropriate time).
\end{corollary}
```

The corollary's proof is the averaging step: apply the Lemma to the threshold atoms $\theta_{n,j,k}$ ($1 \leq k \leq n$) of contract $(n,j)$, giving $A_n(\theta_{n,j,k}) \to v_{n,j,k} = \mathbb{1}[k \leq m^*_{n,j}]$ uniformly in $k$; then
$$|A_n(C_{n,j}) - \text{val}(n,j)| = \Big|\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_k A_n(\theta_{n,j,k}) - \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_k v_{n,j,k}\Big| \leq \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_k |A_n(\theta_{n,j,k}) - v_{n,j,k}| \to 0,$$
the *average* atom error; finally the settled value $m^*_{n,j}/n$ differs from $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ by $\leq 1/(2n) \to 0$, so the two vanishing terms combine.

Two things to decide before you commit the statement:

First, **the uniformity question in the corollary.** The averaging needs the atom errors $|A_n(\theta_{n,j,k}) - v_{n,j,k}|$ to be small *uniformly across the $n$ thresholds of a given contract*, as $n \to \infty$. The Lemma as stated is about a single sequence $(\psi_i)$, so to get uniform-over-$k$ control you apply it to the *doubly-indexed* family flattened into one sequence, and then you need the convergence to be uniform over the $k$-block for each $n$. This is the one spot where you should be careful: a single-sequence convergence $P_i(\psi_i) - v_i \to 0$ does *not* automatically give "uniform over the $k$-block at index $n$" unless the flattening interleaves the blocks appropriately. The clean fix is to state the Lemma's conclusion as $\sup$ over the relevant block, or to note that the averaging only needs the *Cesàro/average* error to vanish, which the flat convergence does give (the average of a convergent-to-0 sequence over a window vanishes). Actually the average over the $k$-block is exactly an average of terms each $\to 0$, and since they're uniformly bounded by 1, the block-average $\to 0$ by a standard argument — but you should make sure the *blocks* are positioned late enough in the flat sequence that their terms are individually small. Worth one sentence of care in the corollary proof; it's the technical heart and the place a referee looks.

Second, **whether to state the Lemma for $\{0,1\}$ values or general $[0,1]$ values.** I've stated it for $v_i \in \{0,1\}$ because the threshold atoms settle to truth values. That's all you need. You *could* state it for $v_i \in [0,1] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ to make it more general (and then the contract tracking is a direct instance rather than going through atoms), but then you're back to needing real-valued shares, which is exactly the LUV complication you avoided. So keep it $\{0,1\}$ — the whole point of the threshold encoding is that the Lemma only ever sees 0/1-valued sentences, and the real-valued contract tracking emerges from averaging. Stating it for $\{0,1\}$ is the honest reflection of what the threshold construction bought you.

So: Lemma at the atom level with $\{0,1\}$ values and a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement time, contract tracking as a corollary via averaging, with care taken in the corollary that the block-average error vanishes. That's the precise statement, and it's the version whose proof is the capacity-1 argument you've already essentially got.

Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function $F: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$.

For each triple $(n,j,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ j\geq 0,\ 1\leq k\leq n$, define a new propositional ``threshold" symbol $\theta_{n,j,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(j)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{n}$." A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with the monotonicity axioms, define the value of contract $(n,j)$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n,j) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq n,\ W(\theta_{n,j,k})=1\}}{n}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n,j)=\frac{m}{n}$. 

Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $(n,j) \mapsto H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $(n,j)$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n+j)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n+j)$ additional elementary steps. Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n,j)\geq \max(n,j+1)$ and $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n,j)$ steps.

Define a deductive process $D_A$ as follows. At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_A$ extends $D_H$
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,j,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,j,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$, $j\leq t$, and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each pair $(n,j)$ with $\sigma(n,j)\leq t$, let $m_{n,j}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,j,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n,j}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,j,k}$ for $k>m_{n,j}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract $(n,j)$ translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every $t\geq \sigma(n,j)$ and every $W$ consistent with $D^t_A$, $\text{val}_W(n,j)=\frac{m^*_{n,j}}{n}$, which differs from $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ by at most $\frac{1}{2n}$. Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each $D_A^t$ is finite. $D_A$ is also computable since $D_H$ is a computable deductive process and each $m^*_{n,j}$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable (because $H_{F(n)}(P^{(j)})$ is computable within $\sigma(n,j)$ steps.) Finally, note that each $D_A^t$ is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from $\mathcal{S}$. Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to $D_A$ is well-posed.

For each $n \geq 1$ and $j \geq 0$, define the contract $C_{n,j}$ as the affine combination $C_{n,j} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,j,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n,j}) = \text{val}_W(n,j)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n,j}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,j,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

\begin{lemma}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values 
        $v_n \in [0,1] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ and a $\mathcal{C}$-computable 
        settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
For every $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable choice of indices $j(n)$,
\[
A_n\bigl(C_{n,j(n)}\bigr) - H_{F(n)}\bigl(P^{(j(n))}\bigr) \to 0 
\quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

Define a deductive process $D_A$ as follows. At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_A$ extends $D_H$
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract $n$ translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every $t\geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W$ consistent with $D^t_A$, $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}$, which differs from $H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ by at most $\frac{1}{2n}$. Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each $D_A^t$ is finite. $D_A$ is also computable since $D_H$ is a computable deductive process and each $m^*_{n}$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable (because $H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is computable within $\sigma(n)$ steps.) Finally, note that each $D_A^t$ is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from $\mathcal{S}$. Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to $D_A$ is well-posed. 

Define $A = (A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to the deductive process $D_A$. A logical inductor $A$ must exist by the same construction as in Garrabrant et al. $\S5$ with the language, deductive process, and trader complexity class substituted.

For each $n \geq 1$, define the contract $C_{n}$ as the affine combination $C_{n} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n}) = \text{val}_W(n)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

\begin{lemma}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values 
        $v_n \in [0,1] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ and a $\mathcal{C}$-computable 
        settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

```

\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma]
Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is
some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely
many $n$. At least one of the two one-sided conditions
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' throughout.

So assume $P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$; call these the
\emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
For each $n$, define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the
day-$n$ price $P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, $\rho_n$ is a continuous function of the market price,
and $\rho_n = 1$ at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable
and $X_n$ is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with
$q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within
$\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ that holds at most one open position at any time. Say the
trader is \emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day
$i < n$ with $\tau(i) > n$ (i.e.\ every previously opened position has already
settled). On day $n$, if the trader is available, it sells $\rho_n$ units of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price; otherwise it trades nothing. Concretely, the
day-$n$ trade is
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr)
\qquad\text{if available, and } T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ denotes selling one unit of the affine combination $X_n$
at price $P_n(X_n)$ (receiving the price in cash, owing one unit of $X_n$).

The trade coefficient $\rho_n$ is a continuous function of the day-$n$ price,
and the availability flag depends only on the deductive process and the
trader's own past behavior, not on the day-$n$ price; hence $T_n$ is a valid
trading strategy. To compute $T_n$ the trader must evaluate $\rho_n$ and
reconstruct its availability, the latter requiring it to recompute its day-$i$
decisions for $i < n$. This is $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the
$\mathcal{C}$-computable data $(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ plus $\operatorname{poly}(n)$
further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead, $T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position
$T_i = \rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
because the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Therefore for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
We claim the trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Suppose not;
then beyond some time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time. But
the trader is unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at
some $i < n$ with $\tau(i) > n$; since $\tau(i)$ is finite, that position
settles by time $\tau(i)$, after which the trader is available again. As trigger
times are infinite, some trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader
becomes available at a trigger time after $N$, a contradiction. Hence the trader
opens a position with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times.

Each such position, once settled, contributes
\[
W(T_n) = P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon
\]
for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ with $t \geq \tau(n)$. Let $R(t)$ be the
number of positions opened by the trader that have settled by time $t$; by the
previous paragraph $R(t) \to \infty$. Combining with the downside bound, for
$t$ large and $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq \varepsilon\, R(t) - 1 \to \infty.
\]

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but not bounded
above. Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical
induction criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}
```

\]

Claude writes:

In your setup, (X_n) is an affine combination:

## 3. The availability/reconstruction step should mention prior market prices are part of the trader’s input/history

It depends on **past prices too**, because whether the trader opened a position at day (i) depended on (P_i(X_i)). That is okay, but the sentence should be:

This matters for continuity: dependence on past prices can be discontinuous without violating the day-(n) continuity condition, because on day (n) those are already fixed historical data.
