\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma]
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}
```

A_n(C_n) - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0. \qedhere

$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}

Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$

$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with

day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing

\[

\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of

$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,

product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.

availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[

\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has

$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position

\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m}{n}$.

This coupled construction is made well-founded with a timing delay: $H^+$ receives a quote for the prices of $A$ at the following time step.



Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable [more detail on this assumption]. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n) > F(n)$ and also that $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n)$ steps.

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_A$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract \(n\) translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every \(t\geq \sigma(n)\) and every \(W\) consistent with \(D^t_A\), \(\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}\), which differs from \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) by at most \(\frac{1}{2n}\). Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each \(D_A^t\) is finite. \(D_A\) is also computable as part of the simultaneous construction: \(D_H\) is a computable deductive process, and each \(m^*_{n}\) is computable because \(\sigma(n)>F(n)\), so the value \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) has already been computed by the time the settlement is inserted. Finally, note that each \(D_A^t\) is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from \(\mathcal{S}\). Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to \(D_A\) is well-posed.

Define $A = (A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to the deductive process $D_A$. A logical inductor $A$ must exist by the same construction as in Garrabrant et al. $\S5$ with the language, deductive process, and trader complexity class substituted.

For each $n \geq 1$, define the contract $C_{n}$ as the affine combination $C_{n} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n}) = \text{val}_W(n)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

\begin{lemma}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values 
        $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ and a $\mathcal{C}$-computable 
        settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable since $m_n^*$ is, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. For hypothesis~2: by the construction of $D_A$, for
every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have
$\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\ $W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since
$C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is an average of $n$ values
$W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have $W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at
every $t$, independently of consistency.

The Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) - \tfrac{m_n^*}{n} \to 0$. By the construction of
$D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n} \to
0$. Combining, we have $A_n(C_n) - H_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0.$ \qedhere
\end{proof}

\end{document}

\begin{lemma}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values

        settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus

$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the

\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}

be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$,

  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values

        W(X_n) = v_n;

        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the

its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination

the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is

every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have

The Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) - \tfrac{m_n^*}{n} \to 0$. By the construction of

\end{proof}

be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]

\]

\begin{proof}

\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}

$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing

\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of

availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is

\[

unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after

\]

\begin{theorem}[Deference]
Under the hypotheses of the Calibration Lemma, $H^+$'s judgment of $P^{(n)}$ 
defers to $A$'s quote. In product form,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\, G_n\bigr] 
- a_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[G_n\bigr] \to 0,
\]
and consequently, conditional on $A$ quoting in the bin,
\[
H^+_{n+1}\bigl(P^{(n)} \,\big|\, a_n \in [r,s]\bigr) \in [\,r - \delta,\; 
s + \delta\,] \quad \text{asymptotically.}
\]
\end{theorem}

$H^+$, whose own future price of $P^{(n)}$ is $Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, 
weighting by the observed constant $G_n$ gives
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] 
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n] + o(1).
\]
By the Calibration Lemma, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] = 
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] + o(1)$. As $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants at 
time $n+1$, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$,

$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)} \mid a_n \in [r,s]) \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]$ asymptotically.
\end{proof}

Since the enumeration can be freely chosen, take $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)}, \ldots$ to be the sequence of propositions of interest. Tying contract $n$ to $P^{(n)}$ therefore loses no generality, as any efficiently computable sequence of propositions can be studied by enumerating it in this way.

For each pair $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ 1\leq k\leq n$, define a new propositional ``threshold" symbol $\theta_{n,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{n}$." Define a new language $\mathcal{L}^+$ that extends $\mathcal{L}$ with all the $\theta$ symbols, and define $\mathcal{S}^+$ to be the sentence set over $\mathcal{L}^+$. 

Define a schema $\{\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}: n\geq 1,\ 2\leq k\leq n\}$ of ``monotonicity" axioms. Each axiom informally says that ``clearing the $\frac{k}{n}$ threshold implies clearing the $\frac{k-1}{n}$ threshold." 

A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with the monotonicity axioms, define the value of contract $n$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq n,\ W(\theta_{n,k})=1\}}{n}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m}{n}$. 

The following simultaneously defines a coupled pair $A$ that represents an AI reasoner and $H^+$ that represents the human reasoner augmented with the ability to observe published quotes of $A$'s outputs. These two mutually referential inductors are defined by recursion on time. Two timing delays to ensure this recursion's well-foundedness: $H^+$ receives the quotes from $A$ one time step after they are posted, and $A$'s contracts settle only at a time step greater than $F(n)$, after which the referenced future price $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ already exists.

Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable [more detail on this assumption]. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n) > F(n)$ and also that $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n)$ steps.

Define a deductive process $D_A$ as follows. At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_A$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract \(n\) translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every \(t\geq \sigma(n)\) and every \(W\) consistent with \(D^t_A\), \(\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}\), which differs from \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) by at most \(\frac{1}{2n}\). Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each \(D_A^t\) is finite. \(D_A\) is also computable as part of the simultaneous construction: \(D_H\) is a computable deductive process, and each \(m^*_{n}\) is computable because \(\sigma(n)>F(n)\), so the value \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) has already been computed by the time the settlement is inserted. Finally, note that each \(D_A^t\) is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from \(\mathcal{S}\). Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to \(D_A\) is well-posed.

Define $A = (A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to the deductive process $D_A$. A logical inductor $A$ must exist by the same construction as in Garrabrant et al. $\S5$ with the language, deductive process, and trader complexity class substituted.

For each $n \geq 1$, define the contract $C_{n}$ as the affine combination $C_{n} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n}) = \text{val}_W(n)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

Define a deductive process $D_H^+$ extending $D_H$ with two additional streams of data. In order for $H^+$ to learn the reliable calibration of $A$, it requires quotes of $A$'s prices and the settlements those quotes are eventually audited against. At each time $t$, $D_H^{+,t}$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_H^+$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item A record of the published quotes $a_i := A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$
  \item For each $i$ with $F(i) < t$, the realized settlement of contract $i$: the threshold profile $\theta_{i,k}$ for $k \leq m_i^*$ and $\neg\theta_{i,k}$ for $k > m_i^*$
\end{enumerate}
Note that items 1 and 3 match the corresponding components of the construction of $D_A$. As part of the simultaneous construction, each $D_H^{+,t}$ is finite, computable, and consistent.

Define $H^+$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.

Write $a_n := A_n(C_n)$ for $A$'s published quote, recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, and $Y_n := H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for $H^+$'s own future price that the quote is audited against. For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, let $g_{r,s,\delta} : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be the continuous function equal to $1$ on $[r,s]$, equal to $0$ outside $[r-\delta, s+\delta]$, and linear in between, and set $G_n := g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$. Since $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, both $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable by $H^+$ from time $n+1$ onward.

\begin{lemma}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a sequence of values $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$, computable 
        within $\mathcal{C}$ given access to $D^{\tau(n)}$, and a 
        $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to 
        \mathbb{N}^+$ such that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$ given
$D^{\tau(n)}$, and $X_n$ is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with
$q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within
$\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the data $(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$, computable
within $\mathcal{C}$ given $D^{\tau(i)}$, together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable since $m_n^*$ is, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. For hypothesis~2: by the construction of $D_A$, for
every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have
$\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\ $W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since
$C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is an average of $n$ values
$W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have $W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at
every $t$, independently of consistency.

The Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) - \tfrac{m_n^*}{n} \to 0$. By the construction of
$D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n} \to
0$. Combining, we have $A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0.$ \qedhere
\end{proof}

\end{document}

\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
Suppose:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item \emph{(Settlement-calibration.)} $A$'s quotes are accurate on the 
        audited record: the realized signed errors satisfy 
        $G_n(a_n - Y_n) \to 0$.
  \item \emph{(Audit-coherence.)} There is an $H^+$-recognizable correspondence 
        $\Phi$ between the settled cases (those $i$ with $F(i)$ already past) and 
        the current case $n$, under which the settlement-calibration established 
        on the former transfers to a bound on the latter.
\end{enumerate}
Then $H^+$ expects no signed audit error in the bin:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \to 0 
\quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Consider the audit quantity $Z_n := G_n(a_n - Y_n)$. By the construction of 
$D_H^+$, the settlement profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ is pinned once $F(n) < t$ and 
the quote $a_n$ is recorded once $n < t$, so with $\tau(n) := F(n)+1$ --- which

with $t \geq \tau(n)$ assigns $Z_n$ its realized value. Since $a_n$ and $G_n$ 
are constants recorded in $D_H^{+,\tau(n)}$ and the pinned profile encodes $Y_n$ 
up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, the quantity $Z_n$ is an affine combination of sentences, 
satisfies $|Z_n| \leq 1$, and has realized value computable within 
$\mathcal{C}_H$ given $D_H^{+,\tau(n)}$. Thus $Z_n$ meets the hypotheses of the 
Computable Tracking Lemma applied to $H^+$, giving 
$H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) - (\text{realized } Z_n) \to 0$, with the $\tfrac{1}{2n}$ 
rounding absorbed into the limit. By settlement-calibration the realized errors 
vanish, and by audit-coherence this convergence transfers from the settled

$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n(a_n - Y_n)] \to 0$.

\begin{theorem}[Deference]
Under the hypotheses of the Calibration Lemma, $H^+$'s judgment of $P^{(n)}$ 
defers to $A$'s quote. In product form,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\, G_n\bigr] 
- a_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[G_n\bigr] \to 0,

and consequently, on the cases where $A$ quotes in the bin with

\[
H^+_{n+1}\bigl(P^{(n)} \,\big|\, a_n \in [r,s]\bigr) \in [\,r - \delta,\; 
s + \delta\,] \quad \text{asymptotically.}
\]
\end{theorem}

= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n] + o(1).
\]
By the Calibration Lemma, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] = 
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] + o(1)$. As $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants at

\end{proof}

downside (now $\pm B$) are identical. The only change is at settlement: a 
settled trigger position opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes 
$\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have 
$|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger position 
($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a bought 
one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and the 
revealed pinned values. Infinitely many settled triggers then give plausible 
net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B$ along a subsequence, unbounded 
above, while the downside stays $\geq -B$. This exploits $P$, contradicting the 
logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}
```

Note hypothesis 2 no longer demands $w_n$ be $\mathcal{C}$-computable — that omission is the whole point of the lemma, so it's correct that the computability clause is gone. The trader uses $\tau$ (computable) and the revealed values, never computing $w_n$ ahead of time.

On "in the bin" — you're right that it's an abstruse gloss, and the issue is that the phrase is compressing something the reader hasn't been set up for. "In the bin" means "weighted by $G_n$," i.e. restricted to the cases where $A$'s quote falls in $[r,s]$ (where $G_n$ is supported). But "in the bin" only reads naturally if "bin" is already established terminology, and you've used $[r,s]$ as "a bin" only glancingly. The cleaner fix is to say what the quantity *is* rather than gloss where it lives. Options, roughly in order of how I'd rank them:

Plainest — just name the object: "On the cases $A$ quotes in $[r,s]$, $H^+$'s expected signed error between quote and settlement vanishes:" — this says exactly what $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n(a_n-Y_n)]$ is (the $G_n$-weighting *is* "on the cases $A$ quotes in $[r,s]$," and $a_n - Y_n$ *is* the signed error between quote and settlement).

Or drop the gloss entirely and let the formula speak: "$H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match the settlement:" followed by the display. This reads $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n(a_n - Y_n)] \to 0$ as "the $G_n$-weighted gap between quote $a_n$ and settlement $Y_n$ vanishes in $H^+$'s expectation," which is "$H^+$ expects quote to match settlement."

I'd use the second — it's the most honest one-line reading of the formula and avoids "bin" entirely:

```
\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
$H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match the settlement:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \to 0 
\quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}
```

The one caveat: "expect $A$'s quote to match the settlement" slightly undersells that it's the *$G_n$-weighted* (i.e. bin-restricted) and *signed* error — a reader who looks at the formula sees the $G_n$ and the signedness, so the gloss being a touch loose is fine as a headline reading, and the formula carries the precision. If you want the gloss to also flag the weighting, "On the cases $A$ quotes in $[r,s]$, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match the settlement:" does both — names the restriction and the content. That's probably the best single version; it trades one extra clause for removing all abstruseness.

Right — $G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ genuinely depends on the bin $[r,s]$ and margin $\delta$, which were introduced back in the derived-quantities block as "for any bin $[r,s]$ and margin $\delta > 0$." So by the time the Calibration Lemma uses $G_n$, the bin is a parameter already in scope. The question is whether the lemma should *remind* the reader of that dependence, and I think yes — partly for precision, partly because the bin is exactly what "calibration" is *about* (it's calibration *on a particular range of quotes*), so naming it sharpens the statement rather than just decorating it.

The cleanest fix is to make the lemma explicitly quantify or recall the bin in its opening, so $G_n$'s dependence is visible at point of use rather than relying on the reader to carry it from the derived-quantities block. Something like:

```
\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, with 
$G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as above, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match 
the settlement on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \to 0 
\quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}
```

This does three things: restates "for any bin... and margin," which makes the universal-over-bins reading explicit (the calibration holds for *every* bin, which is what you want — it's calibration across the whole range of $A$'s quotes, not just one window); recalls $G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ so the reader doesn't have to flip back; and "on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$" glosses the $G_n$-weighting honestly — "near" rather than "in" because $G_n$ is supported on the $\delta$-fattened $[r-\delta, s+\delta]$, not exactly $[r,s]$, so "near" is the precise word.

A couple of refinements depending on how precise you want to be:

If you want to nail the support exactly rather than say "near," you could write "on the cases $A$ quotes within $\delta$ of $[r,s]$" — that's exactly the support of $G_n$. "Near" is the readable version; "within $\delta$ of" is the exact version. I'd use "near $[r,s]$" in the gloss and let the formula (with its explicit $G_n$) carry the exact support, since a reader who wants precision reads $g_{r,s,\delta}$.

One thing to make sure is consistent: if you make the Calibration Lemma open with "For any bin $[r,s]$ and margin $\delta$," then the Deference Theorem, which inherits the bin, should either also open that way or clearly inherit it. Right now Deference says "conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ in a bin $[r,s]$" — which reintroduces the bin, so they're consistent, but you have the bin quantified in three places (derived quantities, Calibration, Deference). That's fine and arguably good for self-containedness, but if you'd rather quantify once, you could say in the derived-quantities block "Fix a bin $[r,s]$ and margin $\delta$ throughout" and then neither lemma nor theorem needs to re-quantify — they just use $G_n$. The tradeoff: "fix throughout" is terser but makes the results about *one* bin (you'd then add "and since $[r,s]$ was arbitrary, this holds for every bin" if you want the universal); "for any bin" repeated in each statement makes each self-contained and the universal explicit. For a clean headline I'd lean toward "fix throughout" in the derived block and let the statements be about that fixed bin, with a remark that it's arbitrary — but repeating "for any bin" in the Calibration Lemma is also perfectly fine and more self-contained. Either works; just pick one and be consistent so the bin isn't quantified inconsistently across the three spots.

For each pair $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ 1\leq k\leq n$, define a new propositional ``threshold" symbol $\theta_{n,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{n}$." Define a new language $\mathcal{L}^+$ that extends $\mathcal{L}$ with all the $\theta$ symbols, and define $\mathcal{S}^+$ to be the sentence set over $\mathcal{L}^+$.

A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with the monotonicity axioms, define the value of contract $n$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq n,\ W(\theta_{n,k})=1\}}{n}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m}{n}$.

These two mutually referential inductors are defined by recursion on time. Two timing delays to ensure this recursion's well-foundedness: $H^+$ receives the quotes from $A$ one time step after they are posted, and $A$'s contracts settle only at a time step greater than $F(n)$, after which the referenced future price $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ already exists.

Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable [more detail on this assumption]. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. \begin{enumerate}[nosep]

  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract \(n\) translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every \(t\geq \sigma(n)\) and every \(W\) consistent with \(D^t_A\), \(\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}\), which differs from \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) by at most \(\frac{1}{2n}\). Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each \(D_A^t\) is finite. \(D_A\) is also computable as part of the simultaneous construction: \(D_H\) is a computable deductive process, and each \(m^*_{n}\) is computable because \(\sigma(n)>F(n)\), so the value \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) has already been computed by the time the settlement is inserted. Finally, note that each \(D_A^t\) is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from \(\mathcal{S}\). Define $A = (A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to the deductive process $D_A$. \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_H^+$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item A record of the published quotes $a_i := A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$
  \item For each $i$ with $F(i) < t$, the realized settlement of contract $i$: the threshold profile $\theta_{i,k}$ for $k \leq m_i^*$ and $\neg\theta_{i,k}$ for $k > m_i^*$
\end{enumerate}
Note that items 1 and 3 match the corresponding components of the construction of $D_A$. As part of the simultaneous construction, each $D_H^{+,t}$ is finite, computable, and consistent.

Define $H^+$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.

Write $a_n := A_n(C_n)$ for $A$'s published quote, recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, and $Y_n := H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for $H^+$'s own future price that the quote is audited against. Since $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, both $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable by $H^+$ from time $n+1$ onward.

\begin{lemma}[Pinning]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a sequence of values $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$, computable 
        within $\mathcal{C}$ given access to $D^{\tau(n)}$, and a 
        $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to 
        \mathbb{N}^+$ such that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$ given
$D^{\tau(n)}$, and $X_n$ is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with
$q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within
$\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the data $(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$, computable
within $\mathcal{C}$ given $D^{\tau(i)}$, together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \textup{ as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Pinning Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable since $m_n^*$ is, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. For hypothesis~2: by the construction of $D_A$, for
every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have
$\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\ $W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since
$C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is an average of $n$ values
$W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have $W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at
every $t$, independently of consistency.

The Pinning Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) - \tfrac{m_n^*}{n} \to 0$. By the construction of
$D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n} \to
0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0.$ \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Vanishing Settled Values]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \to 0 \quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of the Pinning Lemma with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping, admissibility, and bounded 
downside (now $\pm B$) are identical. The only change is at settlement: a 
settled trigger position opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes 
$\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have

revealed pinned values. Infinitely many settled triggers then give plausible

logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, with 
$G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as above, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match 
the settlement on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \to 0 
\quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := G_n(a_n - Y_n)$. By the Tracking Theorem, $a_n - Y_n \to 0$, so 
since $0 \leq G_n \leq 1$ the realized values satisfy

$n < t$ and the settlement profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ encoding $Y_n$ is pinned

realized values.) By the Vanishing Settled Values Lemma applied to $H^+$, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Z_n] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deference]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, $H^+$ defers to 
$A$'s quote: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ in $[r,s]$,
\[
H^+_{n+1}\bigl(P^{(n)} \,\big|\, a_n \in [r,s]\bigr) \in [\,r - \delta,\, 
s + \delta\,] \quad \textup{asymptotically.}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By the No Expected Net Update property (Garrabrant et al.\ 4.12.2) applied to 
$H^+$, whose own future price of $P^{(n)}$ is $Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, and 
since $G_n$ is a constant observable at time $n+1$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] 
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n] + o(1).
\]
By the Calibration Lemma, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] = 
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] + o(1)$, and as $a_n, G_n$ are constants at time 
$n+1$, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$. On 
the cases where $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$ is bounded below, dividing through 
and using that $G_n = 1$ on $\{a_n \in [r,s]\}$ and vanishes outside 
$\{a_n \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]\}$ yields 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)} \mid a_n \in [r,s]) \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]$ asymptotically.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pinning]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive
