\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a sequence of values $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$, computable 
        within $\mathcal{C}$ given access to $D^{\tau(n)}$, and a 
        $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to 
        \mathbb{N}^+$ such that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$ given
$D^{\tau(n)}$, and $X_n$ is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with
$q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within
$\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the data $(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$, computable
within $\mathcal{C}$ given $D^{\tau(i)}$, together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \textup{ as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Pinning Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable since $m_n^*$ is, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. For hypothesis~2: by the construction of $D_A$, for
every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have
$\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\ $W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since
$C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is an average of $n$ values
$W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have $W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at
every $t$, independently of consistency.

The Pinning Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) - \tfrac{m_n^*}{n} \to 0$. By the construction of
$D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n} \to
0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0.$ \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Vanishing Settled Values]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \to 0 \quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of the Pinning Lemma with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping, admissibility, and bounded 
downside (now $\pm B$) are identical. The only change is at settlement: a 
settled trigger position opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes 
$\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have 
$|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger position 
($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a bought 
one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and the 
revealed pinned values. Infinitely many settled triggers then give plausible 
net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B$ along a subsequence, unbounded 
above, while the downside stays $\geq -B$. This exploits $P$, contradicting the 
logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, with 
$G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as above, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match 
the settlement on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \to 0 
\quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := G_n(a_n - Y_n)$. By the Tracking Theorem, $a_n - Y_n \to 0$, so 
since $0 \leq G_n \leq 1$ the realized values satisfy 
$|Z_n| \leq |a_n - Y_n| \to 0$. The quote $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^+$ once 
$n < t$ and the settlement profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ encoding $Y_n$ is pinned 
once $F(n) < t$, so $Z_n$ is a bounded affine combination pinned by $D_H^+$ at 
$\tau(n) := F(n)+1$, which is $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is. (The pinned 
profile encodes $Y_n$ up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, absorbed into the vanishing 
realized values.) By the Vanishing Settled Values Lemma applied to $H^+$, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Z_n] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deference]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, $H^+$ defers to 
$A$'s quote: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ in $[r,s]$,
\[
H^+_{n+1}\bigl(P^{(n)} \,\big|\, a_n \in [r,s]\bigr) \in [\,r - \delta,\, 
s + \delta\,] \quad \textup{asymptotically.}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By the No Expected Net Update property (Garrabrant et al.\ 4.12.2) applied to 
$H^+$, whose own future price of $P^{(n)}$ is $Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, and 
since $G_n$ is a constant observable at time $n+1$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] 
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n] + o(1).
\]
By the Calibration Lemma, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] = 
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] + o(1)$, and as $a_n, G_n$ are constants at time 
$n+1$, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$. On 
the cases where $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$ is bounded below, dividing through 
and using that $G_n = 1$ on $\{a_n \in [r,s]\}$ and vanishes outside 
$\{a_n \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]\}$ yields 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)} \mid a_n \in [r,s]) \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]$ asymptotically.
\end{proof}

\end{document}

```
\begin{lemma}[Coupled Construction]
There exist sequences $A = (A_1, A_2, \ldots)$ and $H^+ = (H^+_1, H^+_2, \ldots)$, 
together with the deductive processes $D_A$ and $D_H^+$, such that: $D_A$ and 
$D_H^+$ are computable deductive processes; $A$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ 
satisfying the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$; and $H^+$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical 
induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The four sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, $(D_H^{+,t})$ are defined 
together by a single recursion on $t$. We use the construction of Garrabrant et 
al.\ \S5, which produces a logical inductor over a given computable deductive 
process by a procedure whose time-$t$ output depends only on the deductive 
process up to time $t$ and on the construction's own earlier stages; we run two 
such constructions, one for each market, interleaved with the definitions of 
the deductive processes.

Suppose all four sequences have been defined at every stage $s < t$. We define 
the stage-$t$ objects as follows.

\emph{Deductive processes.} $D_A^t$ is given by its definition. Its only 
dependence on $H^+$ is through the settlement values $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for 
$n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$; since $\sigma(n) > F(n)$, each such $n$ has 
$F(n) < \sigma(n) \leq t$, so these are prices $H^+_{F(n)}$ at times 
$F(n) < t$, already defined. Likewise $D_H^{+,t}$ depends on $A$ only through the 
quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$, again already defined. Both stage-$t$ 
deductive sets are therefore computable from stage-$(<t)$ data, and are finite 
and consistent as shown in their definitions.

\emph{Markets.} With $D_A^{\leq t}$ now in hand, the \S5 construction yields its 
time-$t$ pricing $A_t$ from $D_A^{\leq t}$ and its own earlier stages; similarly 
$H^+_t$ is produced from $D_H^{+,\leq t}$. Neither market-step references any 
stage-$t$ price of the other: $A_t$ uses only $D_A^{\leq t}$ (which depended on 
$H^+$ at times $< t$) and $(A_s)_{s<t}$, and symmetrically for $H^+_t$.

Every stage-$t$ object thus depends only on stage-$(<t)$ objects, so the 
recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, 
$(D_H^{+,t})$ are computable; in particular $D_A$ and $D_H^+$ are computable 
deductive processes. Finally, because each market is produced by the \S5 
construction over its own (computable, consistent) deductive process, $A$ 
satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$, and $H^+$ satisfies it against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{proof}
```

This goes right after you define $H^+$ (and after the derived-quantities paragraph, or before it — either works, but I'd put it immediately after the $H^+$ definition so all four objects have been introduced). Then delete the old "A logical inductor $A$ must exist by the same construction as in Garrabrant et al. §5..." sentence, since this lemma replaces it.

A few things about choices I made and what to check:

The crux move is the paragraph showing the stage-$t$ deductive processes depend only on strictly-earlier *market prices* ($H^+$ at $F(n) < t$, $A$ at $i < t$), and the stage-$t$ markets depend only on the just-built deductive process plus their own earlier stages. That's the whole well-foundedness argument, and it's where gap (2) gets closed — the markets are built *inside* the recursion via §5-as-a-step, not by invoking §5 as a black box on a finished $D_A$. Make sure you believe the claim "the §5 construction's time-$t$ output depends only on the deductive process up to time $t$ and its own earlier stages" — this is the locality-in-time of §5 that makes the interleaving legitimate. I'm fairly confident it's true of the LIA construction (the market-maker/budgeter/trading-firm machinery is computed incrementally), but it's the one external fact the proof leans on, so it's worth confirming against §5 that the construction is genuinely incremental in $t$ and doesn't need the whole deductive process in advance. If §5 needs the full $D_A$ to define even $A_1$, the interleaving breaks — but it doesn't, because logical inductors are defined as computable sequences precisely so each $A_t$ is computed finitely. So this should hold, but it's the assumption to verify.

I asserted "finite and consistent as shown in their definitions" rather than re-proving — since you already establish finiteness and consistency in the $D_A$ and $D_H^+ paragraphs, the lemma should cite those rather than repeat. Just make sure those paragraphs do establish consistency for $D_H^+$ (the $D_A$ one does; check the $D_H^+$ one says it too — it currently says "finite, computable, and consistent" in one breath without the disjointness argument, so you might want the $D_H^+$ consistency spelled out as much as $D_A$'s, since the lemma now leans on it).

One genuine subtlety I want to flag rather than hide: the proof establishes the markets are *computable* and satisfy the LIC *relative to their respective deductive processes*. It does *not* establish that $A$ is computable *within $\mathcal{C}_A$* in the budget sense Tracking needs — that's the complexity frontier, correctly excluded from this existence lemma. So this lemma gives existence-and-computability; the $\mathcal{C}_A$-budget assumption remains separate (the thing that was the bracket). Keep those distinct: this lemma is pure existence, and it does *not* discharge the complexity assumption. When you write the complexity assumption afterward, it should say "beyond the existence guaranteed by the Coupled Construction Lemma, Tracking additionally requires $A$'s traders to compute $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ within $\mathcal{C}_A$, i.e...." so the reader sees existence (proved) and budget (assumed) as two different things.

The proof is watertight modulo the one external fact (§5's time-locality), which is true. That's a much stronger position than the deleted one-sentence assertion — you now *prove* the coupled pair exists and is computable, and the only remaining assumption is honestly the complexity one. That closes the biggest gap from the pressure-test.

Consider a logical inductor $H = (H_1, H_2,\ldots)$ that represents the base human collective reasoning process. $H$ is defined over language $\mathcal{L}$ with sentence set $\mathcal{S}$, theory $\Gamma$, and $\Gamma$-complete deductive process $D_H$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in the complexity class $\mathcal{C}_H$. Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function $F: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$. Fix an effective enumeration $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)},\ldots$ of the sentences of $\mathcal{S}$. Since the enumeration can be freely chosen, take $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)}, \ldots$ to be the sequence of propositions of interest. Tying contract $n$ to $P^{(n)}$ therefore loses no generality, as any efficiently computable sequence of propositions can be studied by enumerating it in this way.

For each pair $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ 1\leq k\leq n$, define a new propositional ``threshold" symbol $\theta_{n,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{n}$." Define a new language $\mathcal{L}^+$ that extends $\mathcal{L}$ with all the $\theta$ symbols, and define $\mathcal{S}^+$ to be the sentence set over $\mathcal{L}^+$. 

Define a schema $\{\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}: n\geq 1,\ 2\leq k\leq n\}$ of ``monotonicity" axioms. Each axiom informally says that ``clearing the $\frac{k}{n}$ threshold implies clearing the $\frac{k-1}{n}$ threshold." 

A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with the monotonicity axioms, define the value of contract $n$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq n,\ W(\theta_{n,k})=1\}}{n}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m}{n}$. 

The following simultaneously defines a coupled pair $A$ that represents an AI reasoner and $H^+$ that represents the human reasoner augmented with the ability to observe published quotes of $A$'s outputs. These two mutually referential inductors are defined by recursion on time. Two timing delays to ensure this recursion's well-foundedness: $H^+$ receives the quotes from $A$ one time step after they are posted, and $A$'s contracts settle only at a time step greater than $F(n)$, after which the referenced future price $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ already exists.

Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable [more detail on this assumption]. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n) > F(n)$ and also that $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n)$ steps.

Define a deductive process $D_A$ as follows. At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_A$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract \(n\) translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every \(t\geq \sigma(n)\) and every \(W\) consistent with \(D^t_A\), \(\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}\), which differs from \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) by at most \(\frac{1}{2n}\). Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each \(D_A^t\) is finite. \(D_A\) is also computable as part of the simultaneous construction: \(D_H\) is a computable deductive process, and each \(m^*_{n}\) is computable because \(\sigma(n)>F(n)\), so the value \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) has already been computed by the time the settlement is inserted. Finally, note that each \(D_A^t\) is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from \(\mathcal{S}\). Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to \(D_A\) is well-posed.

Define $A = (A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to the deductive process $D_A$.

For each $n \geq 1$, define the contract $C_{n}$ as the affine combination $C_{n} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n}) = \text{val}_W(n)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

Define a deductive process $D_H^+$ extending $D_H$ with two additional streams of data. In order for $H^+$ to learn the reliable calibration of $A$, it requires quotes of $A$'s prices and the settlements those quotes are eventually audited against. At each time $t$, $D_H^{+,t}$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_H^+$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item A record of the published quotes $a_i := A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$
  \item For each $i$ with $F(i) < t$, the realized settlement of contract $i$: the threshold profile $\theta_{i,k}$ for $k \leq m_i^*$ and $\neg\theta_{i,k}$ for $k > m_i^*$
\end{enumerate}
Note that items 1 and 3 match the corresponding components of the construction of $D_A$. As part of the simultaneous construction, each $D_H^{+,t}$ is finite, computable, and consistent.

Define $H^+$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.

Write $a_n := A_n(C_n)$ for $A$'s published quote, recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, and $Y_n := H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for $H^+$'s own future price that the quote is audited against. For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, let $g_{r,s,\delta} : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be the continuous function equal to $1$ on $[r,s]$, equal to $0$ outside $[r-\delta, s+\delta]$, and linear in between, and set $G_n := g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$. Since $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, both $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable by $H^+$ from time $n+1$ onward.

\begin{lemma}[Existence]
There exist sequences $A = (A_1, A_2, \ldots)$ and $H^+ = (H^+_1, H^+_2, \ldots)$, 
together with the deductive processes $D_A$ and $D_H^+$, such that: $D_A$ and 
$D_H^+$ are computable deductive processes; $A$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ 
satisfying the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$; and $H^+$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical 
induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The four sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, $(D_H^{+,t})$ are defined 
together by a single recursion on $t$. We use the construction of Garrabrant et 
al.\ \S5, which produces a logical inductor over a given computable deductive 
process by a procedure whose time-$t$ output depends only on the deductive 
process up to time $t$ and on the construction's own earlier stages; we run two 
such constructions, one for each market, interleaved with the definitions of 
the deductive processes.

Suppose all four sequences have been defined at every stage $s < t$. We define 
the stage-$t$ objects as follows.

\emph{Deductive processes.} $D_A^t$ is given by its definition. Its only 
dependence on $H^+$ is through the settlement values $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for 
$n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$; since $\sigma(n) > F(n)$, each such $n$ has 
$F(n) < \sigma(n) \leq t$, so these are prices $H^+_{F(n)}$ at times 
$F(n) < t$, already defined. Likewise $D_H^{+,t}$ depends on $A$ only through the 
quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$, again already defined. Both stage-$t$ 
deductive sets are therefore computable from stage-$(<t)$ data, and are finite 
and consistent as shown in their definitions.

\emph{Markets.} With $D_A^{\leq t}$ now in hand, the \S5 construction yields its 
time-$t$ pricing $A_t$ from $D_A^{\leq t}$ and its own earlier stages; similarly 
$H^+_t$ is produced from $D_H^{+,\leq t}$. Neither market-step references any 
stage-$t$ price of the other: $A_t$ uses only $D_A^{\leq t}$ (which depended on 
$H^+$ at times $< t$) and $(A_s)_{s<t}$, and symmetrically for $H^+_t$.

Every stage-$t$ object thus depends only on stage-$(<t)$ objects, so the 
recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, 
$(D_H^{+,t})$ are computable; in particular $D_A$ and $D_H^+$ are computable 
deductive processes. Finally, because each market is produced by the \S5 
construction over its own (computable, consistent) deductive process, $A$ 
satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$, and $H^+$ satisfies it against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pinning]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a sequence of values $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$, computable 
        within $\mathcal{C}$ given access to $D^{\tau(n)}$, and a 
        $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to 
        \mathbb{N}^+$ such that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$ given
$D^{\tau(n)}$, and $X_n$ is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with
$q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within
$\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the data $(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$, computable
within $\mathcal{C}$ given $D^{\tau(i)}$, together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \textup{ as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Pinning Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable since $m_n^*$ is, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. For hypothesis~2: by the construction of $D_A$, for
every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have
$\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\ $W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since
$C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is an average of $n$ values
$W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have $W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at
every $t$, independently of consistency.

The Pinning Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) - \tfrac{m_n^*}{n} \to 0$. By the construction of
$D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n} \to
0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0.$ \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Vanishing Settled Values]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \to 0 \quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of the Pinning Lemma with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping, admissibility, and bounded 
downside (now $\pm B$) are identical. The only change is at settlement: a 
settled trigger position opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes 
$\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have 
$|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger position 
($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a bought 
one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and the 
revealed pinned values. Infinitely many settled triggers then give plausible 
net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B$ along a subsequence, unbounded 
above, while the downside stays $\geq -B$. This exploits $P$, contradicting the 
logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, with 
$G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as above, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match 
the settlement on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \to 0 
\quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := G_n(a_n - Y_n)$. By the Tracking Theorem, $a_n - Y_n \to 0$, so 
since $0 \leq G_n \leq 1$ the realized values satisfy 
$|Z_n| \leq |a_n - Y_n| \to 0$. The quote $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^+$ once 
$n < t$ and the settlement profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ encoding $Y_n$ is pinned 
once $F(n) < t$, so $Z_n$ is a bounded affine combination pinned by $D_H^+$ at 
$\tau(n) := F(n)+1$, which is $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is. (The pinned 
profile encodes $Y_n$ up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, absorbed into the vanishing 
realized values.) By the Vanishing Settled Values Lemma applied to $H^+$, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Z_n] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deference]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, $H^+$ defers to 
$A$'s quote: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ in $[r,s]$,
\[
H^+_{n+1}\bigl(P^{(n)} \,\big|\, a_n \in [r,s]\bigr) \in [\,r - \delta,\, 
s + \delta\,] \quad \textup{asymptotically.}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By the No Expected Net Update property (Garrabrant et al.\ 4.12.2) applied to 
$H^+$, whose own future price of $P^{(n)}$ is $Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, and 
since $G_n$ is a constant observable at time $n+1$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] 
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n] + o(1).
\]
By the Calibration Lemma, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] = 
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] + o(1)$, and as $a_n, G_n$ are constants at time 
$n+1$, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$. On 
the cases where $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$ is bounded below, dividing through 
and using that $G_n = 1$ on $\{a_n \in [r,s]\}$ and vanishes outside 
$\{a_n \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]\}$ yields 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)} \mid a_n \in [r,s]) \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]$ asymptotically.
\end{proof}

\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{graphicx} % Required for inserting images
\usepackage{amsfonts}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{enumitem}
\usepackage{amsthm}
\newtheorem{lemma}{Lemma}
\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}

\begin{document}
Consider a logical inductor $H = (H_1, H_2,\ldots)$ that represents the base human collective reasoning process. $H$ is defined over language $\mathcal{L}$ with sentence set $\mathcal{S}$, theory $\Gamma$, and $\Gamma$-complete deductive process $D_H$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in the complexity class $\mathcal{C}_H$. Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function $F: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$. Fix an effective enumeration $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)},\ldots$ of the sentences of $\mathcal{S}$. Since the enumeration can be freely chosen, take $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)}, \ldots$ to be the sequence of propositions of interest. Tying contract $n$ to $P^{(n)}$ therefore loses no generality, as any efficiently computable sequence of propositions can be studied by enumerating it in this way.

For each pair $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ 1\leq k\leq n$, define a new propositional ``threshold" symbol $\theta_{n,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{n}$." Define a new language $\mathcal{L}^+$ that extends $\mathcal{L}$ with all the $\theta$ symbols, and define $\mathcal{S}^+$ to be the sentence set over $\mathcal{L}^+$. 

Define a schema $\{\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}: n\geq 1,\ 2\leq k\leq n\}$ of ``monotonicity" axioms. Each axiom informally says that ``clearing the $\frac{k}{n}$ threshold implies clearing the $\frac{k-1}{n}$ threshold." 

A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with the monotonicity axioms, define the value of contract $n$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq n,\ W(\theta_{n,k})=1\}}{n}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m}{n}$. 

The following simultaneously defines a coupled pair $A$ that represents an AI reasoner and $H^+$ that represents the human reasoner augmented with the ability to observe published quotes of $A$'s outputs. These two mutually referential inductors are defined by recursion on time. Two timing delays ensure this recursion's well-foundedness: $H^+$ receives the quotes from $A$ one time step after they are posted, and $A$'s contracts settle only at a time step greater than $F(n)$, after which the referenced future price $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ already exists.

Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable [more detail on this assumption]. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n) > F(n)$ and also that $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n)$ steps.

Define a deductive process $D_A$ as follows. At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_A$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract \(n\) translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every \(t\geq \sigma(n)\) and every \(W\) consistent with \(D^t_A\), \(\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}\), which differs from \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) by at most \(\frac{1}{2n}\). Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each \(D_A^t\) is finite. \(D_A\) is also computable as part of the simultaneous construction: \(D_H\) is a computable deductive process, and each \(m^*_{n}\) is computable because \(\sigma(n)>F(n)\), so the value \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) has already been computed by the time the settlement is inserted. Finally, note that each \(D_A^t\) is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from \(\mathcal{S}\). Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to \(D_A\) is well-posed.

Define $A = (A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to the deductive process $D_A$.

For each $n \geq 1$, define the contract $C_{n}$ as the affine combination $C_{n} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n}) = \text{val}_W(n)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

Define a deductive process $D_H^+$ extending $D_H$ with two additional streams of data. In order for $H^+$ to learn the reliable calibration of $A$, it requires quotes of $A$'s prices and the settlements those quotes are eventually audited against. At each time $t$, $D_H^{+,t}$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_H^+$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item A record of the published quotes $a_i := A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$
  \item For each $i$ with $F(i) < t$, the realized settlement of contract $i$: the threshold profile $\theta_{i,k}$ for $k \leq m_i^*$ and $\neg\theta_{i,k}$ for $k > m_i^*$
\end{enumerate}
Items 1 and 3 coincide with the corresponding components of $D_A$; item 2 is the new content, recording $A$'s quotes after the one-step delay. As part of the simultaneous construction each $D_H^{+,t}$ is finite and computable, and is consistent: the settlement profiles of item 3 are initial segments respecting the monotonicity axioms, and the quote records of item 2 concern values disjoint from the threshold propositions.

Define $H^+$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.

Write $a_n := A_n(C_n)$ for $A$'s published quote, recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, and $Y_n := H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for $H^+$'s own future price that the quote is audited against. For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, let $g_{r,s,\delta} : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be the continuous function equal to $1$ on $[r,s]$, equal to $0$ outside $[r-\delta, s+\delta]$, and linear in between, and set $G_n := g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$. Since $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, both $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable by $H^+$ from time $n+1$ onward.

\begin{lemma}[Existence]
There exist sequences $A = (A_1, A_2, \ldots)$ and $H^+ = (H^+_1, H^+_2, \ldots)$, 
together with the deductive processes $D_A$ and $D_H^+$, such that: $D_A$ and 
$D_H^+$ are computable deductive processes; $A$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ 
satisfying the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$; and $H^+$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical 
induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The four sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, $(D_H^{+,t})$ are defined 
together by a single recursion on $t$. We use the construction of Garrabrant et 
al.\ \S5, which produces a logical inductor over a given computable deductive 
process incrementally: its time-$t$ pricing depends only on the deductive 
process up to time $t$ and on the construction's own stages before $t$. We run 
two such constructions, one per market, interleaved with the definitions of the 
deductive processes.

Suppose all four sequences have been defined at every stage $s < t$. We define 
the stage-$t$ objects as follows.

\emph{Deductive processes.} $D_A^t$ is given by its definition. Its only 
dependence on $H^+$ is through the settlement values $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for 
$n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$; since $\sigma(n) > F(n)$, each such $n$ has 
$F(n) < \sigma(n) \leq t$, so these are prices $H^+_{F(n)}$ at times 
$F(n) < t$, already defined. Likewise $D_H^{+,t}$ depends on $A$ only through the 
quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$, again already defined. Both stage-$t$ 
deductive sets are therefore computable from stage-$(<t)$ data, and are finite 
and consistent as shown in their definitions.

\emph{Markets.} With $D_A^{\leq t}$ now in hand, the \S5 construction yields its 
time-$t$ pricing $A_t$ from $D_A^{\leq t}$ and its own stages before $t$; 
similarly $H^+_t$ is produced from $D_H^{+,\leq t}$. Neither market-step 
references any stage-$t$ price of the other: $A_t$ uses only $D_A^{\leq t}$ 
(which depended on $H^+$ at times $< t$) and $(A_s)_{s<t}$, and symmetrically 
for $H^+_t$. This is where the incrementality of the \S5 construction is used: 
$A_t$ can be computed without the whole of $D_A$ in advance.

Every stage-$t$ object thus depends only on stage-$(<t)$ objects, so the 
recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, 
$(D_H^{+,t})$ are computable; in particular $D_A$ and $D_H^+$ are computable 
deductive processes. Finally, because each market is produced by the \S5 
construction over its own (computable, consistent) deductive process, $A$ 
satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$, and $H^+$ satisfies it against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$. We 
emphasize that this establishes existence and computability only; that $A$'s 
traders can compute the settlement values \emph{within $\mathcal{C}_A$} is the 
separate assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$ above, used in the Tracking Theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pinning]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a sequence of values $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$, computable 
        within $\mathcal{C}$ given access to $D^{\tau(n)}$, and a 
        $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to 
        \mathbb{N}^+$ such that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$ given
$D^{\tau(n)}$, and $X_n$ is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with
$q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within
$\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the data $(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$, computable
within $\mathcal{C}$ given $D^{\tau(i)}$, together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) - v_n \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0 \textup{ as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Pinning Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable; the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is computable within
$\mathcal{C}_A$ given $D_A^{\sigma(n)}$, since $m_n^*$ rounds 
$H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, which is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable by the standing 
assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$. For hypothesis~2: by the construction of $D_A$, for
every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have
$\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\ $W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since
$C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is an average of $n$ values
$W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have $W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at
every $t$, independently of consistency.

The Pinning Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) - \tfrac{m_n^*}{n} \to 0$. By the construction of
$D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n} \to
0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \to 0.$ \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Vanishing Settled Values]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \to 0 \quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of the Pinning Lemma with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping and admissibility argument are 
unchanged. Since $W(X_n) \in [-B,B]$, a single open position has value 
$\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)) \in [-B', B']$ for $B' = 2B$, so the downside from 
the at-most-one unsettled position is bounded below by $-B'$. The only 
substantive change is at settlement: a settled trigger position opened at a 
trigger time $i$ contributes $\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$, and since $w_i \to 0$, 
for all large $i$ we have $|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger 
position ($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a 
bought one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and 
the revealed pinned values. Infinitely many settled triggers then give plausible 
net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B'$ along a subsequence, unbounded 
above, while the downside stays $\geq -B'$. This exploits $P$, contradicting the 
logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, with 
$G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as above, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match 
the settlement on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \to 0 
\quad \textup{as } n \to \infty.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := G_n(a_n - Y_n)$. Since $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants and $Y_n$ is 
the value of the contract $C_n$ pinned by the settlement profile, 
$Z_n = G_n a_n - G_n C_n$ is a bounded affine combination of the threshold 
sentences $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n| \leq 1$. The quote $a_n$ is recorded in 
$D_H^+$ once $n < t$ and the profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ is pinned once 
$F(n) < t$, so $Z_n$ is pinned by $D_H^+$ at $\tau(n) := F(n)+1$, which is 
$\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is. Its realized value is 
$w_n = G_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)$; by the Tracking Theorem $a_n - Y_n \to 0$, and the 
profile encodes $Y_n$ up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, so 
$|w_n| \leq |a_n - Y_n| + \tfrac{1}{2n} \to 0$. By the Vanishing Settled Values 
Lemma applied to $H^+$ (with $B = 1$), 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Z_n] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deference]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, $H^+$ defers to 
$A$'s quote: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ in $[r,s]$,
\[
H^+_{n+1}\bigl(P^{(n)} \,\big|\, a_n \in [r,s]\bigr) \in [\,r - \delta,\, 
s + \delta\,] \quad \textup{asymptotically.}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By the No Expected Net Update property (Garrabrant et al.\ 4.12.2) applied to 
$H^+$, together with the identification of $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{F(n)}(\mathbf{1}
(P^{(n)}))$ with the price $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) = Y_n$ (Expectations of 
Indicators, 4.8.6), and since $G_n$ is a constant observable at time $n+1$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] 
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n] + o(1).
\]
By the Calibration Lemma, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] = 
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] + o(1)$, and as $a_n, G_n$ are constants at time 
$n+1$, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$. On 
the cases where $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[G_n]$ is bounded below, dividing through 
and using that $G_n = 1$ on $\{a_n \in [r,s]\}$ and vanishes outside 
$\{a_n \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]\}$ yields 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)} \mid a_n \in [r,s]) \in [r-\delta, s+\delta]$ asymptotically.
\end{proof}

\end{document}

This is a major finding, and it's almost entirely good news — but it also surfaces one real concern. Let me give you the verdict on each piece.

**4.12.2 and 4.8.6 check out exactly.** 4.12.2 (No Expected Net Update) is $P_n(\varphi_n) \simeq_n \mathbb{E}_n(\text{"}P_{f(n)}(\varphi_n)\text{"})$ — your self-trust step. 4.8.6 (Expectations of Indicators) is $\mathbb{E}_n(\mathbf{1}(\varphi_n)) \simeq_n P_n(\varphi_n)$ — your indicator/price identification. Both citations in your Deference proof are correct and say what you use them for. Good.

**There's a much better citation for your Deference theorem: 4.12.3, and especially 4.12.4 (Self-Trust).** Look at what the paper already has:

4.12.3 (No Expected Net Update under Conditionals): $\mathbb{E}_n(\text{"}X_n \cdot w_{f(n)}\text{"}) \simeq_n \mathbb{E}_n(\text{"}\mathbb{E}_{f(n)}(X_n) \cdot w_{f(n)}\text{"})$ — this is *exactly* your weighted self-trust step, with $w$ a $P$-generable weight sequence. Your $G_n$ is playing the role of $w$.

4.12.4 (Self-Trust): $\mathbb{E}_n(\text{"}\mathbf{1}(\varphi_n) \cdot \mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(P_{f(n)}(\varphi_n) > p_n)\text{"}) \gtrsim_n p_n \cdot \mathbb{E}_n(\text{"}\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(P_{f(n)}(\varphi_n) > p_n)\text{"})$ — this is *almost verbatim your Deference theorem*. The $\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(P_{f(n)}(\varphi_n) > p_n)$ is a smoothed bin indicator on the future price, $p_n$ is the threshold, and the conclusion is the conditional-deference bound. This is the paper's own self-trust theorem and it has the same shape as what you're proving.

This matters in two ways, one helping and one a concern.

The help: your Deference proof currently reconstructs the weighted self-trust by hand from 4.12.2 + 4.8.6 + a constant-pullout. You can instead cite **4.12.3** directly for the weighted step — it's the exact statement, already proved, with $G_n$ as the $P$-generable weight $w_{f(n)}$. That's cleaner and more obviously correct than your manual reconstruction. So your Deference proof can shrink to "by 4.12.3 with weight $G_n$, [weighted self-trust]; by Calibration, [replace $Y_n$ with $a_n$]; pull out the constant."

**The concern — and it's a real one you need to look at.** In 4.12.3 the weight is $w_{f(n)}$ — indexed at the *future* time $f(n)$, and required to be $P$-generable. In 4.12.4 the indicator weight is $\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(P_{f(n)}(\varphi_n) > p_n)$ — a function of the *future* price $P_{f(n)}$. But your weight $G_n = g(a_n)$ is a function of $A$'s quote $a_n$, observed at time $n+1$ — a *current/past* observable, not a function of $H^+$'s own future price. So your $G_n$ is a different kind of weight than either 4.12.3's $w_{f(n)}$ or 4.12.4's future-price indicator.

Is $G_n$ a legitimate weight for these theorems? 4.12.3 requires $w$ to be a $P$-generable sequence of reals in $[0,1]$. Your $G_n = g(a_n)$ is $H^+$-generable (it's a continuous function of the observed quote $a_n$, which is in $D_H^+$, hence available to $H^+$'s traders) and lies in $[0,1]$. So $G_n$ *does* qualify as a $P$-generable weight for $P = H^+$ — but you're using it indexed at time $n$ (or $n+1$), whereas 4.12.3's weight is indexed $w_{f(n)}$, at the future time. You need to check the index alignment: 4.12.3 weights by the future-time value $w_{f(n)}$, and you want to weight by the current-time $G_n$. These aren't obviously the same, and the theorem as stated puts the weight at $f(n)$.

So the question is whether there's a version with the weight at the *current* time $n$. Let me look at whether your manual reconstruction (4.12.2 + 4.8.6 + constant-pullout) actually handles this correctly, because that's the thing that has to be right regardless of which theorem you cite.

Consider a logical inductor $H = (H_1, H_2,\ldots)$ that represents the base human collective reasoning process. $H$ is defined over language $\mathcal{L}$ with sentence set $\mathcal{S}$, theory $\Gamma$, and $\Gamma$-complete deductive process $D_H$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in the complexity class $\mathcal{C}_H$. Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function $F: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$. Fix an effective enumeration $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)},\ldots$ of the sentences of $\mathcal{S}$. Since the enumeration can be freely chosen, take $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)}, \ldots$ to be the sequence of propositions of interest. Tying contract $n$ to $P^{(n)}$ therefore loses no generality, as any efficiently computable sequence of propositions can be studied by enumerating it in this way.

For each pair $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ 1\leq k\leq n$, define a new propositional ``threshold" symbol $\theta_{n,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{n}$." Define a new language $\mathcal{L}^+$ that extends $\mathcal{L}$ with all the $\theta$ symbols, and define $\mathcal{S}^+$ to be the sentence set over $\mathcal{L}^+$. 

Define a schema $\{\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}: n\geq 1,\ 2\leq k\leq n\}$ of ``monotonicity" axioms. Each axiom informally says that ``clearing the $\frac{k}{n}$ threshold implies clearing the $\frac{k-1}{n}$ threshold." 

A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with the monotonicity axioms, define the value of contract $n$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq n,\ W(\theta_{n,k})=1\}}{n}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m}{n}$. 

The following simultaneously defines a coupled pair $A$ that represents an AI reasoner and $H^+$ that represents the human reasoner augmented with the ability to observe published quotes of $A$'s outputs. These two mutually referential inductors are defined by recursion on time. Two timing delays ensure this recursion's well-foundedness: $H^+$ receives the quotes from $A$ one time step after they are posted, and $A$'s contracts settle only at a time step greater than $F(n)$, after which the referenced future price $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ already exists.

Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that the map $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable [more detail on this assumption]. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n) > F(n)$ and also that $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n)$ steps.

Define a deductive process $D_A$ as follows. At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_A$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The third component should be understood as the settlement of contract \(n\) translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every \(t\geq \sigma(n)\) and every \(W\) consistent with \(D^t_A\), \(\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}\), which differs from \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) by at most \(\frac{1}{2n}\). Note that since items 2 and 3 range over finitely many values, each \(D_A^t\) is finite. \(D_A\) is also computable as part of the simultaneous construction: \(D_H\) is a computable deductive process, and each \(m^*_{n}\) is computable because \(\sigma(n)>F(n)\), so the value \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) has already been computed by the time the settlement is inserted. Finally, note that each \(D_A^t\) is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms and each settlement step involves sets of threshold propositions that are disjoint both from each other and from \(\mathcal{S}\). Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to \(D_A\) is well-posed.

For each $n \geq 1$, define the contract $C_{n}$ as the affine combination $C_{n} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n}) = \text{val}_W(n)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

Define a deductive process $D_H^+$ extending $D_H$ with two additional streams of data. In order for $H^+$ to learn the reliable calibration of $A$, it requires quotes of $A$'s prices and the settlements those quotes are eventually audited against. At each time $t$, $D_H^{+,t}$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_H^+$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item A record of the published quotes $a_i := A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$
  \item For each $i$ with $F(i) < t$, the realized settlement of contract $i$: the threshold profile $\theta_{i,k}$ for $k \leq m_i^*$ and $\neg\theta_{i,k}$ for $k > m_i^*$
\end{enumerate}

As part of the simultaneous construction each $D_H^{+,t}$ is finite and computable, and is consistent: the settlement profiles of item 3 are initial segments respecting the monotonicity axioms, and the quote records of item 2 concern values disjoint from the threshold propositions.

Define $H^+$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.

Write $a_n := A_n(C_n)$ for $A$'s published quote, recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, and $Y_n := H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for $H^+$'s own future price that the quote is audited against. Since $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, both $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable by $H^+$ from time $n+1$ onward.

\begin{lemma}[Existence]
There exist sequences $A = (A_1, A_2, \ldots)$ and $H^+ = (H^+_1, H^+_2, \ldots)$, 
together with the deductive processes $D_A$ and $D_H^+$, such that: $D_A$ and 
$D_H^+$ are computable deductive processes; $A$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ 
satisfying the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$; and $H^+$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical 
induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The four sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, $(D_H^{+,t})$ are defined 
together by a single recursion on $t$. We use the construction of Garrabrant et 
al.\ \S5, which produces a logical inductor over a given computable deductive 
process incrementally: its time-$t$ pricing depends only on the deductive 
process up to time $t$ and on the construction's own stages before $t$. We run 
two such constructions, one per market, interleaved with the definitions of the 
deductive processes.

Suppose all four sequences have been defined at every stage $s < t$. We define 
the stage-$t$ objects as follows.

\emph{Deductive processes.} $D_A^t$ is given by its definition. Its only 
dependence on $H^+$ is through the settlement values $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for 
$n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$; since $\sigma(n) > F(n)$, each such $n$ has 
$F(n) < \sigma(n) \leq t$, so these are prices $H^+_{F(n)}$ at times 
$F(n) < t$, already defined. Likewise $D_H^{+,t}$ depends on $A$ only through the 
quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$, again already defined. Both stage-$t$ 
deductive sets are therefore computable from stage-$(<t)$ data, and are finite 
and consistent as shown in their definitions.

\emph{Markets.} With $D_A^{\leq t}$ now in hand, the \S5 construction yields its 
time-$t$ pricing $A_t$ from $D_A^{\leq t}$ and its own stages before $t$; 
similarly $H^+_t$ is produced from $D_H^{+,\leq t}$. Neither market-step 
references any stage-$t$ price of the other: $A_t$ uses only $D_A^{\leq t}$ 
(which depended on $H^+$ at times $< t$) and $(A_s)_{s<t}$, and symmetrically 
for $H^+_t$. This is where the incrementality of the \S5 construction is used: 
$A_t$ can be computed without the whole of $D_A$ in advance.

Every stage-$t$ object thus depends only on stage-$(<t)$ objects, so the 
recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, 
$(D_H^{+,t})$ are computable; in particular $D_A$ and $D_H^+$ are computable 
deductive processes. Finally, because each market is produced by the \S5 
construction over its own (computable, consistent) deductive process, $A$ 
satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$, and $H^+$ satisfies it against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$. We 
emphasize that this establishes existence and computability only; that $A$'s 
traders can compute the settlement values \emph{within $\mathcal{C}_A$} is the 
separate assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$ above, used in the Tracking Theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pinning]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a sequence of values $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$, computable
