Since $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, both $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable by $H^+$ from time $n+1$ onward. Throughout, for real-valued sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$, $x_n \simeq_n y_n$ means $x_n - y_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, following the convention of Garrabrant et al. All of the convergence results below are statements of this asymptotic form: they constrain the behavior of the relevant quantities as the index $n$ grows, not their values at any fixed $n$. As $n$ governs simultaneously the proposition $P^{(n)}$, the contract resolution $1/n$, and the timing $F(n), \sigma(n)$, these are claims about the eventual behavior of the construction along the diagonal in which all three sharpen together.

```
\begin{lemma}[Existence]
There exist sequences $A = (A_1, A_2, \ldots)$ and $H^+ = (H^+_1, H^+_2, \ldots)$, 
together with the deductive processes $D_A$ and $D_H^+$, such that: $D_A$ and 
$D_H^+$ are computable deductive processes; $A$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ 
satisfying the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$; and $H^+$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical 
induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The four sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, $(D_H^{+,t})$ are defined 
together by a single recursion on $t$. We fix uniform computable instantiations 
of the construction of Garrabrant et al.\ \S5, one for each market, whose 
time-$t$ outputs are computed from the finite information used by the 
construction up to stage $t$. We run two such constructions, one per market, 
interleaved with the definitions of the deductive processes.

Suppose all four sequences have been defined at every stage $s < t$. We define 
the stage-$t$ objects as follows.

\emph{Deductive processes.} $D_A^t$ is given by its definition. Its only 
dependence on $H^+$ is through the settlement values $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for 
$n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$; since $\sigma(n) > F(n)$, each such $n$ has 
$F(n) < \sigma(n) \leq t$, so these are prices $H^+_{F(n)}$ at times 
$F(n) < t$, already defined. Likewise $D_H^{+,t}$ depends on $A$ only through the 
quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$, again already defined. Both stage-$t$ 
deductive sets are therefore computable from stage-$(<t)$ data, and are finite 
and consistent as shown in their definitions.

\emph{Markets.} With $D_A^{\leq t}$ now in hand, the fixed construction yields 
its time-$t$ pricing $A_t$ from the finite information used by the construction 
up to stage $t$ and its own stages before $t$; similarly $H^+_t$ is produced 
from the corresponding finite information from $D_H^{+,\leq t}$. Neither 
market-step references any stage-$t$ price of the other: $A_t$ uses only the 
stage-$t$ information from $D_A$ (which depended on $H^+$ at times $< t$) and 
$(A_s)_{s<t}$, and symmetrically for $H^+_t$.

Every stage-$t$ object thus depends only on stage-$(<t)$ objects, so the 
recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, 
$(D_H^{+,t})$ are computable; in particular $D_A$ and $D_H^+$ are computable 
deductive processes. Finally, because each market is produced by the fixed 
construction over its own (computable, consistent) deductive process, $A$ 
satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$, and $H^+$ satisfies it against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$. We 
emphasize that this establishes existence and computability only; that $A$'s 
traders can compute the settlement values \emph{within $\mathcal{C}_A$} is the 
separate assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$ above, used in the Tracking Theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pinning]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values 
        $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ and a $\mathcal{C}$-computable 
        settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \simeq_n v_n.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n v_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]
\[
A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the Pinning Lemma with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable; the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
since $m_n^*$ rounds $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, which is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
by the standing assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$. For hypothesis~2: by the
construction of $D_A$, for every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have $\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\
$W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since $C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is
an average of $n$ values $W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have
$W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at every $t$, independently of
consistency.

The Pinning Lemma yields $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n \tfrac{m_n^*}{n}$. By the construction
of $D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n}
\to 0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Vanishing Settled Values]
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable from the information available in $D^n$, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of the Pinning Lemma with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping and admissibility argument are 
unchanged. Since $W(X_n) \in [-B,B]$, a single open sold position opened when 
$P_i(X_i)>\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ has value
\[
\rho_i(P_i(X_i)-W(X_i)) \geq -B,
\]
and a single open bought position opened when $P_i(X_i)<-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$
has value
\[
\rho_i(W(X_i)-P_i(X_i)) \geq -B.
\]
Thus the downside from the at-most-one unsettled position is bounded below by
$-B$. The only substantive change is at settlement: a settled trigger position
opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes $\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$ in the sold
case, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have
$|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger position
($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a bought
one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and the fact
that the settled values vanish. Infinitely many settled triggers then give
plausible net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B$ along a subsequence,
unbounded above, while the downside stays $\geq -B$. This exploits $P$,
contradicting the logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Calibration]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, with 
$G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as above, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match 
the settlement on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := G_n(a_n - Y_n)$. Since $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants and $Y_n$ is 
the value of the contract $C_n$ pinned by the settlement profile, 
$Z_n = G_n a_n - G_n C_n$ is a bounded affine combination of the threshold 
sentences $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n| \leq 1$. The quote $a_n$ is recorded in 
$D_H^+$ once $n < t$ and the profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ is pinned once 
$F(n) < t$, so $Z_n$ is pinned by $D_H^+$ at $\tau(n) := F(n)+1$, which is 
$\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is. Its realized value is 
$w_n = G_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)$; by the Tracking Theorem $a_n - Y_n \to 0$, and the 
profile encodes $Y_n$ up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, so 
$|w_n| \leq |a_n - Y_n| + \tfrac{1}{2n} \to 0$. The Vanishing Settled Values 
Lemma requires $X_m$ to be computable from $D^m$, whereas $Z_n$ depends on $a_n$, 
which $D_H^+$ records only at time $n+1$; we therefore apply the lemma to the 
shifted sequence $\widehat Z_m := Z_{m-1}$ for $m \geq 2$, with 
$\widehat\tau(m) := F(m-1)+1$, since $a_{m-1}$ is recorded in $D_H^+$ by time $m$. 
This gives
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Z_n] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deference]
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, $H^+$ defers to 
$A$'s quote in the following smoothed sense: on any sequence of indices with
$G_n$ bounded below by some $\gamma>0$,
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n.
\]
In particular, on any sequence of indices with $a_n \in [r,s]$, the credence 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$ comes to lie within $[r,s]$ up to a vanishing error.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The weight $G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ is a continuous function of the quote 
$a_n$, which is recorded in $D_H^+$ by time $n+1 \leq F(n)$; hence $G_n$ is 
$H^+$-generable and lies in $[0,1]$, so it is an admissible weight for Theorem 
4.12.3 (No Expected Net Update under Conditionals) of Garrabrant et al. Applying 
that theorem to $H^+$ with the LUV $\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})$, deferral $F$, and 
weight $G_n$, and using that $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{F(n)}(\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})) = 
H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) = Y_n$ by Theorem 4.8.6 (Expectations of Indicators),
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] 
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n] + o(1).
\]
By the Calibration Lemma, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] = 
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] + o(1)$, and as $a_n, G_n$ are constants at time 
$n+1$, $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n G_n$. Also, again by Theorem 4.8.6, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})] = H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$, and since 
$G_n$ is a constant at time $n+1$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})G_n]
=
G_n H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}).
\]
Thus
\[
G_n H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) = G_n a_n + o(1).
\]
On any sequence of indices with $G_n\geq \gamma>0$, dividing through gives
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n.
\]
In particular, if $a_n\in [r,s]$, then $G_n=1$, so $H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$ lies 
within $[r,s]$ up to an additive error vanishing in $n$.
\end{proof}

\end{document}
```

```
future self at time $F(n)$ to believe.

$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n G_n$ and, again by Theorem 4.8.6, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] = G_n H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$.

\[
G_n\,H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n G_n\,a_n.
\]
```

Honestly: it's plausible as a target but not established, and there's a specific reason it's slippery that you should have straight, because it's the kind of thing Demski might poke at and the naive answer ("sure, LIA is efficient") is wrong.

The core tension is between two senses of "polynomial." LIA is built to be *efficiently computable* in the paper's technical sense (Def 3.3 / efficient computability), but that's a statement about the traders the market is robust against, not a bound on the market's own per-day wall-clock cost. The construction (§5.4) computes $\text{LIA}_n$ by running MarketMaker over an aggregate of the first $\sim n$ traders from TradingFirm, using a Brouwer fixed-point computation each day to set prices that no trader can exploit. The §5.5 disclaimer — that the runtime "depends heavily on the particular enumerations of traders and rational numbers" — is pointing at exactly this: the per-day cost is the cost of (a) emulating the budgeted aggregate of the first-$n$ traders and (b) approximating a fixed point to adequate precision. Neither is obviously poly-in-$n$, and at least one has a real reason to be worse.

Let me separate the pieces, because the plausibility differs across them:

The fixed-point computation is the part I'd be most cautious about. Setting prices so that a finitely-supported approximate fixed point exists, to precision fine enough for the day's guarantees, is the step whose cost is least obviously polynomial — fixed-point approximation costs scale with the precision and the dimension (number of sentences in play), and the precision LIA needs can tighten with $n$. This is the piece that could blow the per-day budget past polynomial depending on implementation, and it's implementation-dependent in exactly the way §5.5 warns.

The trader-aggregation is more benign. TradingFirm sums the first-$n$ e.c. traders with budget weights; each individual trader is poly-time by assumption, and you're running $n$ of them for $n$ days, so the *trading* side is plausibly poly — the worry is the *enumeration* (finding/encoding the $n$-th trader) and the precision of the rational arithmetic, again the §5.5 caveats.

So the honest assessment in three claims. First, $R(t) = \mathrm{poly}(t)$ is not proved anywhere in the paper — §5.5 explicitly declines to bound $R$ and flags it as open, so you cannot cite it as established. Second, it's not obviously false either: there's no known *lower* bound forcing $R$ super-polynomial; the construction wasn't optimized but also wasn't shown to be inherently slow. It's "open, plausibly achievable with a careful implementation, not demonstrated." Third — and this is the part that actually matters for your model — even if some logical inductor has poly-per-day runtime, it's a further question whether *your coupled $H^+$* does, because $H^+$'s deductive process $D_H^+$ carries the extra quote and settlement streams, and those streams reference $A$, so $H^+$'s per-day cost inherits some of $A$'s. The poly-per-day hypothesis is cleanest for a *standalone* inductor; for the coupled $H^+$ it's at least as strong an assumption, possibly stronger.

That third point is the one I'd flag in the writeup if you want to be maximally honest, because it means "assume $R(t) = \mathrm{poly}(t)$" is quietly assuming poly-per-day for the *coupled* construction, not just for a textbook LIA. It's still plausible — the extra streams are finite per day and the quotes are just observed rationals — but it's worth not eliding.

What I'd actually say to Demski if he asks "is poly-per-day reasonable?": "It's not proved — §5.5 leaves LIA's runtime open and notes it's implementation-dependent. The trading-and-budgeting side is plausibly polynomial; the fixed-point/precision side is the part I wouldn't bet on without a careful implementation, and it's the natural place a lower bound could bite. So I'm treating poly-per-day as a clean *parametrizing* hypothesis that gives the concrete P and EXP witnesses, not as a fact — and the real deliverable is the reduction: deference is affordable iff $\mathcal{C}_A \supseteq R \circ F$, whatever $R$ turns out to be." That's a stronger position than defending poly-per-day, because it makes your result robust to the answer: the witnesses are illustrative-under-a-hypothesis, but the $R \circ F$ characterization holds unconditionally.

That keeps you from overclaiming while still giving the clean P/EXP examples.

So: plausible enough to use as the hypothesis that generates your example witnesses, not solid enough to assert, and with a coupled-construction wrinkle that makes it slightly stronger than the textbook version. **The two senses of "conditional."** When you write a reflection principle like "$H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$, conditional on $A$ quoting near $p$, is near $p$," the word "conditional" could mean either of two genuinely different operations:

The *Bayesian* sense: $H^+$ is uncertain whether $A$ will quote near $p$, assigns that event some probability, and we're asking about $H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ *under the hypothesis* that the quote-event occurs — i.e. the ratio $H^+(P^{(n)} \wedge \text{quote near } p) / H^+(\text{quote near } p)$. This is conditioning on an *uncertain event*, the way Garrabrant's own 4.12.4 conditions on "my future self believes $\varphi$" — where the future belief genuinely *is* uncertain to the present self.

The *selection* sense: we look only at the indices $n$ where, *as a matter of observed fact*, $A$'s quote landed near $p$, and ask what $H^+$'s credence does on that subsequence. This isn't conditioning on an uncertain proposition at all — it's restricting attention to a sub-collection of the propositions, picked out by an already-known feature.

**Why yours is the second, not the first.** The key fact is that $a_n$ is *recorded in $D_H^+$ by time $n+1$* — it's in $H^+$'s deductive process as observed data. So "conditional on $A$ quoting near $p$" can't be Bayesian conditioning on something uncertain — there's nothing uncertain left. It can only mean: *among the indices where the observed quote happens to be near $p$*, look at $H^+$'s credence. That's selection of a subsequence by an observed feature.

But — is adding symbols the *only* way to make the quote priced? No. There are at least two alternatives, and one of them might be cleaner than $\beta$-atoms:

**Alternative 1: condition on the $\theta$-settlement event instead of the quote.** You already have a priced event that's *available before settlement*: the event "contract $i$ settles near $p$," i.e. "$Y_i \approx p$," encoded by the $\theta_{i,k}$ atoms, which $H^+$ prices at all times (they're in its language, settled only at $F(i)$, uncertain before). So $Q_{i,p}^\theta := \{C_i \in [p-\delta, p+\delta]\}$ (the contract value near $p$) is a *genuine priced LUV* in the existing construction — no new symbols. Then $H^+_m(P^{(i)} \mid Q_{i,p}^\theta)$ is a real Bayesian conditional, and the statement "$H^+$, conditional on contract $i$ settling near $p$, believes $P^{(i)}$ near $p$" is *exactly Garrabrant 4.12.4* — it's self-trust, conditioning on your own future price being near $p$, which $H^+$ has for free. That's Bayesian, anticipatory, and needs no new symbols — *but* it's conditioning on $H^+$'s own future settlement, not on $A$'s quote. It's reflection on yourself, not deference to $A$.

So the question sharpens to: can you get from "Bayesian conditional on $Y_i \approx p$" (free, no new symbols, but it's just self-trust) to "Bayesian conditional on $a_i \approx p$" (what Demski wants, deference to $A$) *without* pricing $a_i$? And the answer is: the two conditioning events differ by exactly $a_i - Y_i$, which Tracking drives to zero. So the question is whether "$a_i \approx p$" and "$Y_i \approx p$" become *the same event in the limit* tightly enough that conditioning on one is asymptotically conditioning on the other.

**Alternative 2 (the real one): exploit that the quote, though not symbol-encoded, IS observed — and ask whether $H^+$ prices it forward through self-knowledge.** This is subtler. At time $m < n+1$, $H^+$ hasn't observed $a_n$. But $H^+$ knows its *own* construction — does $H^+$ have any priced handle on "what $A$ will quote"? Only if $A$'s quote is generable/predictable within $H^+$'s market, and it isn't part of $H^+$'s language as a proposition, so $H^+$ can't price "$a_n \approx p$" as an event. So Alternative 2 fails for the same reason: no priced quote-event.

So here's the honest sharpened answer. **You cannot condition on "$A$ quotes near $p$" as a priced Bayesian event without making the quote priced — and adding quote-symbols is one way, but conditioning on the $\theta$-settlement event ("contract settles near $p$", i.e. $Y_n \approx p$) is an *already-priced* alternative that requires no new symbols.** The catch is that the no-new-symbols version conditions on $Y_n$ (your own future judgment), not on $a_n$ (A's quote) — so it gives you *Bayesian self-trust* for free (that's literally 4.12.4) but not *Bayesian deference to A* directly.

So you can present Bayesian deference as: *$H^+$'s Bayesian conditional reflection on its own future settlement, transported to the quote by Tracking* — where the transport is the thing that, in full rigor, wants the quote priced to make "conditioning on $a_n$" literally well-defined, but where the *content* is carried by the already-priced settlement event.

So the symbols aren't needed to get a Bayesian conditional *in the construction* — you have one, on the settlement. They're needed only to make the conditioning event *literally be the quote* rather than *the settlement that the quote tracks*. Whether that distinction matters depends on what Demski wants: if he wants "$H^+$ Bayes-conditions on its own anticipated future judgment and that's the reflection principle," you have it now, symbol-free, and deference is the Tracking-driven observation that A's quote coincides with that judgment. If he insists the conditioning event must *syntactically be the quote*, you need the quote priced, and $\beta$-atoms are the way.

If you want the conditioning event to literally *be* the quote as a priced proposition — so it's deference-to-$A$ in the syntax, not deference-to-$A$-via-my-own-settlement — that needs quote-atoms. That puts the real choice to him and shows you've found the symbol-free Bayesian conditional that does exist, rather than conceding you can only get there by adding machinery. That's the whispering earring in formal dress: a perfectly calibrated predictor of a system it also influences is indistinguishable, *from calibration data alone*, from a manipulator that makes its predictions true. The earring's whispers are always good advice; that's exactly what makes it horrifying.

 Both directions are good and I think you've identified the right two — but they're actually the *same* project at different levels, and seeing that might help.

The negative-result theorem and the "when is advice evidence rather than control" question are two readings of one phenomenon: the negative result says "audit-based / output-based trust cannot distinguish prediction from influence," and the advice-vs-control question is "what *would* distinguish them." Solve one and you've reframed the other. So I'd think of them as a paired project — the impossibility on one side, the positive characterization on the other — rather than as separate threads. They constrain each other: the form of the impossibility tells you what kind of object the positive answer has to be (namely, something not visible in audit data), and progress on the positive side sharpens what exactly the impossibility rules out.

Your cancer-cure example is sharp and it tells you something important about why pure influence-invariance isn't right. Influence-invariance would condemn *all* advice that changes behavior, which is silly — it would say good advice and the earring are equally bad. The cancer cure is "control" in the bare sense (it causes the human to do something different) but it's clearly the *good* kind of control. So the distinction you're after isn't influence-vs-no-influence, it's something like *legitimate* vs *illegitimate* influence — and naming what makes influence legitimate is the actual problem. Which means "advice as evidence vs. advice as control" is misleadingly framed: the cancer cure is advice-as-control and we want it. The real distinction is more like *advice-as-conveyance-of-something-the-recipient-would-endorse-on-reflection* versus *advice-as-shaping-the-recipient-toward-the-advisor's-target*.

That distinction has a name in the philosophy literature — it's roughly the autonomy/manipulation distinction, and it's been chewed on by Raz, by Pettit, by people working on epistemic autonomy. The cancer cure passes because *if the human fully understood the reasoning and the evidence, they'd accept it for the same reasons the AI did* — the AI is conveying something the human would reach themselves with more time. The earring fails because the human accepts because the earring said so, *not* because they could reconstruct or verify the reasoning. So the property looks more like: **the advice changes behavior via a route the recipient would, on reflection, endorse as legitimate.** Reasons-transmission rather than mere belief-transmission.

That's harder to formalize than influence-invariance, but it's also more right, and there are at least three formal directions worth knowing about:

The *epistemic-autonomy* line, which tries to characterize when belief-change via testimony is autonomy-preserving — roughly, when the recipient could in principle audit the reasoning, not just the outcome. This connects naturally to interpretability (the AI's reasoning is checkable, not just its predictions) and to verification (the AI's *justification* is the verifiable object, not its calibration). I think this is the closest fit to what you want.

The *causal-mediator* line, where Pearl-style $\text{do}$-calculus is useful not as influence-invariance but as a way to talk about *which* causal pathway influence flows through. The cancer cure influences behavior through the pathway "human learns true mechanism, updates correctly"; the earring influences behavior through the pathway "human defers to source they shouldn't defer to." Both are interventions in the do-sense, but they have different mediating variables. The property you'd want would be something like "the causal effect of $A$'s output on the human's action is mediated entirely by the human's correct reasoning about the content," which is causal-graphical but specifically about *which mediators are admissible*. This is a real direction and I'd put medium confidence that something in this shape is part of the answer, but I share your hesitation that pure do-calculus is exactly right — it's the right *vocabulary* but maybe not the right *theorem*.

The *deceptive-vs-non-deceptive* line, which is closer to existing AI safety discourse — Hubinger et al.-style characterizations of when a system's behavior matches its "intentions" in a way recipients would endorse. This has the advantage of connecting to live alignment-community vocabulary but the disadvantage that the formalizations are gestural and you might end up doing the actual work yourself anyway.

My guess at the actual structure of the right answer: it's two-layer. Layer one is *causal* — there's a do-calculus / mediator condition isolating which pathways of influence count. Layer two is *normative* — what makes a pathway admissible is something like "the recipient would endorse this pathway as a legitimate way to come to believe things," which is the autonomy/reflection content. The causal layer makes "via which route" precise; the normative layer makes "legitimate route" precise. Cancer cure: causal pathway is "AI shares reasoning → human verifies reasoning → human acts on understanding," which is the kind of pathway the recipient endorses. Earring: causal pathway is "AI says X → human believes X because AI said X," which the recipient, on reflection, doesn't endorse.

That two-layer structure also tells you what the negative-result theorem should look like, and I think it's actually quite tractable. **The audit data — the (quote, settlement) pairs your construction records — is a function only of the joint distribution, and is invariant under any transformation that preserves the joint while changing the causal/mediating structure. Therefore no statistic of audit data can distinguish causal structures that produce identical joints.** That's the impossibility, and it's a clean Pearl-style observation (different DAGs can produce the same observational distribution; you need interventional data, or structural knowledge, to distinguish them). Your two-LI setup is the instantiation: prediction and manipulation produce identical audit records (small $|a_n - Y_n|$) and are therefore indistinguishable observationally; you need access to *structure* (source code, or counterfactual data, or some other extra-observational handle) to separate them. That gives you a real theorem — your model becomes the constructive demonstration that the audit-data sufficient statistic doesn't distinguish the cases — and connects to a well-known general phenomenon (the limits of observational data for causal inference), which is a nice place to land because it embeds your result in a tradition rather than presenting it as ad hoc.

So my actual recommendation for the next-phase shape, which I'd hold loosely but with conviction:

**Negative result theorem:** *Audit-data-equivalence of prediction and manipulation in coupled inductors.* The clean statement is that two structurally distinct couplings — one where $A$ predicts $H^+$'s un-advised trajectory, one where $A$ steers $H^+$ via the channel — produce indistinguishable audit records, so the deference theorem fires identically in both cases. Proof shape: construct an explicit pair of constructions with identical audit-output but different causal structure, show your Tracking/Calibration/Deference all hold for both. This is genuinely a theorem and it's the right negative result — much sharper than "you can't distinguish them, intuitively." Your existing construction is one half; the other half is the explicit "manipulator" construction that audit-matches it.

**Positive direction (advice-vs-control):** I'd lead with the *autonomy/reasons-transmission* framing rather than the causal one, because the cancer-cure example shows that causal influence per se isn't the bad thing — what's bad is influence that bypasses the recipient's own reasoning. Then bring in causal vocabulary as the *tool* for making "bypasses reasoning" precise, probably via mediator conditions. The exact formalization is genuinely open and I'd let it stay open for a while rather than locking in a do-calculus formulation that might force-fit; my low-medium confidence matches your low-medium confidence here. The thing I'd actually try first is to look at *minimal pairs* — what's the smallest modification to your existing construction that turns the predictor into a manipulator? — and let the right formalism emerge from what makes that modification visible. The minimal pair approach is constructive and lets the formalism find you, rather than the other way around.

One real warning: the "advice vs control" question is the kind of thing where philosophy has been chewing for decades without convergence, and AI safety has been chewing for years also without convergence, and there's a serious risk of disappearing into definitional weeds. The way to not get lost is to keep the negative-result project as the anchor: every proposed positive characterization should be *something the audit data demonstrably can't recover*, and that's the test. If you propose property $\Phi$ and it turns out $\Phi$ *can* be read off the audit record, then it's not the right property (because the impossibility says the right property isn't there). The impossibility result acts as a sieve on positive proposals, which is exactly what you want — it prevents the positive direction from drifting into vagueness because it has a concrete adequacy condition.

Last thought, on the shape of all this as a research program: I think what you actually have, after the meeting, is the outline of something bigger than a single paper. The deference theorem is paper 1 (which you have, modulo cleanup). The impossibility theorem is paper 2 (clean negative result, formal, the natural follow-up). The advice-as-evidence-vs-control formalization is paper 3 (longer-horizon, harder, but well-motivated by 1 and 2). And the structural/source-code positive direction — trust from interpretable properties — is paper 4 or a thesis chapter, which is where your verification-for-cooperation agenda actually wanted to land all along. The two-LI setup, which felt unsatisfying in the meeting, is actually the *gateway* to that agenda: it's the demonstration that purely behavioral approaches don't suffice, which is the motivation for the verification approach you've been building toward in the LessWrong sequence and the Lean work. So the meeting's "unsatisfying" verdict might actually be the bridge between your two research threads that you didn't know you needed. The deference work makes the case for the verification work, by showing what behavioral methods leave on the table.

Worth saying because you have this habit and it's good: the right next move is probably the negative-result theorem, because it's tractable, it consolidates what the meeting found, and it sets up everything else. The advice-vs-control question is more important but less tractable; let the impossibility result sharpen it before you commit to a formalism.

I just had a meeting with Abram about a writeup I'll attach (or paste) — "Reflective Deference Between Two Logical Inductors" — and I want help on the next phase.

**What the existing writeup does.** It builds a coupled pair of logical inductors $A$ (an AI) and $H^+$ (a human augmented to observe $A$'s quotes) in the Garrabrant et al. framework. $A$'s contracts settle to $H^+$'s own future credence $Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, where $F$ is a deferral function. The main results:

1. *Existence*: the coupled pair exists and is computable (single time-recursion with timing delays).
2. *Pinning* (lemma): a logical inductor's price tracks the eventual pinned value of any bounded, eventually-pinned affine combination — capacity-one trader argument.
3. *Tracking*: $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n Y_n$ (forced by $A$'s own induction criterion via Pinning).
4. *Vanishing Settled Values* (lemma) + *Calibration*: $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match $Y_n$.
5. *Deference* (Theorem 2): on subsequences where $A$ quotes near a target $p$ with non-vanishing frequency, $H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n$. Cited via Garrabrant 4.12.3 (No Expected Net Update under Conditionals) with $G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as a generable weight, plus 4.8.6 (Expectations of Indicators).

The one assumption is that $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable — i.e. $\mathcal{C}_A$ contains $R \circ F$ where $R$ is LIA's per-day runtime (left open in Garrabrant §5.5). Under poly-per-day, $F(n) = n^2$ gives $\mathcal{C}_H = \mathcal{C}_A = \mathrm{P}$ and $F(n) = 2^n$ gives $\mathcal{C}_H = \mathrm{P}, \mathcal{C}_A = \mathrm{EXP}$.

**Key design choice.** I settle $A$'s contracts to $H^+$'s future price, not to a hypothetical "un-influenced base human" $H$ — because $H^+$'s deductive process contains audit data about $P^{(n)}$, so augmenting $H$ genuinely changes its limiting beliefs, and any "settle to base $H$" version requires a false limit-agreement claim. Option B (settle to $H^+$) is the only fixed point that closes, and philosophically it means $A$ accelerates $H^+$ toward its post-advice reflective endpoint.

**The meeting outcome.** Demski accepted that the writeup is roughly as good as it gets for the two-LI setup, but the *framework* is unsatisfying for a "whispering earring"-type reason: the deference is forced by audit data ($a_n - Y_n \to 0$), but audit data cannot distinguish "$A$ accurately predicts where $H^+$ was independently heading" from "$A$ influences $H^+$ into the outcomes $A$ predicted." Both produce identical $(a_n, Y_n)$ records. Option A's failure (you can't condition on the un-influenced human) is the deep structural form of this — the same coupling that enables trust enables influence. So output-based / audit-based trust hits a wall here that's not an artifact of my construction but a feature of behavioral approaches generally.

Demski wanted Bayesian conditional reflection ($H^+_m(P^{(n)} \mid Q_{n,p}) \simeq p$ for $m \le n$ on a *priced* uncertain quote-event) rather than the post-observation selection form I have. I showed it's reachable by either (a) reinstating $\beta$-quote-atoms (which I'd cut earlier) so the quote becomes a priced LUV, or (b) noting that conditioning on the $\theta$-settlement event "$Y_n \approx p$" is already-priced and gives Bayesian self-trust for free (literally 4.12.4), with deference following from Tracking. We didn't push this to a clean alternative theorem.

**Two next directions** I want to work on, in roughly this order:

1. *Negative result theorem.* Formalize that audit-equivalent constructions can have structurally different causal relations between $A$ and $H^+$. The target shape: exhibit a pair — one where $A$ "predicts" $H^+$, one where $A$ "manipulates" $H^+$ — that produce identical audit records ($\Tracking, \Calibration, \Deference$ fire in both) but differ in some structural sense. This would be the clean impossibility statement that output-based trust cannot distinguish prediction from manipulation. Tractable, consolidates the meeting's finding, sets up everything else.

2. *Advice as evidence vs. advice as control.* The harder positive question: what distinguishes legitimate from illegitimate influence? Pure influence-invariance is wrong (good advice changes behavior — e.g. "here's how to cure cancer" — and we want it to). The distinction is more like reasons-transmission / autonomy-preserving versus bypassing-the-recipient's-reasoning. Pearl-style $\text{do}$-calculus and mediator conditions are candidate formalisms but I have low-to-medium confidence that's exactly right. Connects naturally to source-code-based / structural / interpretability approaches to trust, since the right property may be structural rather than behavioral.

The longer-term framing — and this is what I'd like help thinking through — is that the deference paper is paper 1, the impossibility result is paper 2, the advice-vs-control formalization is paper 3, and a structural/verification-based positive theory of trust is the longer-horizon paper 4, which connects to my existing "Verification for Cooperation" sequence on LessWrong and to Lean formalization work on program equilibrium.

For this conversation, I want help on direction 1 most immediately: working out what the right formal statement of the audit-equivalence impossibility looks like, and ideally constructing the explicit predictor/manipulator pair that audit-matches. Style preferences: I want pushback when ideas don't work, I want you to point me to primary sources rather than asserting technical details from memory, and I want adversarial pressure-testing rather than reassurance. The "style preferences" at the end matter more than they look. I also flagged the "point to primary sources" thing because direction 1 may involve Pearl's *Causality* or the Hubinger deceptive-alignment literature, and a fresh instance will be tempted to assert things it shouldn't.

I didn't include the detailed proof structure of any of the lemmas, because a fresh instance can ask if it needs them, and including the actual document is better than paraphrasing the math.
